speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to pay tribute to the Union des producteurs agricoles on the 60th anniversary of its founding. For many years, the UPA has defended the interests of farmers in the region of Nicolet-Drummond- Bois Francs, and it has a great deal to be proud of.
With 225 officers working in 14 sectorial unions and 14 unions specialized in areas such as milk, beef cattle, eggs and so forth, the UPA's real challenge is defending the socio-economic interests of its 5,000 strong constituency. The Federation de l'UPA de Nicolet is synonymous with the many services that have become available to producers over the years.
Mr. Speaker, this is thanks to the perseverance and energy of farm producers who take part of their precious time to defend the interests of other farmers, and I want to congratulate them for their dedication and the tremendous job they have done.

Mr. Speaker, this week the commission responsible for examining the consequences of expanding the Tracadie military camp received the report on the environmental impact study prepared by National Defence.
After waiting for five years, residents of the region of Tracadie and Allardville-Saint-Sauveur are very worried, considering the many questions that have some unanswered.
We are all aware of the drawbacks of being near a firing range that would allow National Defence aircraft to train in low-level flying near inhabited areas.
The federal government should immediately identify, clearly and precisely, all the components for an economic development program for the region directly affected by this project.
I am willing to listen to all parties, but I repeat my commitment to the people of my riding: I will be the most difficult person to convince that expanding the Tracadie military camp is a good thing.

Mr. Speaker, today I rise to draw your attention to an article which appeared in The Financial Post on June 14, regarding Canada's jobless. It stated the statistics of Canada's contribution toward job training in relation to other industrialized countries.
Canada falls behind Germany, Japan, Britain and Italy, to name a few. I believe if the Senate was acting for the good of Canada, like it says it is, then it would pass Bill C-21 so that the government can begin to address the need to do more in the area of job training. Of course, this is only one area of concern that is being held up in the Senate.
I continue to hear from many expectant mothers who had planned to take advantage of the extended maternity leave benefits offered in Bill C-21. They are most upset that the stalling of the Senate is playing havoc with then-lives and those of their unborn children.
The Senate's partisan gamesmanship is certainly not in the best interests of these mothers-to-be.

Mr. Speaker, many members of Parliament have received letters and

June 20, 1990
petitions from Canadians who are concerned about the funding cuts to heritage language classes.
I have here hundreds of letters from constituents which state that the total Secretary of State budget has been cut by only 5 per cent, but heritage schools have been cut by 100 per cent for a total of $4.1 million. There are 129,000 students across the country enrolled in heritage schools receiving instruction in 60 languages.
By cutting heritage language schools the government is destroying the most cost-effective program ever offered for the delivery of an effective language training program.
In Vancouver East over $138,000 has been cut from 30 heritage classes, many of which will have to close or charge a higher tuition fee making them inaccessible to children from low income families.
I call on the government to reinstate full funding for heritage language classes today.

Mr. Speaker, from June 23 to July 1, the city of Beauport will host the 4th World Children's Folk Festival, a major event of the summer in the Quebec City area.
Nearly 100,000 spectators are expected to attend this great popular festival featuring ten young folk troupes from eight countries, including France, Mexico, Hungary, Colombia and the Soviet Union.
Today I would like to pay tribute to the organizers of this festival, especially to the president, Marc-Andre Touzin, and the hundreds of volunteers throughout the riding of Montmorency-Orleans who will house the 400 young dancers and singers who are to perform in a dazzling display of rhythm and colour until July 1.
Mr. Speaker, I invite the people of Montmorency- Orleans and all the Quebec City region to join in this great festival of children of the world.

Mr. Speaker, we witnessed the Prime Minister put on a pathetic performance in the House yesterday.
He tried to blame everyone in the country except himself for the Meech Lake mess. Well, he won't get away with it, Canadians will make sure of that.
Who decided to leave the First Ministers' Conference until it was too late? Was it the premier of Manitoba? No. Was it Sharon Carstairs? No. Was it the NDP leader in Manitoba? No. Was it Brian Mulroney? You betcha.
In fact, he admits the timing was all very deliberate. He said he rolled the dice. He bragged about it. He even gloated over it. Now we know the result. The Prime Minister blew it. He has made a complete and utter mess of Meech Lake.
It is time the Prime Minister stopped looking for scapegoats. It is time he accepted responsibility for his own actions. Canadians do not deserve such a poor performance from the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, the first nominee for the corporate welfare bum of the week is Consolidated HCI Holdings Corporation. It had profits of $20 million in 1988 without paying a penny of tax.
The second nominee is Cairn Capital Inc. which had profits of $17 million in 1988. For producing these profits, it received a tax credit of $243,000.
The third nominee is BMO NT Financial Corporation. It did not pay any tax on profits of $8 million in 1988.
The envelope, please.
And the winner is: From these financial corporations that play shell games, the winner is BMO NT Financial, because the "NT" stands for "no tax". BMO NT Financial is the corporate welfare bum of the week.
June 20, 1990

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Veterans Affairs announced that maximum rates payable for funeral expense assistance for eligible veterans has been increased from $2,000 to $2,940, a 50 per cent increase.
This announcement is yet more positive news. Hon. members will recall that last week the Department of Veterans Affairs signed an agreement with British Columbia for 200 long-term beds for veterans worth up to $35 million.
In addition to this, there will be increased income protection for spouses of veterans who are in long-term care centres, a special trust fund for the benefit of needy veterans, using moneys left unclaimed on the death of a veteran, payment of attendance allowance to widows for one year after the death of a veteran, and interest on moneys administered by the Department of Veterans Affairs on behalf of veterans.
These continuing improvements are evidence of this government's high regard for veterans and their families.

Mr. Speaker, this month and the following summer months in Prince Edward Island will be exciting times for Islanders.
Numerous festivals and events across the province will take place to celebrate the heritage and tradition of the Island.
From Anne of Green Gables to our Malpeque oysters to fresh lobsters and potatoes, the Island has so much to offer.
Visitors keep coming back because the quality and richness of Island life is hard to match.
Islanders make visitors feel at home. Our glorious beaches and beautiful landscape make it even harder to leave.
1990-91 is special in the tourism industry as we remember our rich Celtic heritage and celebrate a special Irish homecoming. The theme for this celebration is We're Akin to Ireland.
I would like to take this opportunity to invite my fellow colleagues on all sides of the House to come to Prince Edward Island and enjoy one of the world's greatest Islands.

Mr. Speaker, for several months, the Mayor of Amos, Jean-Paul Veilleux, council members and the general manager, Real Borde-leau, have been trying to obtain justice from CN with respect to renewal of the lease for a community parking lot.
The City of Amos does not agree with the rent increases proposed by CN management; it considers them to be excessive and unfair. The City of Amos is prepared to accept a normal rent increase based on the cost of living, especially since the city receives no revenue from this community parking lot.
Once again, CN property management in Montreal show that they could not care less about the people of Amos by charging an exorbitant price for this community parking lot.
Mr. Speaker, I ask CN property management to consider the request of the City of Amos for the welfare of the people of Amos and surrounding areas.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay tribute to Dr. Helen Graves, organizer of the 1990 Comparative Political Internship Program and the 26 university students from Michigan who have worked with us in Parliament as our interns since May 9.
For the record, these interns are: Nawal Amori, Jennifer Bednar, Paul Berg, Kristen Brown, Lee Colum-bino, Renu Daga, Darrell Donakowski, Jeremy Efroym-son, Elizabeth Gnegy, Jodi Goldman, James Green,

June 20, 1990
Oral Questions
Donald Kennedy, Denise Legault, Kimberlyn McNally, Michael Morris, Anthony Nitsos, Gerrald Ottenbreit, Brian Parillo, Jennifer Perlove, Kenneth Ross, Judy Samp, Dennis Santillan, Ona Sostakas, Laura Van Hav-ermaat, Julie Zazula, and Stephen Pancratz, my excellent intern.
Dr. Graves and interns, we wish you much success in your future and we thank you for your contribution to us.

Mr. Speaker, as our constitutional problems unfold, Canadians are rightly asking how we got into this mess. The people in my riding, like the rest of Canadians, do not understand all that is happening. I do not understand it either. It leaves me frustrated and angry. I want my country back; I want my country back from the extremists; I want it back from the regionalists; I want it back from the special interest groups; I think all Canadians want their country back right now.
Premier Peterson said in Newfoundland this morning that what unites us is our ability to solve problems, not to create them.

Mr. Speaker, it is obvious, it is common sense, it is now time for all Canadians to say: Long live Quebec! Long live Canada! Our country first and foremost!
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, as the critical path which the Prime Minister established for resolving the constitutional impasse continues to unfold, I would like to ask him for an update on developments in Newfoundland and Manitoba.

Mr. Speaker, the latest developments of which I am aware are that Premier Peterson accepted the invitation of the
premier of Newfoundland and Labrador to visit the Newfoundland and Labrador House of Assembly this morning.
I believe I can fairly say that he made one of the most impressive speeches that has been my pleasure to listen to on behalf of the unity of Canada and the desirability of passing Meech Lake.
Hear, hear!

It was clearly an accurate statement because the member for Willowdale is in agreement.
It was a most impressive statement in which Premier Peterson, who had participated at the 1987 Meech Lake Agreement, and then the 1990 agreement, brought forward arguments on behalf of the unity of Canada and the compelling and urgent nature of concluding Meech Lake so that the country could move on to other important matters such as aboriginal concerns that we wish to deal with on an urgent and comprehensive basis. I understand that Premier McKenna is before the legislature in Newfoundland and Labrador as we speak.
My hon. friend will remember that Premier McKenna was the first to have some reservations about Meech Lake, but those were fully satisfied in the meetings in Ottawa 10 days ago. He went back, and the legislature of New Brunswick passed the Meech Lake Accord, bringing the number to eight legislatures representing 94 per cent of the population of Canada that, as of this moment, have already passed the Meech Lake Accord. I think that is very good and encouraging news.
With regard to Manitoba, I understand that the House is meeting, or will be meeting very shortly. I know that there is a unique situation in Manitoba because of the difficulties inherent in a minority situation. It has the only one that exists in a legislature in Canada. So there have been special problems for Premier Filmon and for Mrs. Carstairs and Mr. Doer that we recognize and seek to accommodate. I think on behalf of all Canadians, and in the same spirit of generosity that Premier Peterson put forward this morning in Newfoundland and Labrador, we simply ask the leaders of the three parties in Manitoba to please, on behalf of Canada, make an extra effort to make sure that the Meech Lake Accord is ratified.

Hear, hear!
June 20, 1990

Mr. Speaker, considering the very real problems with the time frame in Manitoba, I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether he has considered the various suggestions that have been made for extending the deadline for ratifying the accord, and whether he sees any possible solutions?

Mr. Speaker, if I can say in a non-critical way without any recrimination, I think it is probably fair to say, at least the reports were, that the problem 11 days ago originated from a procedural fault in the introduction of the original motion. That was used to delay by some 10 or 11 days consideration of this important matter by the legislature of Manitoba.
Human mistakes do occur everywhere. They occur in this Parliament, they occur in all freely elected Parliaments. But, it is our belief that this flaw of procedure can be corrected. I believe the premier and the two other leaders wish to have it corrected and that there is time under the rules of the Manitoba legislature to correct this situation and to move on and to cause that legislature to do within the timeframe, namely, before the twenty-third, what legislatures are elected to do, to be seized of a problem and to vote it either up or vote it down.
I believe that if it comes to the Manitoba legislature for a vote, pursuant to the undertakings given by the three leaders that the Manitoba legislature will substantially support the Meech Lake Accord with the companion resolution because of what it does for Canadian unity and what it does for aboriginal justice in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, certainly no one in this House denies the importance of solving the problem. Can we take it from the answer the Prime Minister has given that the government, having examined all of the various proposals made for ways of extending the deadline, is not able to propose any way which would be effective for doing that?
I want to ask the Prime Minister further whether he is prepared to meet with aboriginal leaders to see if he can earn their co-operation in seeing the constitutional impasse resolved?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend asks about extending the deadline. I have just tried to indicate to him that the present deadline suffices. Irrespective of the fact that the Manitoba legislature has already lost 11 days from what appears to have been a defect in the procedure in the bringing in of the resolution on June 11 after the signing ceremony, it is our advice that under the rules of the Manitoba legislature, if the three party leaders and the three parties are in agreement, while time is short, it can be done. It should not be forgotten that the Manitoba legislature and the people of Manitoba have had and have taken a great deal of time by committee to consider the implications of Meech Lake over many months prior to June of this year. There have been very extensive public hearings held on Meech Lake already. Under the rules of the Manitoba legislature, we are informed that the Meech Lake Accord could indeed be passed by the twenty-third with ample time left for public hearings in respect of the companion resolution which would ensure that all Manitobans are heard again, if need be, on the implications of the companion resolution.
It should never be forgotten that full and complete hearings have already been held on the Meech Lake Accord. Meech Lake, we are told, could be passed within the present time frames. There would be ample opportunity for public participation in respect of the companion resolution and so Canada would conserve and strengthen its unity and Manitoba would have done its duty toward the people of Manitoba by ensuring that they are heard again in respect of all the considerations in the companion resolution.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State. I want to ask if it is now a condition for getting a grant for Canada Day celebrations that a mayor or other official must have their picture taken with the local Tory MR In this respect, has the minister received a complaint from Mayor Steve Olynik of Greenfield Park in Quebec that the member of Parliament for Saint-Hubert made such a request, made such a condition for delivering the Canada Day cheque? Does the minister think that this sort of behaviour is consistent with the spirit of Canada Day?

June 20, 1990
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there were some 270 projects approved by a remarkable Canada Day committee under the chair of Mrs. Geraldine Doucet.
The committee worked very hard and I think brought forward some very excellent proposals which were all, of course, approved and will bring great credit to our ability to celebrate together a very important Canada Day.
From what I understand, there were on some rare instances, opportunities for an MP to deliver some of the larger cheques. I am not fully conversant with how all of this takes place, nor am I really conversant with what took place between the mayor and the MP. I personally have not spoken to the mayor. He has not called me on the subject.
I will certainly look into the matter and get back to the member at my earliest convenience.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the minister when he or his department decided to have these cheques delivered by local Conservative MPs instead of having them mailed, and why is he making assistance for Canada's national day into a partisan act? What is the rationale for this abhorrent policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the committee operated in a very honourable fashion and examined all of the projects that were brought forward. Those projects were all approved by this independent, impartial committee and it is my understanding that all of the projects that will go forward will be carried out with a great deal of enthusiasm and will be very helpful in celebrating Canada Day this year in the country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Last week, the Prime Minister admitted he had planned the countdown, rolled the dice and then convinced first New Brunswick, then Manitoba, and finally Newfoundland.
Clearly, his plan has fizzled. I therefore want to ask the Prime Minister when he will show some leadership. What is he going to do next? What are his plans today? Canada deserves a definite reply today!

Mr. Speaker, inadvertently, the hon. member misrepresented what I said because she refused to go on and quote the rest, when I said we had no intention of isolating anyone, and that we proceeded this way because it seemed reasonable to do so, and because by doing so, we were pursuing the fundamental goal of Canada's unity. In any case, you have to have some idea where you are going when you get involved in complex negotiations, and we abided by some very important principles which were hailed as such, not only by the hon. member but also by other members of her political party, following the successful outcome on June 9.
Today, the hon. member is asking me about our plans for the future. I can inform the Leader of the New Democratic Party that we remain confident that MPPs in Newfoundland and Manitoba, who still have enough time, will agree to vote for the Meech Lake Accord. There will be a vote Thursday evening or Friday morning in Newfoundland. According to the Standing Orders of the Manitoba legislature, they still have enough time to proceed with the required vote. I am therefore confident that the leaders of the three political parties in Manitoba and the premier and the Leader of the Opposition in Newfoundland and Labrador will ensure that these votes take place, so that Canada will be able to preserve and reinforce its unity by the evening of the 23rd.

My supplementary question is for the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister talks about the confidence he has in other legislatures to take the action to further the constitutional process. I would then have to question the Prime Minister as to why his government wants to bring forward a resolution today that talks about exerting influence on those legislatures, if he has such confidence.
The Prime Minister talks about what Manitoba can do, and I want to remind the Prime Minister that the agreement that was signed on June 9 by the premier of Manitoba, clearly states underneath the premier of Manitoba's signature: "subject to the public hearing
June 20, 1990

process". I will further draw to the Prime Minister's attention the Standing Orders of Manitoba which state:
(2) Prior to the sixth day of debate on such a motion, that motion shall be referred to a Standing or Special Committee of the House ordered to receive submissions from the general public and to report back to the House.
Clearly Manitoba has Standing Orders, and I guess the Prime Minister is asking Manitoba to break this agreement.
Is the Prime Minister saying, by his comments today and by the resolution he wants to bring forward, that Manitoba should break its own rules and the rules that the premier signed with the agreement of June 9, 1990?

Mr. Speaker, I do not want Manitoba or anyone to break any rules. I indicated to the member from Toronto in an earlier exchange that it was the view of the Government of Canada that, notwithstanding the fact that 11 days have already been lost because of a procedural defect in the introduction of the original motion, there still remains under the rules of the Manitoba legislature time to pass the Meech Lake Accord by June 23.
That is not just the view of the government. I would point out to my hon. friend that on June 11 in the Winnipeg Free Press the NDP House leader stated:
The rules for dealing with constitutional amendments are quite clear, (NDP House leader Steve) Ashton said, adding none of the votes in the process require unanimous consent-
A simple majority vote is required to move the legislature into committee, he said.
Since that time there has been paralysis in the Manitoba legislature, not because of anything that has been done by my hon. friend or a member of this House. But I ask her to reread the statements made by the House leader of the NDP who said on the 11th that a majority was all that was required, the implication being that one person could not and should not be allowed to hold up such an important, vital, national matter.
My hon. friend asks a question about the matter coming for consideration before the House this afternoon. On October 6, 1983 the then Prime Minister of the day introduced a resolution in this House which con-
Oral Questions
eluded with the House inviting the government and Legislative Assembly of Manitoba to take action as expeditiously as possible in order to fulfil their constitutional obligations and protect effectively the rights of the French speaking minority of the province.
On February 24, 1984 the same government introduced another resolution which concluded with the House urging the Government of Manitoba to persist in its efforts to fulfil the constitutional obligations of the province and protect effectively the rights of its French speaking minority, and so on.
This is not an intrusion into the rights of a legislature of another jurisdiction. This is simply, with ample precedent to guide us, the Parliament of Canada saying to the nation and saying respectfully to the legislators in Manitoba that "there is a most serious constitutional matter before the nation. You have it within your power to resolve this matter within the time frames of the 23rd, and please, in the interests of Canadian unity, use your best efforts to make sure that it is done".

Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister would like to quote from 1983, I too would like to quote from 1983 from a book entitled Where I Stand by the Prime Minister, in which he said that he was concerned about the constitutional process and he felt that the debate should be open to the public at all times. He stated:
There would be no sessions behind closed doors.
At that time the Prime Minister also stated:
The test of great leadership is to harmonize divergent views into
an eloquent and thoughtful declaration of national purpose.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I can understand the government wanting to applaud because I think any of us could applaud that fine statement. But I want to ask the Prime Minister: in order to live up to those fine words, what is rthe Prime Minister's plan now? We are now just a couple of days away from the deadline. Canadians have a right to know what is the plan of the leader of the country for the constitution of the country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
You have answered that.

June 20, 1990
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my friend, the member from Vanier, says that I answered that and he is quite right, but I will be happy to try again.
I should tell my hon. friend that I thank her for that quote. It was one of the finer ones.
I want to tell my hon. friend that the resolutions from Mr. Trudeau and his colleagues, supported by the member for Winnipeg South Centre, then Winnipeg-Fort Garry, led the debate on both of these important resolutions.
I supported both of these resolutions because I thought it was important that the Parliament of Canada send a signal, however respectful, to the legislature of Manitoba or to any other legislature that in the national interest the time had come to act to protect minority rights, and in this case, to help bring about a more united Canada.
I think it is entirely appropriate that this be done by the Parliament of Canada. That is what we are here for, to speak for Canada, and now is the time for all Canadians to speak for Canada.
I tell my hon. friend that one of the things she might do, and I say this respectfully, is to call the member of the Manitoba legislature of her own political persuasion, Mr. Doer, who is doing a tremendous job, and call the others who may have doubts and ask them in the national interest to support Meech Lake so that we can move to questions of aboriginal justice.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Prime Minister and it concerns the administration of the Montreal Port Authority.
The Prime Minister will know of reports whereby the insurance firm of Charbonneau Dulude acting as consultants for the port authority recommended the awarding of a contract to Pratte-Morrissette, a company having as chairman one of the partners of the consulting firm recommending the award of the contract to start with.
Has the Prime Minister verified these allegations? Is he satisfied that the Parliament of Canada Act and the spirit of the conflict of interest rules have been strictly adhered to?

Mr. Speaker, I read the same article in The Globe and Mail today, and quite frankly, I saw nothing in it that would cause me to believe that there had been any conflict of interest or that the insurance contracts in question went to anybody other than the lowest bidder back in 1984 when, as my hon. friend knows, there was a Liberal administration in the land up until September 4, 1984. My hon. friend knows those contracts were let before September 4, 1984. I see no reason to go back into my hon. friend's administration to investigate.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister of Transport or the Deputy Prime Minister the following supplementary question in the same regard.

This is the third time in less than a week that the Port of Montreal Corporation has been the subject of controversy for the way it awards contracts, for its purchasing policy and, earlier last week, for wasting public funds.
I would like to ask the government opposite if they are prepared to ask the Auditor General of Canada to investigate the contracting and administration policy of the Port of Montreal Corporation.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
In its report tabled Monday the Tory dominated House of Commons Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations denounced the Government Information Bureau on the GST as having an impossible, time consuming and costly task.
Will the minister show respect toward the consumers of Canada and simply call off this ridiculous and excessively expensive PR job that members of his own party disagree with and that now clearly lacks credibility?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)

Mr. Speaker, I am a little surprised by the hon. member's comment. I have here the report that was tabled by the standing committee and I would just like to quote the summary, Mr. Speaker, where it says that the committee believes that competition and consumer information are the best assurances of protection from business people who might abuse the GST. That is exactly what the government has done.
A little further, it says: "The government should subsidize an independent body with full power to educate consumers on the effects of the GST on prices with the elimination of existing federal sales taxes. This body would be composed of representatives from business and consumer groups; of limited size, it would be active for a short period and should be profitable."
Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what we have done.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
By accepting his position, Mr. Nickolas Murray clearly put himself in conflict of interest. Given his lack of judgment-

-and therefore lack of credibility, should the government not at least now withdraw his appointment as chairman of the government's GST information office?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the hon. Prime Minister. His government's February budget launched another in a series of vicious, ideological attacks on aboriginal peoples and brutally slashed the government's program for native peoples in this country.
How can the Prime Minister now blame aboriginal leaders for delaying approval of the Constitutional Accord? Does he not see that their position is a direct consequence of his actions in the February budget?

June 20, 1990
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I think my hon. friend would want to correct a serious misstatement. I never once blamed the aboriginal peoples for anything. I have believed from the very beginning that, if anything, the aboriginal peoples were, are and continue to be victims of historic injustice which this nation must seek to correct.
As a result of which, my hon. friend will recognize that this year the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development will have a budget of in excess of $3.5 billion, up nearly $200 million from last year, and total funding for aboriginal peoples from all departments will be over $4 billion, which is the largest amount ever expended in history by the Government of Canada, and we plan to do more each year on behalf of the aboriginal peoples.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister says that the native people in this country have been victimized for years and years. How does he expect cutting their media budget this year will reverse that victimization? How does he expect cutting programs for their language retention and for their cultural organizations will reverse that victimization? How does he expect that cutting the funds for their representative organizations, which also assist natives in making representations to constitutional debates, is going to reverse that victimization?
He did blame Phil Fontaine of the Manitoba Chiefs yesterday.
When the roll of the dice was taking place, did the Prime Minister expect that the native people of this countiy would be paying the price?

Mr. Speaker, on the contrary. My hon. friend continues to do a disservice to the facts by suggesting that I blamed Chief Phil Fontaine. I did no such thing and the record will sustain what I have just said. I also said that the Manitoba Metis Federation, representing approximately 80,000 native Manitobans, on June 18 actively supported and called on the Manitoba Legislature to stop the procedural blockage of the resolution. I quote Mr. Dumas who stated: "We have considered the latest undertaking by the Prime Minister and believe it is now
in our interests more than at any time in the past, that we take advantage of the provisions now before us which are possible following the approval of the accord".
The Manitoba Metis Federation is calling on the Manitoba legislature to pass it now because there are untold benefits to come from the proposals.
What about aboriginal organizations in this country? What about the cuts?
What about the SFIN? Check the SFIN.

Mr. Speaker, I have already indicated to my hon. friend that the Government of Canada now expends in excess of $4 billion a year, up $200 million from last year.
My friend talks about communications programs. Let me talk to him about the negotiations which led to the final agreements with the Dene-Metis on their comprehensive land claim, and others in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. The Government of Canada has concluded all of these agreements-
What about money for representative organizations?

I ask my hon. friend to listen to this. The Arctic claims will put 575,000 square kilometres of land firmly and irrevocably under Indian and Inuit ownership and transfer $1.3 billion to the native peoples of Canada, making the natives the largest single land holders on the North American territory. That is what they wanted. That was refused for decades.
As Le Devoir states this morning, and my hon. friend should listen to this-

"By saying no to Brian Mulroney, the Manitoba chiefs have turned down the only hand that was seriously extended to them in six years. The Conservatives have an undeserved reputation as shallow, unscrupulous business people, but it was under their administration that the historic wrongs done to native people began to be righted. It is Brian Mulroney, 'the company lawyer' who gave back to northerners the land that Mr. Trudeau, 'the father of the Charter', reserved for the oil companies."

Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel knows perfectly well, about a year or a year and a half ago, the Canadian government, through the Secretary of State for External Affairs, was one of the most vigourous critics of the former administration in Romania. Industry was particularly insistent on this point. Chemicals Abstracts Services is not tasked with the provision of any information relative to the import, manufacture, use, distribution or availability of substances with Canada.
Background Information
Environment Canada is in the process of building the Domestic Substances List (DSL) required for the Canadian Environmental Protection Act (CEPA). Until this list is finalized, the new substance notification provisions of the Act can not be implemented.
In compiling the DSL, the Department has adhered as closely as possible to the recommendations of the Environmental Contaminants Act Amendments Consultative Commitee, a multistakeholder consultation group consisting of representatives of the federal government, the provinces, labour, industry and non-governmental environmental interest groups. Accordingly, all substances considered for the DSL are based on nominations submitted by Canadian industry. Environment Canada evaluates these submissions to determine their consistency with statutory and administrative criteria for inclusion on the list. Consequently, Canadian industry and the Department jointly determine the ultimate contents of the DSL.
In order that the Domestic Substances List (DSL) required by the Canadian Environmental Protection Act (CEPA) be prepared as expeditiously as possible, Environment Canada has contracted Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) of Columbus, Ohio to assist in its compilation.
Environment Canada is committed to formatting the DSL in terms of CAS Registry Numbers and substance names structured according to CA nomenclature rules. As CAS is the originator of the CAS numbering system, it would be impossible to proceed without their involvement.
CAS has also advised Environment Canada on approaches to the collecting and compiling of DSL data and is assisting with the development of publication procedures.
Five contracts ($3.8 M total) have been awarded to CAS on a sole-source basis.

June 20, 1990

CAS has a unique experience in the area of chemical substances inventory development as a result of its participation, as prime contractor, in the two main inventory exercises that have been carried in the world so far, namely in the U.S.A. (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Washington) and in Europe (Commission of European Communities, Brussels).
Environment Canada has been advised by both these agencies that the involvement of CAS in the Canadian inventory project must be viewed as a necessary and essential condition for the success of the exercise and the credibility of its output.
One country, Australia, has attempted to prepare a similar list without the benefit of outside expertise. The effort has been in progress for four years and has been less than successful. To our knowledge, the level of expertise and highly qualified assistance required to build the DSL is not available from any other source, neither in Canada nor elsewhere.
The comprehensive assessment process specified in CEPA for new substances, imported into or manufactured in Canada, cannot be implemented until this list is completed.
CAS is owned by the American Chemical Society and operates on a non-profit basis.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Holcombe Wilson (Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
The Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985, which came into effect on January 1, 1987 established new minimum standards for federally-regulated pension plans. It included a requirement that pension plans provide a survivor benefit. Hence, since January 1, 1987, the pension benefit paid to a plan member or former member who has a spouse at the time the pension benefit commences, must be in the form of a joint and survivor pension benefit. Plans are allowed to reduce benefits on the death of either spouse to an amount not less than 60 per cent of the amount payable when both were alive. Further, the plan sponsor is permitted to reduce the initial pension benefit payable provided that the actuarial present value of the benefit in joint and survivor form is no less than the actuarial present value of the unreduced initial pension benefit payable in the normal form provided by the plan. At the same time, plans may be more generous, i.e., have no reductions on first death, have no actuarial adjustment for the joint and survivor provision, etc.
A plan member or former member may elect to receive pension benefits as though there were no spouse. This option requires, however, that in cases where such an election would reduce the pension benefit on the death of the plan member or former member to an amount less than 60 per cent of the amount which would have been payable if both spouses were still alive, that the non-member spouse sign an agreement which effectively waives his/her entitlement to a joint and survivor pension benefit. This written agreement must be deposited with the pension plan administrator.
In cases where a separation or divorce has taken place, a pension plan may provide for the payment of a joint and survivor pension benefit as two separate pensions. When this occurs, the actuarial present value of the two pensions must not be less than the actuarial present value of the joint and survivor pension benefit.
In cases where a plan member or former member dies before becoming eligible for early retirement, the surviving spouse is entitled to that portion of the pension benefit credit to which the plan member or former member would have been entitled to on the day of death, (calculated as though termination of employment and not death had occured) and attributable to that member or former member's membership in the plan after December 31, 1986. A pension plan may provide for an immediate pension benefit equal to or greater than what

June 20,1990
Routine Proceedings
is provided by the pension benefit credit just described. Where a member or former member of a pension plan died before payments begin but after becoming eligible for retirement, the person is deemed to have retired for purposes of the survivor benefit and to have been entitled to a joint survivor pension benefit.
In cases where the surviving spouse is entitled to a payment under a group life insurance plan on the death of a spouse, the pension benefit payable may be reduced by an amount equal to that part of the group life insurance payment that can be considered to have been paid by employer premiums. There are two conditions placed on this reduction: the actuarial present value of the reduction may not be greater than the amount of the payment to which the surviving spouse is entitled under the group life insurance plan; and if the pension plan is a contributory one, the reduction may not lower the benefit payable to the surviving spouse to an amount which is less than the member's required contributions plus interest.
When the new act came into effect on January 1,1987, plan sponsors were given a period of grace to actually re-draft the texts of their plans, providing they gave an undertaking to make the benefit changes effective to the date of the new act. Hence, the new provisions of the act are now in place.

CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the accord has been a subject about which there has been a great deal of public mystification. As often as possible I have tried to demystify it. I believed in 1987, as I do now, that the Meech Lake Accord is good for all of Canada. As a British Columbian, I believe it is good for western Canada.

The Meech Lake Accord brings Quebec back into the Canadian family under very reasonable conditions. It puts an end to the bitterness and ostracism experienced by Quebec since the patriation of the Constitution in 1982, and makes Quebec a full-fledged Canadian province.
The Meech Lake Accord paves the way to a stronger Canada in which the federal government will work with stronger provinces, not against them, and in which all provinces will be treated equally.
The Meech Lake Accord recognizes the distinct identity of Quebec society within Canada. It gives the provinces a voice in federal institutions such as the Supreme Court. It confirms the power of the Canadian government to establish new shared-cost programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction and the right of the provinces to withdraw from such programs and receive reasonable compensation, provided they offer their own programs on a basis compatible with national programs.

The Meech Lake Accord recognizes the need to move on to the next phase of our constitutional reform, to close out the agenda of the 1980s so that we can get on with the agenda of the 1990s.
I believe passionately and deeply in the importance of the accord as a device for enabling us to continue the kind of nation building that has created the most extraordinary country in the world today.
The accord will allow us to deal with the kind of problems and issues that a dynamic society like Canada constantly faces with each new generation.
I also believe that failure of the accord would be deeply injurious to the future of our country. That is not to say that the accord is perfect and could not be improved.
Indeed, at the recent first ministers' meeting, Meech Lake was improved as a result of proposals put forward by Manitoba, Newfoundland, and New Brunswick and the negotiations of all First Ministers.
Newfoundlanders and Manitobans have every reason to be proud of the contributions that they have made to this process.
As a British Columbian, I am keenly aware of the vital importance of Senate reform to western Canada. It is clearly of great importance to many Canadians in Atlantic Canada as well. The Meech Lake Accord guarantees Senate reform will be on the agenda at annual conferences on the Constitution.
Pursuant to the 1990 constitutional agreement, Senate reform based on agreed objectives will now be the key constitutional priority. The process will be accelerated and an intergovernmental commission will hold hearings based on objectives approved by all First Ministers, leading to a First Ministers' Conference on Senate reform by the end of this year.
If Senate reform is not achieved by June 1, 1995, the representation of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Newfoundland in the Senate will automatically rise from six to eight.
As Premier Filmon noted, this provides a commitment to Senate reform every bit as strong as the commitment that was originally given to Quebec for the current round of constitutional negotiations.

June 20,1990
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, another important issue discussed at the First Ministers' meeting was incorporating in the Constitution a general clause stating the fundamental characteristics of Canada.
The First Ministers made a thorough review of this question and took note of repeated and unsuccessful attempts over the past twenty years to draft a clause that would satisfy all concerned.
Finally, they agreed to refer drafts submitted by the federal government and Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Ontario and British Columbia to an all-party Special Committee for public hearings.
Premier Filmon called this "a major step forward" and noted that we now have "an open process that allows Canadians to actively participate in the definition of their national identity".
At the urging of Manitoba and Newfoundland, First Ministers also re-examined the distinct society clause and, in particular, its relation to charter rights and its impact on the distribution of powers.
The view of the federal government and the vast majority of legal experts has always been that inclusion of the distinct society clause in the accord does not endanger charter rights or alter the distribution of powers, as some have claimed.
Reassurance was provided by six eminent jurists that charter rights will not be infringed or denied by the linguistic duality distinct society clause, and that the clause will not create new legislative authority for Parliament or any provincial legislature.
The 1990 agreement also improves the possibilities for resolution of the concerns of the aboriginal peoples. As minister responsible for aboriginal constitutional matters, I restate this government's commitment to completing unfinished business in this area. As we stated in the last Speech from the Throne, aboriginal matters will be among the government's top constitutional priorities following ratification of the accord.

If all governments sit down at the same table and break the constitutional impasse, the accord will make it possible to achieve progress on the constitutional amendments required to meet the native people's concerns.
Furthermore, as a result of the agreement reached in 1990, it will be possible to establish a separate constitutional process for native peoples; a constitutional conference of first ministers will be held every three years, the first one in the year following proclamation of the Accord.
Obviously, the solution to questions affecting native people is closely tied to passage of the Meech Lake Accord.

Its failure is the real threat to making progress on aboriginal matters and on other important constitutional matters, as our present constitutional impasse would continue and the environment for constitutional discussions would likely be polluted for many years.
The consequences of the failure of the Meech Lake Accord should not be overstated, but neither should they be ignored.
I am deeply concerned that many people across Canada underestimate the effect of the rejection of the accord. Three times in the last decade-in the referendum, at Meech Lake, and most recently at the first ministers' meeting, Quebecers have said "yes" to Canada.

In 1980, Quebecers voted strongly for Canada. Imagine their disappointment when an agreement was negotiated in 1982 without their signature, without the province that is the homeland of one of the two founding peoples of this country.
Quebec's constitutional proposals are the most modest ever put forward in modem times.
Two provinces have yet to ratify the Meech Lake Accord and time is almost up. We are at a turning point in our national life and the stakes are high, very high.
We are at a critical period in our history. Without the accord, our existence as a united country and our will to continue to live together will be in question.
June 20, 1990

We do not want to leave this problem as an inheritance to the next generation of Canadians; we do not have the right to do that.

Let us not jeopardize the gains made in the Meech Lake Accord and the 1990 constitutional agreement. More important, let us not jeopardize the future viability of our nation.
It has struck me in the course of the public debate about the Meech Lake Accord how young we are as a nation when it comes to constitutional amendment. It is only since the repatriation of the Constitution in 1981 that Canadians have had the opportunity to enter into this process in a serious way and that the final decision about amendments to our Constitution has lain in the hands of our own governments.
The amending formula that was part of the repatriated Constitution in 1982 requires that constitutional amendments be put into effect through a ratification process in the legislatures of this country. The process leading up to the Meech Lake Accord is perhaps the first serious, nation-wide use of the process that came to us through the 1981 constitutional repatriation.
We have discovered in this process that there are difficulties with it. In the course of the negotiation of the Meech Lake Accord and the process that arose after it leading to the negotiation of the companion resolution just recently, there have been critics who have said that the process is not sufficiently open, who have criticized the meetings of First Ministers in attempting to come to a solution to our constitutional problems.
We face before us a challenge of trying to reconcile, on the one hand, the desire of Canadians to participate broadly in the constitutional process and, on the other hand, the requirements of the Constitution that at some point consensus be reached and ratified through the legislative processes in the Parliaments of the nation and the provinces.
This requires that at some point during the process responsible, accountable, political leaders must take the responsibility to articulate what they have heard from Canadians in resolutions and present those resolutions before the legislatures.
Government Orders
Clearly, for constitutional amendments to take effect, those resolutions must be similarly worded in all of the legislatures of the country. Therefore, there has to be consensus reached among First Ministers as to precisely what they will present to their legislatures.
We have learned a great deal from the process leading to the Meech Lake Accord and the companion resolution. I believe that the challenge of trying to reconcile these two broad concerns, on the one hand to be able to use effectively the amending process set out in the 1981 Constitution to achieve constitutional gains through the ratification of amendments by our legislatures and, on the other hand, to involve a broad range of Canadians, will be a challenge that will continue to be with us for some time ahead.
But what I find most difficult to understand about the process since the ratification of Meech Lake is the concern of some Canadians to somehow deal at once with every issue of constitutional reform that faces us as a country.
We are new to this process. In many ways we are children in the area of constitutional development. This has not been something that we have had solely in our hands for a long period of time in our country, unlike many of our neighbours and associates around the world. So we have to learn that there are processes of setting an agenda, of establishing priorities, of dealing with issues one at a time and gradually, over the years, building a corpus of a made-in-Canada Constitution.
My concern is that many Canadians have lost sight of precisely what it was that the Meech Lake Accord was intended to accomplish. The Meech Lake Accord is in many ways a small chapter in Canadian constitutional development. The Meech Lake Accord was designed to address a very specific problem, and that was the exclusion of Quebec from the constitutional process in 1981.
My own province was a very active participant in the negotiations leading to the repatriation of the Constitution. In fact, my province and other western provinces were very strongly concerned about the implications of a repatriated Constitution on the ability of those provincial governments to continue to operate.
There was much concern in the early 1980s about the effect of an entrenched Charter of Rights, for example, particularly the effect of that Charter of Rights to impose upon the prerogatives that under our system of

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
parliamentary supremacy had been so important to the Parliaments of Canada's provinces.
So, in the impasse that existed around the repatriation of the Constitution, there was a deadlock at that time as well. My province, the province of British Columbia, contributed very significantly to breaking that deadlock when it brought to Ottawa an expert in constitutional matters who devised the compromise which was at that time the nothwithstanding clause.
For my province, as well as others, the notwithstanding clause was the key to reassuring them that the patriation of the Constitution of Canada and the entrenchment of the Charter would not infringe upon their legislative prerogatives.
Mr. Speaker, we may have a different view about the notwithstanding clause now, but in the early 1980s it was hailed by many as a great and classic Canadian compromise, notwithstanding the fact that it permitted provincial legislatures and the Government of Canada to clearly override charter rights.
I believe that at the time, because it permitted repatriation of the Constitution and permitted the beginning of a process that has matured us in many ways, that has created enormous legal challenges for us, that has created great challenges to all governments in trying to work and operate consistent with the principles of the charter, that it was a positive contribution. But I would be the first to recognize that it may be a contribution that Canadians want to rethink.
What is important is that at that time there was a spirit of give and take and a willingness to make concessions on the part of the federal government and the governments of most of the provinces in order to ensure that there was support for the repatriation of the Constitution.
What we have been asked to address in the Meech Lake Accord is infinitely more modest than the challenges that faced us in the repatriation process. We are asked to recognize the aspirations of Quebec to ensure that it can defend and protect its own particular cultural entity.
So the process that led to the Meech Lake Accord was initiated at the instigation of the other nine provincial premiers who wanted to deal with that unfinished business. It is of great concern to me that there are those now who criticize the Meech Lake Accord because, in fact, it was designed only to deal with a limited agenda. The Premiers at that time recognized that the limited agenda addressed by the Meech Lake Accord was of fundamental significance because once dealt with it opened up the possibility of dealing with serious, fundamental, broad-ranging issues in Canadian society, that it was the key to unlocking a door that would open up a bright, constructive and fruitful future in Canadian constitutional development.
I think it is important at this time to remind Canadians that the Meech Lake Accord is simply the step in a long path that will continue to occupy us as long as we are a dynamic, changing, growing and developing society.
So, Mr. Speaker, we should not jeopardize the gains made in the Meech Lake Accord and the 1990 constitutional agreement. More important, let us not jeopardize the future viability of our nation.

As Premier Wells said in his closing remarks after the meeting of First Ministers, we must think of Canada first, consider the national interest first and our individual regions second.
That is why we are here today to take a stand for Canada, not as westerners or easterners, not as British Columbians or Newfoundlanders, but as Canadians.

Now is a time for Canadians to come together. It is a time for bridge-building and nation-building by all Canadians. It is time we came together in this country, not for the sake of Meech Lake but for the sake of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I urge the legislatures of Newfoundland and Manitoba to put Canada first and ratify the Meech Lake Accord.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin by taking the minister up on her closing remark. I agree it is time to come together and to see the Meech Lake Accord proceed to get through this constitutional impasse. I rise to support this resolution which urges the
June 20, 1990

two provinces which have not yet ratified the Meech Lake Accord to do so.
The minister recalled her own situation when the Meech Lake Accord was first introduced three years ago when she was a member of a legislature. I, myself, at that time was a member of this House. I served on the Meech Lake committee with my colleague the member for Papineau-St. Henri in the summer of 1987 when we reviewed the Meech Lake Accord. I sat again with the committee of the House of Commons, now called the Charest Committee, which reviewed the McKenna resolution submitted by the province of New Brunswick and which made recommendations unanimously supported by the House. So, like the minister, I have had some association with the process of this matter over the last three years.
I wish I could agree with the minister that the problems which she acknowledges so fully, the crisis to which she has alluded several times during her speech, are the result of us being new to the process of constitutional amendment, of us not having had the responsibility of amending our Constitution under present rules except since 1982.
But from where I sat I could see a very different problem. When I see this resolution, which may be interpreted by some as positioning two provinces for holding out, being brought before the House now, although I support the resolution, I feel bound to say in my remarks that I think the problem lies somewhere other than with two provinces and somewhere other than where the minister has suggested, with inexperience.
I suggest that what has gone wrong-and so much has gone wrong that I think even members of the government are hastening to characterize this as a critical situation with serious implications for financial markets, with serious implications for the future of our country- has been the approach that the Government of Canada, under the leadership of the Prime Minister, has taken since the Meech Lake Accord was passed to try to make it part of the Constitution of this country.
In light of the strong feelings that I and so many Canadians have on that subject, on the subject of how this file has been handled for the last three years, it is appropriate for me to put on the record my own experiences and some of my own observations about this very sorry story.
Government Orders
We all knew from the time of patriation in 1982 that it would be essential that the province of Quebec, as a government in Canada, give its approval of the patriation and of the establishment of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, not for the legalities of it or for the constitutionality of it, but because we knew we had a lot of constitutional work yet to do and we knew that the participation of the province of Quebec was an essential element in that.
It was with joy, for my own part, that I received, as we all did, the agenda put forward by the Government of Quebec after the Bourassa government took office. It put forward five points for what could be called, in the context of the debate, renewed federalism. I had been here for a while and I recognized that this list, these five points, were a reasonable agenda. Unlike past sets of agendas put forward, this was a reasonable agenda that could work in a federal system, and I supported it as a basis for negotiation. When the Meech Lake Accord resulted, I looked forward to the work that the committee would do to try to assure that the Meech Lake Accord would lead, as the patriation had, to a kind of consensus in the country and, even more, to an act that would unify the whole country. However, the strategy that the government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister, adopted was the opposite.
The minister tried to answer the critics about the idea that constitutional amendment can be done by a small group of men sitting behind closed doors. I do not have too much difficulty with that idea. I agree with her to a point. It is impossible for the amending procedures to be met unless there is some element of negotiation and compromise to produce a resolution that has a hope of acceptance in all the legislatures of the country and in the Parliament of Canada. So there has to be an element of what you could call executive federalism.
It took place back in 1981, that famous "kitchen cabinet" meeting at which representatives of three governments sat together and worked out compromises which resulted in the patriation and the Charter of Rights. You need something like that. I am not critical that Meech Lake was produced at a meeting like that. But to say that the Constitution limits the process to that is a misrepresentation. It is obvious that a strong element of public participation, support and contribution needs to be part, in any democratic society, of the amending of the constitution of a country. Ever since the Charter of Rights and Freedoms became part of the constitution of this country, for the first time the Canadian people

began to feel that they owned the Constitution of Canada. It did not just belong to governments to adjust, to wheel and deal, to pass powers back and forth. It belonged to the people of this country.
I recognize that some kinds of compromises cannot be made in public and need to be made in private. However, I do not believe that the whole deal should be one from which the public is excluded. That just will not wash.
Mr. Speaker, you might think-I see you looking a little suspiciously-that this is something I gained by the wisdom of hindsight, looking back at this process. I want to say that my Liberal colleague and I, when we sat on the Meech Lake committee, saw instantly, as I think most Canadians did, that there was room for improvement of the Meech Lake Accord.
I think I can quote the minister and what she said a few moments ago: "The week long meetings of First Ministers resulted in substantial improvements in the Meech Lake Accord."
Well, you know something, Mr. Speaker? The Liberal caucus recommended in August, 1987, a list which contains all of the improvements that she says occurred to First Ministers a few weeks ago when they met to see if they could improve the Meech Lake Accord.
We called for public participation. We recognized something so important that I think it is worth putting on the record. Although you could say that Quebec's problems, Quebec's demand for renewed federalism, Quebec's agenda, should be given priority it is a mistake to have a constitutional round that is described as the Quebec round.
I will tell you why. In a country like this with so many regions, every round has to be the Canada round. You cannot tell people we are just looking at Quebec's priorities now and as soon as they are finished we are going to look at yours.
Most Canadians, and I say this with respect to my fellow Canadians, tune in late. They may not be aware that in August, 1986, the premier of their province agreed that we would deal with Quebec's problems first and then deal with Manitoba's, Alberta's, New Brunswick's, or Newfoundland and Labrador's, or some other province. They tune in late and they see that the only thing on the agenda is the Quebec issue.
We in the Liberal caucus knew that and recommended in our minority report, which the government would not even allow us to include in the majority report, a broader agenda, not to take anything out of Quebec's list. We wanted Quebec's list to be there and you can see that from the record. We also wanted every region of this country to have its own reasons for supporting the Meech Lake Accord.
We urged the government to broaden it, to have public participation. People can read our report. It is a short report that we wrote back in 1987 which shows that if the government had not taken the tactic that it did, and if the minister is right in saying that the thing was much improved a week ago, I think we would have achieved those improvements two and a half years ago. We would have had broader public participation and a package in which every part of the country could see something of their priorities. It would have been truly a Canada round.
I am not sure how far she meant to go in her remarks, but I was pleased to hear the minister saying that we should think again about the notwithstanding clause, whether that has any place now that the constitution has been patriated.
In the Liberal minority report in 1987 we recommended seeking to remove the notwithstanding clause. That would have been a good item on the agenda for that meeting, not for the next one.
I know you cannot completely reform the Constitution all in one step. I know that. It cannot be done. You cannot deal with a thousand different items in every kind of detail. The goal would have been, as we recommended, to give every Canadian and region of this country a reason for wanting to see the Meech Lake Accord succeed. You know, that is what happened in 1981. After the executive federalism feature, real public
June 20, 1990

hearings were held, very different from the public hearings that this government allowed on the Meech Lake Accord where only egregious errors could be admitted.
In 1981 an honest committee sat. Opposition members, the public, and others made suggestions for amendments and they were taken. They were taken in order to give the people who submitted those ideas a real sense of participation in their Constitution.
I want to come now to the Charest Committee. The Charest Committee which had a majority of government members referred back to the meetings that took place in 1987. I am quoting two sentences from page 7 of the report: "The First Ministers who signed the accord back in 1987 took the position that it should be passed, unchanged, unless there was some egregious error. The body of evidence presented to your committee"-that is the Charest Committee-"is that most Canadians perceived at least one such oversight and that was the failure to include the Yukon and the Northwest Territories in the selection process".
Well, we saw many more egregious errors and so did the rest of the Canadian people, but for a committee with a government majority to put out a report recognizing even one egregious error is, I think, some support for the thesis I am advancing here that the problem has been the leadership provided by this government since the Meech Lake Accord was achieved.
I want to move forward to the work of the Charest Committee and close my remarks as quickly as I can. If there was one thing we concluded from the public hearings when we went all over the country in such a great rush, and where we sat late on nights when the public was willing to appear at eight or nine o'clock in the evening, it was that there was nothing wrong with their country. They told us they were proud of our country, that they wanted our country to stick together, that they were not fed up with having to accommodate regions with different ideas, different values or a different language. They told us the opposite, that they could not understand how we could have been led into so much trouble for a country where the desire for national unity was so strong.
They told us what is, in a sense, the explanation for why I am standing to support this resolution today. They told us that they wanted their political leaders to solve
Government Orders
these problems. They did not fully understand whether June 23 was a real date, or whether it was an arbitrary date, perhaps imposed by Quebec. In our report we were able to explain the significance of June 23 and why it is so important that the constitutional impasse be resolved, if it can be, by that date. They want the political leadership of this country to keep this country going, not to lead us into further division.
I recall so well the arguments that this government made to try to stick-handle or manipulate the support for the Meech Lake Accord that the constitutional process requires. I remember when the government accused the opponents of Meech Lake of being anti-Quebec. I remember when it accused them of being anti-French. I remember, and I am glad the minister did not do it today, the government using a heavy reliance on the disaster scenario, that if we do not support this accord and if we do not see it go through, there is going to be a terrible disaster, one argument after the other put forward to try, in a way, to force support for the Accord to take us through the constitutional impasse.
The reason that these extreme means have had to be used is because of a refusal by the government to follow a more democratic process, to open this process to public participation and to open it to improvement. The agreement was reached on a Saturday night, which in many ways can be called the Saturday night special because people felt, and some premiers have said, they had a gun held to their heads. Subsequently, by the Prime Minister's own admission, we learn this was a calculation of his and a belief he had. I did read today's Globe and Mail, and I saw very clearly that one counts backwards. The idea was to put maximum pressure on participants. I am characterizing this as putting maximum pressure on the participants so that the agreement would go through.
I rise to support this resolution. I hope that the constitutional impasse will be traversed and that Canada will get through it. But also, I cannot believe that the Canadian people will ever forget how we were led here. I believe that the government will be held to account for it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to the motion before us. Before I get into my remarks, I would like to mention what the motion is. This is not a debate on the Meech Lake Accord. The Meech Lake Accord was passed by this House in 1987. It is not a debate on the package that was signed on June 9, 1990 by the First Ministers.

First of all, I think it is very important to bring to the attention of those watching and to the people in this House that we are not debating the merits of the Meech Lake Accord. That has been done in this House. Therefore, I want to say that I feel very strongly that the bringing forward of this resolution at this particular time is simply another manoeuvre by this government to manoeuvre a process, rather than to show leadership on this issue.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES

subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my opposition to this motion. I am not expressing opposition to the content of the Meech Lake Accord, the companion resolutions and what is in the June 9 agreement. That is not the object of this motion. But I do object to this motion which is brought at this time simply as a manoeuvre, rather than this government showing some leadership.

Mr. Speaker, the government is trying to put the blame on someone else. That is clear. It is a cynical approach and it won't work.
Canadians have watched the constitutional process evolve. For three years, Canadians have been on the outside looking in. They wanted to participate but the government refused to let them.

Canadians have expressed legitimate concerns. They have proposed imaginative solutions but have been told by the government that they are causing problems and getting in the way. Canadians have been shut out of the constitutional process, and they know who shut them out. They know who has brought Canada to the brink. The government can try to shift the blame, but the people of Canada know that it is the Prime Minister who is responsible for this crisis. He must accept that responsibility.
Instead of wasting the House's time with yet more manoeuvres, perhaps he should be looking for solutions and providing leadership, working to unite and not divide this country.
The Minister of Justice spoke about building bridges. Well, I suggest to the Minister of Justice that the Prime Minister is not building bridges, he is blowing them up.

Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party voted for the Meech Lake Accord in 1987. It did so, fully aware the accord was not perfect. My party voted yes, although it was unable to get the amendments it had proposed through the House, and today it still thinks these amendments would have improved the Accord. Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party voted for Meech Lake because it supports Quebec's five conditions, including the one on a distinct society.
We have not changed our position during the past three years, Mr. Speaker. At its convention in 1989, the NDP confirmed its support for Quebec's conditions. At the same time we realized it was necessary to deal with other issues in the Meech Lake Accord, so that Canadians would be able to support the accord. We made some sound proposals.

June 20, 1990

Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, in 1987 we made specific recommendations, not a long list, three simple recommendations for amendments. Had they been adopted at the time, I believe we would not be in the situation we are in today.
These amendments address three basic issues; the ability of the north to become a province in consultation with the federal government when the people of the north felt that this was an appropriate time. Second, to acknowledge the multiracial, multicultural heritage of our country, to address the issues of aboriginal people, as well as to ensure that minority rights and sexual equality were maintained.
Throughout, our criticism of the accord has been a criticism of process. Three years ago, 11 men signed an agreement which would have incredible ramifications for the future of Canada. We believed that it should be the Quebec round. We wanted to see Quebec fully in the Constitution of Canada because we believe in a united Canada, of which Quebec is a part.
