speechtext:
But, those 11 men who signed that constitutional amendment in 1987 did so without understanding just exactly what it was that would cause the people of Canada to raise questions in subsequent years. It is crucial to emphasize that it was 11 people who signed that accord, 11 people of privilege in a nation that is 50 per cent women, with a multicultural population, and with aboriginal peoples who were here long before any of us.
The 11 people around that table could not fully comprehend how the Meech Lake Accord would affect these Canadians. Input should have been invited, but it was not. Instead, the Prime Minister and the other First Ministers came out of that meeting and said: "We have formed a seamless web. We will only discuss egregious errors". The first egregious error was that nobody knew what egregious meant. It seems to me that at least politicians should speak in a language that people can understand.
Excluded from the process were native peoples, women, the north and Canada's multicultural and multiracial population.
In 1987 there were public hearings. There were hearings for one month, August, in Ottawa. If there was ever a process designed to ensure that very few people would be able to come, that was it. Not only was a wide diversity of groups from across Canada excluded from that limited process, but following that, in each subsequent budget in 1988, 1989 and 1990, this government has made those excluded groups the victims of its attacks in the budget.
Women's groups saw their funds slashed by the government. The budget for the communications programs of aboriginal peoples was slashed. The Assembly of First Nations, a principal organization representing the aboriginal people of this country, had their core funding completely eliminated as did 29 other aboriginal organizations. What kind of a message is that to aboriginal people when this government is saying that it wants to include them in the process and we decimate their organizations so that they do not have the ability to be in that process?
This government has systematically silenced the voices of women and the voices of aboriginal people and, at the same time, it is saying: "Trust us, we will look after you". Canadians do not trust this government, and that is quite clear. It is my belief that if there had been an open constitutional process from the beginning, one in which all Canadians were included, we would not be in the situation we are in today.
I believe there would be much more understanding between Quebec and the rest of Canada. We are a large and diverse country, and we often do not know each other well. That is true for all provinces and territories of this country. The Constitution of Canada must be written by the people of Canada.

After the proposals by the NDP and those by Mr. McKenna, the Conservative government decided to appoint a constitutional committee. The Charest Committee, although it had very little time, did a remarkable job. It heard witnesses and answered their questions. The Charest report contains a number of important proposals.

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
It was really encouraging for our caucus, Mr. Speaker. However, we soon realized that the Prime Minister had no intention of taking the report's recommendations seriously.

When the Charest report was being written, the New Democratic Party tried very hard to ensure that it could be a unanimous report, and it tried to negotiate in that report a way to address the concerns that the witnesses had expressed to that committee. We tried to be as conciliatory as we could because we felt that it was important for the country at that time for all three parties to be unanimous in saying: "yes" to Quebec at the same time as addressing the other outstanding issues.
The NDP felt that it could be done, that it was not an impossible task to do. We did not have a list of many things, but there were a few essential issues.
The Charest report should have been followed up by an immediate, open and public meeting of First Ministers. Time and again in this House I urged the Prime Minister to call for such a meeting. The Prime Minister continually responded that the time was not right and that there was not enough consensus among the First Ministers.
We now know that the Prime Minister had no intention of calling a meeting until a crisis situation was created. He had no intention of holding open public meetings where the people of Canada could see what was going on. I think we make a big mistake here if we say that the flaws in the process were just the flaws of the last two weeks. It is the flaw from 1987. It is the flaw of not beginning to deal with the issues, to listen to the voices that were out there throughout Canada: in Quebec, in the provinces, in the maritimes, the Atlantic, the west and the north. It is the flaw of ignoring all those voices and continuing to say: "This is a seamless web".
During those three years, there was time to have adequate public hearings so that we would not have the situation now in Manitoba where apparently there is not sufficient time to complete the process, a process under their regulations.
When the Prime Minister finally called the First Ministers together at the beginning of this month, we
saw the same mistakes repeated over again; closed doors, long sessions and isolation for the First Ministers.
The environment and the process created is not a rational process for deciding the constitution of a democratic nation, and subsequent events have certainly shown that. This motion today serves no purpose. We have no authority to tell Manitoba and Newfoundlanders what to do. We have made the statements in this House about how we feel about the Meech Lake Accord and what our position is as a House of Commons. Are we now proposing, through this motion, to tell the people and the elected leaders of Manitoba and the people of Newfoundland and the leader of Newfoundland, what they should do? I can tell you, coming from an area of Canada that is not central Canada, if you wanted to inflame the regions in this country and say your democratic processes, your First Minister who signed that agreement cannot be trusted and tell them what to do, this will assure it.
We could support a motion brought forward by this government that enhances the positive process of constitutional development. We cannot support a motion that ensures there will be a negative result in those very two provinces which are mentioned in this motion.

If we are to save this country, if we are to move on and build another society, we need to find a resolution to the crisis. This motion put before us today is not a resolution. The decision has been taken in this House. It is simply a cynical way of trying to out-manoeuvre. We do not need more manoeuvres. We need some real leadership.
I call once more upon the Prime Minister to make immediate and positive efforts to find that solution. It is in his hands. I assure him, if he does, that he will have the whole-hearted support of my party.
We have to look at a new process, a meaningful constitutional process. I want to make a suggestion because, yes, it is easy to criticize. I was not a part of that process in 1987, 1988, 1989, or 1990. We have to look for a new process because this one is not working. I would like to make a recommendation because at our last convention the New Democratic Party called for the

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
establishment of a standing committee on the Constitution which would look at such things as public education, the funding of conferences to bring together a cross-section of people to discuss the Constitution, the requirement to hold hearings, and the encouragement of public participation in forming the Constitution of this country.
Constitution building is not an ad hoc crisis oriented process. I think this is a positive suggestion. I would like to say that over 43 years ago F. R. Scott and David Lewis in their book Make This Year Canada suggested the notion of a constituent assembly in order to construct a just and fair Constitution.
I would suggest to the House that this is a notion worth considering. Executive federalism is not working. We see it now; we have seen it over the last three years.
I remind the House that this is a system that France used in 1958. It was interesting when I met with Nelson Mandela this week that he raised that this was a proposal he had for his country, that there be an elected constituent assembly to form the constitution of his country, a constitution formed by the diverse groups in his country that would reflect that.
It is an issue and a suggestion that I think requires some study. That is again why I propose that this House consider such a standing committee and this proposal because it is clear that we need a new process. Yes, the existing process is fatally flawed, but I feel as leader of the New Democratic Party that I have a responsibility. I have a responsibility to show some leadership, even if the leader of this country is not prepared to do so.
Now we must turn to looking at a new process that will involve all Canadians. Whether or not Meech Lake and the companion amendments, we are going to be continuing constitutional talks. I want to suggest that there is great validity in looking at how we are going to do that in the future.
In summation, I cannot support this motion because this motion is presented cynically, not to advance any particular cause, not to advance constitutional discussions, and I would assume not to debate the merits or the demerits of Meech Lake. That decision has been taken in this House. For that reason I cannot support this motion.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us today a motion which is a motion of encouragement, a motion whereby members of the House of Commons urge the members of the legislatures of my province, Manitoba, and the province of Newfoundland to exert their efforts to bring about full ratification of the constitutional amendment, 1987 by June 23,1990. However the motion does not stop there; the motion goes on.
The reason for it is so that Canadians can complete an important act of nation building and thereby open the process of Canada's future constitutional development, including the important issues of Senate reform, of aboriginal rights and linguistic rights, of territorial participation in the federation, and of providing a process for a continuing review of the operation of the Constitution of Canada. It is the body of that motion which I want to address this afternoon.
There are those who would say that this motion is inappropriate. While I speak today I remind my colleagues that both in the House of Assembly of Newfoundland and in the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba the leaders and elected members of those two provinces in their respective Houses are debating the same issue.
I have just heard the speech of my premier, Mr. Filmon. In my mind, as he made his address to the legislature, he put before members of that House the achievements that were made respecting Meech Lake, the need to bind the wounds of our country, and the need to pass Meech Lake. The issues discussed in Ottawa some two weeks ago resulted in the companion resolution. He just made the recommendation that members of the Manitoba legislature should adopt the Meech Lake resolution.
As I stand here I know also that the Leader of the Opposition, the Leader of the Liberal Party of Manitoba, is addressing the legislature on the basis that we are not only members from specific or particular provinces and territories, but that we are Canadians first.
I thank both of them for the manner in which they are conducting the debate. I know that members in this House would want to conduct the debate on exactly that same level. It is also important to note that we are elected members of Parliament. In this Chamber we have the right and indeed the responsibility to speak for our constituents, to speak for the entire country, and to bring to the issues of the day a spirit, a vision, or an experience which has been moulded by the fact that we
June 20, 1990

sit in a national House and that we are from day to day on the great issues of the day confronted or faced in debate, in conversation and in association with the aspirations of the people of Canada from the various regions.
It is always easier to take a specific view and hold to that view. It has been my experience over the some 18 years I have been here that it is always more difficult but extremely necessary to mould one's views on the basis of what one has heard from one's colleagues and what one has experienced throughout the breadth of our wonderful country.
It is not the Parliament of Canada telling Manitoba legislators or members of the House of Assembly of Newfoundland what to do. Rather, Parliament speaks for all Canadians. I believe that we cannot simply seek public office in order to hold office, but the requirements of office demand us to speak on the great issues of the day.
In 19811 had the opportunity as the then spokesperson for the Official Opposition to lead our committee in the long debate on the patriation of the Constitution, both during the special House of Commons and Senate hearings as well as in this House.
There were three issues which faced us at that time. One was patriation of the Constitution. Should the Constitution be in Canada and should we as Canadians and as a mature country have the opportunity to discuss our Constitution, to debate it, and to change it?
I was a strong supporter of patriation. In those days as well, I had some misgivings and indeed criticisms of the process. We also said that if we had a Constitution in Canada we had to have a method, a formula, whereby we could amend the Constitution.
Colleagues will recall that there was a proposal at that time which was generally referred to as the Victoria proposal. It found its way also into the 1980-81 proposals. Through the process the amending formula was changed. I had the privilege in committee to move the 7/50 formula which today is the central part of the debate
Government Orders
as we look at unanimity and what effect it would have as we try to change the Constitution.
The third issue was the matter of a Charter of Rights and Freedoms and how we balanced a charter and the protection it gives or, more important, the symbolic protection it gave to those Canadians who did not have the heritage of the British parliamentary system? How did we blend a Charter of Rights and Freedoms with the supremacy of Parliament?
At that time I had disagreements with some of my Conservative colleagues in the provinces. I say that and take this historic journey but for a moment is for this reason: After we were through the process and after we had been through the Supreme Court where, as members will recall, there was a reference made as to how much support a government needed in order to change the Constitution and bring it from England, a decision had to be made.
The decision that had to be made was that after the process is complete, despite the criticisms whatever they may be, there was only one decision that every member of the House had to decide upon and that was: Were these constitutional amendments right for Canada?
I remember the debates within the caucus. Members know that we cannot discuss those debates here but I remind members that a decision was made at that time by the opposition party that we would support patriation, we would support the amending formula and we would support a Charter of Rights of Freedom. The issue at the time was, what in our hearts and our minds did we believe was right for Canada.
There were members of the House at that time and they are still here as members today, who opposed it at that time. One of the reasons they opposed it was the unfinished business. Primarily, there were two examples of unfinished business in 1981. This is not put forward as criticism because I am a sincere believer that, through the British parliamentary system, constitutions evolve and develop. One never has, at any point in time, the perfect document.
There were two issues that concerned us. One was the fact that the province of Quebec was not a signatory to the constitution. There are those in this House and especially members opposite who, at that time, convinced me that the signature had to take place because the government of the day, in the province of Quebec, would never sign the constitution. You have to remem-

June 20, 1990

ber that that came one year after there had been a referendum, and a solemn commitment on the part of all of us, that we would ask what was Quebec's expectation and how could we mould them into the constitution. That was the Meech Lake Accord.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset, I would like to say that I will support this motion because I think that it is important and useful at this time when not only elected federal officials but also representatives of the various provincial governments are involved in this great constitutional process. I think that this resolution is in no way unfair to the legislature of Manitoba or Newfoundland. And unlike my colleagues in the New Democratic

Party, I think that the Parliament of Canada can very well express its wishes and hope that two provincial legislatures support a constitutional process approved not only by the Prime Minister of Canada but by the ten provincial premiers as well.
That being said, I nevertheless remind you that the present constitutional impasse goes back several months, I would even say a few years. As soon as a new government was elected in New Brunswick, it was clear that it would be difficult to obtain from this legislature the same consent given previously by the former premier of the province. I can only regret that it took so long to decide to seek an appropriate compromise in response, first of all, to the questions of Premier McKenna, and subsequently to the objections raised by the Manitoba legislature following an election that produced minority government with Premier Filmon, and finally, to the objections raised by a newly elected government in Newfoundland. In any event, I want to say, first of all, that I voted for the Meech Lake Accord, probably because I felt that Quebec's five demands were and still are reasonable, moderate and a good basis for arrangements that would benefit all Canadians.
It formed the basis for negotiating a constitutional agreement which at the time received the unanimous support of the First Ministers. If the proposals made by the Government of Quebec were reasonable and still are, as I believe they are, then why did the present text of the Meech Lake Accord cause such aggressive debate, such dissension, suspicion and distrust? Why did this draft accord a rouse greater anxiety about the future of our country than any other event or initiative had done in the past years? Having watched the Meech Lake debate very closely, I am convinced that the problem was not the five demands of Quebec but the process by which these five demands were met. The Prime Minister, who I am sure was acting in entirely good faith, thought that, by giving the other provinces the same terms he gave Quebec, he would be able to settle this constitutional problem. Unfortunately for the Prime Minister, although many Canadians are prepared to accept a strong Quebec, there are many people in this country who do not necessarily want a weak Canada. Personally, as a
Quebecer and a Canadian, I feel it is very important to obtain the full consent of the Government of Quebec to the provisions of the Constitution Act, 1982, which was and still is the objective of all parties.
Unfortunately for many Canadians, the Prime Minister of Canada abdicated his role as defender of the interests of the Government of Canada to obtain a constitutional accord, apparently at any price. However, I was delighted with the action taken by Premier McKenna of New Brunswick, who on March 21 proposed a way to try and resolve the constitutional impasse.
This suggestion, which I think came very late in the day, was a praiseworthy initiative that should have come, not from a provincial premier but from the Prime Minister of Canada himself, many months ago.
The Government of Canada, in response to the companion resolution proposed by the Government of New Brunswick, appointed a parliamentary committee, commonly referred to as the Charest Committee, which held public hearings across the country, heard hundreds of witnesses, received thousands of written submissions and made a series of suggestions not to undo Meech Lake but to renew the support previously given by the Parliament of Canada through the three party leaders in the House. There was support for Meech Lake, but the report also recommended some additions and improvements, somewhat along the lines of the suggestions made by Premier McKenna, to resolve this constitutional impasse and thus ratify the Meech Lake Accord.
I am glad to say that throughout this political process, the Liberal Party of Canada set aside political considerations and fully co-operated with the government. From the outset, the Leader of the Liberal Party, the Right Hon. John Tbrner, supported the government's action on Meech Lake. Subsequently, the vast majority of Liberal members in this House voted in favour of the accord when the debate on Meech Lake was held. And quite recently, when the Charest Committee was appointed, all four Liberal members signed the Charest Committee's proposals and joined forces with the government and the New Democratic Party to seek a solution to the constitutional impasse.

There were those marathon meetings that lasted nearly a week between the Prime Minister of Canada and the provincial premiers to try to find a compromise that would enable the various legislatures that had not yet ratified the Meech Lake Accord to do so.
I must say that some of the suggestions made by the members of the Charest Committee were accepted and I think that is an important factor which made it possible for the Prime Minister of Canada to obtain the co-operation of all First Ministers who were present at those week long negotiations. An agreement was finally reached because some proposals that had been unanimously accepted by all members of the parliamentary committee chaired by our colleague, Jean Charest, were acted on.
But I must say that I had a feeling right after this agreement was reached following that long week of negotiations among the first ministers- I say that because I saw in the newspaper the day after the agreement that some representatives were very disappointed with what had happened. I quote from an article in The Globe and Mail that said:
"Agreement is faulted by women and natives". The article states:
But Judy Rebick, president of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, said she was "disgusted" by the process. "Women, aboriginal people and multicultural groups were excluded. The decisions are still being made by middle-class white men in Ottawa".
The article goes on to state:
The Assembly of First Nations, which represents native groups, was not available for comment. But Ethel Blondin, Liberal MP for the Western Arctic and a leading native spokeswoman, said she feels betrayed by Mr. Mulroney.

It is obvious that what is now happening in the Manitoba Legislature is a reaction quite similar to the spontaneous reaction of our colleague, Ms. Blondin, who found it wrong that at the end of this long discussion that lasted nearly a week, the Prime Minister invited the representatives of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon in to talk and publicly consent, in front of the nation, to this process that had just been accepted by the First Ministers of Canada. But those who were most

conspicuous by their absence from that happy Saturday evening were of course the representatives of the native peoples. I wonder why the Prime Minister of Canada did not have the good idea to bring these people into the final moments of this long discussion that lasted nearly a week, so that they too might accept this compromise in Canada's interest.
I must say that the recommendations of the Charest Report, in particular recommendations 9, 10 and 18, were not followed up either by the Prime Minister of Canada or probably by the provincial premiers. If more serious, sustained attention had been given to these recommendations of the Charest Report, I do not think we would have the objections now being raised in the Manitoba Legislature. In any event, I can only regret what is happening.
I sincerely hope that the legislatures of Manitoba and Newfoundland will approve this compromise agreed to by the Prime Minister of Canada and the provincial premiers. What is at stake is our concern that each and everyone of us can live in harmony in our country. The original objectives of the 1987 constitutional exercise must be realized. I think that if the Prime Minister makes it a point of honour to say that the 1982 round was incomplete, he too must admit that the 1987-1990 round is also incomplete.
The resolution before us clearly indicates that if, on one hand, we hope for the ratification of the 1987 Constitution Amendment before June 23, 1990, on the other hand there is also an important step which will have to be taken in the future constitutional development process with a view to dealing with, as the resolution puts it, the important issues of Senate reform, of aboriginal rights and linguistic rights, of territorial participation in the federation, and of providing a process for a continuing review of the operation of the Constitution of Canada.

I hope that on the evening of June 23 all Canadians will be able to celebrate the

Mr. Speaker, I have just come from a meeting with the agricultural leaders of Canada in preparation for the Houston Summit. I was advised of the very gracious gesture by the member for Papineau-Saint-Michel in accommodating my speaking here today. I wanted to thank him personally for that.
It is with some poignancy that I recall it was some 30 years ago that the member for Papineau-Saint-Michel and I as fellow students at Laval University in Quebec City were discussing at great length some of the same constitutional problems that are before this House today.
I remember the member as an active participant in those debates. Some of the questions raised then, as I think back, have bedevilled Canada ever since. I think some of the solutions that he and other members have put forward have been incorporated into a broader perspective that we all hope will bring greater unity and harmony to Canada.

I personally thank the hon. member for Papineau- Saint-Michel, former minister in the Liberal government, for his kindness in offering his place so that I could take part in this debate today.

This week, as few times before, Canadians feel the weight of our history. After a long and sometimes difficult journey, we are now only three days away from June 23. Today, the past of which we are all so proud is balanced against the future that we all so ardently desire.
In April 1987, in the Gatineau hills, we began a voyage that has led so far to the ratification of the Meech Lake Accord by eight provinces representing 94 per cent of the Canadian population and by the Parliament of Canada. The path has led us to the legislatures of Newfoundland and Labrador and Manitoba, on whose steps an anxious nation now waits.
When First Ministers met on June 3, the concerns raised in the three years since the accord was first signed were all part and parcel of the problems that were on the table for resolution. For seven difficult days these issues were debated, analysed, and discussed at great length. Proposals were exchanged and ultimately an agreement
June 20, 1990

was arrived at. This agreement is reflected in the final communique dated June 9, 1990, with the appropriate caveats as expressed by the premier of Newfoundland and Labrador and the premier of Manitoba.
The Premiers of New Brunswick, Manitoba, and Newfoundland and Labrador undertook to submit the Constitution Amendment, 1987, the Meech Lake Accord, for appropriate legislative or public consideration and "to use every possible effort to achieve decision prior to June 23, 1990".
Since then the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick has unanimously adopted the Meech Lake Accord, together with two companion resolutions.
Today, with this motion, Mr. Speaker, we as members of the Parliament of Canada simply and respectfully urge the Legislative Assemblies of Manitoba and Newfoundland to bring about the full ratification of the Meech Lake Accord.
There is no attempt by the Parliament of Canada to intrude upon anyone else's jurisdiction, but the national Parliament, using precedent from past decades and past years, has both the opportunity and the obligation from time to time to speak out and respectfully urge other legislatures to take cognizance of important matters, and this is one that is important to the future of the country.
We all appreciate the heavy responsibility which now rests on our fellow legislators in those provinces who must complete the ratification process. We have the greatest respect for the rules of their legislatures and for the procedures to which they have chosen to subject their decisions. But there is a compelling national interest that the Meech Lake Accord be brought to a vote before June 23.
As all parliamentarians know from experience, political will can always overcome procedural obstacles.
I am advised by Premier Wells that the free vote which he plans for the Newfoundland and Labrador House of Assembly will take place either late Thursday evening or early Friday morning. I salute him on selecting this method which included consultation by the members of the House of Assembly with their electors for voting on the accord and on the companion resolution. True to his signature, he has asked the members of his legislature to
Government Orders
express their opinions and to vote on this crucial question before the deadline.
Premier Wells has extended an invitation to myself and to the other First Ministers who signed the communique to address the Newfoundland House of Assembly on the subject of the Meech Lake Accord.
Earlier today 1 had the opportunity to watch part of a quite remarkable address by the premier of Ontario to the legislature of Newfoundland and Labrador, a very compelling and eloquent statement on national unity, strongly urging the ratification of the Meech Lake Accord in the interests of Canada's well-being. Premier McKenna, I understand, was there this afternoon.

speechtext:
Provincial first ministers recognized this in Edmonton in August, 1986 when they issued the unanimous declaration designed to bring about Quebec's full and active participation in the Canadian federation.

The unanimous decision by the provincial premiers in Edmonton to promote Quebec's return to the constitutional fold was an intelligent and generous response to the legitimate demands formulated by the Bourassa government.

In 1985, with a federalist Liberal government in office in Quebec, five principles for the resolution of our problem were laid out and the way began to be cleared to continue to build our common destiny. The success of Meech Lake in 1987 was, above all, a gain for Canada, for all of Canada, for the strength and unity of Canada. That is why I think that this House twice adopted the Constitution Amendment, 1987.
Meech Lake affirms the principle of the equality of the provinces. It clarifies and confirms the spending power of the federal Parliament in respect of programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. It strengthens through entrenchment the Supreme Court of Canada as the
highest court in the land. It provides the provinces with a say in the selection of senators, although in all cases the final decision on appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada and appointments to the Senate rests with the Government of Canada.

Like many of my colleagues in this House and like many Canadians, I realize that this agreement, essential though it is to our country's future, will never be able to respond to all the aspirations nor appease all the fears of certain groups or individuals.
Mr. Speaker, that is not its purpose. As a Parliament cannot be defined by the stones used to build it, no constitutional text can ever contain the entire soul of a nation. It is my profound conviction that we can judge the effectiveness of a Constitution by its ability to inspire respect for institutions and affection and compassion for humankind.
Like thousands of Canadians, I felt the breath, the spirit of Meech Lake on that Saturday night, on June 9, 1990, when the Premiers of all Canadian provinces and the leaders of the Northwest Territories and Yukon appeared in turn before the television cameras to express, in terms most eloquent, their pride in having been able to contribute to the unity of this country, a country we all love: Canada.
Through the voices of the Premiers the same message came through, loud and clear: Canada is a magnificent country, and we have a responsibility to future generations to preserve it and make it grow. And that is exactly what we are doing with the Meech Lake Accord.!

With our constitutional process unblocked by Quebec's return to the table, we will be able to turn our attention to an agenda such as Senate reform and aboriginal constitutional matters.
Premier Penikett of Yukon said on June 9:
After three years of debate and discussion it is clear to us that constitutional evolution is not a series of discrete steps but a fluid process. We will meet again as we have in the past and I hope work together to create a Constitution which all Canadians, aboriginal and non-aboriginal, French and English, east and west, south and north recognize as the sum of this country.
June 20,1990

If, despite the agreement reached at the Ottawa Conference Centre, the remaining ratifications were not obtained, no one here or anywhere else can say for sure what our future might be. I for one, cannot tell this House if or when another opportunity to make the changes so important to so many Canadians-Senate reform, further gender equality rights and aboriginal rights-would present itself again.
Quebec, in confidence and maturity, has proposed to return to the Canadian constitutional family. If we do not seize this chance now, if we do not seize this glorious chance now, who can say if and when it would arise again.
The uncertainty caused by the failure to resolve our constitutional problems could harm our chances to regenerate the outstanding economic and employment growth that we have known in the recent past, and I believe are poised to achieve again over the next few years.
I am deeply encouraged that the legislators of Manitoba and Newfoundland and Labrador are now debating this historic accord. I express the fervent hope of members from all parties of this House that they will pass it within the time frames.
I also call upon the other legislatures to ratify the companion resolution agreed to in Ottawa which provides progress toward the goal of Senate reform; the protection of gender equality rights; a fairer deal for the territories and for linguistic minorities; and important gains on aboriginal constitutional issues.
The aboriginal peoples have the assurance of a separate constitutional process dedicated to aboriginal constitutional matters that would involve their participation in First Ministers' Conferences every three years.
We placed before a meeting of the representative group of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs on Sunday a proposal that would provide for, first, a federal-aboriginal process to set the agenda for the First Ministers' Conference on aboriginal matters and the acceleration of the holding of the first conference.
Second, a commitment by the Government of Canada to full constitutional recognition of the aboriginal peoples as a fundamental characteristic of Canada.
Government Orders
Third, the participation of representatives of the aboriginal peoples of Canada at any future First Ministers' Conference held to discuss the recognition's clause.
Fourth, an invitation to participate in all First Ministers' Conferences where matters being discussed directly affect the aboriginal peoples.
Fifth, a most important historic matter for the aboriginal peoples, the joint definition of treaty rights.
Sixth, the establishment of a royal commission on native affairs of the scope and the impact of the historic Bilingualism and Biculturalism Commission that made such a beneficial change 25 years ago, and this new royal commission on native affairs can do at least as much to advance the cause of aboriginal justice now and into the future in Canada.
This six-point proposal is, I think, generous and comprehensive in response to the legitimate demands of aboriginal peoples. It highlights as well the consequences to all of us in not succeeding in restoring the full constitutional family to the table.
I have said in this House, and others have remarked upon it as well, that I remember well under the 1982 Constitution being called upon as Prime Minister of Canada to chair a First Ministers' Conference seeking an amendment to provide for justice for the aboriginal peoples of Canada. I believed then and I believe today that that amendment so vital to the well-being of the aboriginal peoples of Canada would have been achieved had Quebec been at the constitutional table at the time, because the government of Quebec had clearly signalled that it would support that kind of an aboriginal initiative for justice.
The absence of Quebec already at that time had taken a terrible toll on something that we all hold dear, and that is the promotion of instruments of greater justice, greater fairness and greater equality for the aboriginal peoples.
In spite of the very comprehensive nature of the proposal that we have put forward on behalf of all parliamentarians to secure greater justice for the aboriginal peoples, clearly a condition precedent to this taking place is the return of Quebec to the constitutional table because Quebec is an ally of the aboriginal peoples and it is in Canada's interest and in the interest of the aboriginal peoples that Quebec come safely home to the

constitutional table and thereafter the first matter that will achieve greater justice and greater dignity will be the aboriginal peoples themselves.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I have to begin by saying that it is very clear, in spite of the Prime Minister's words and the applause of his supporters, that it is his mishandling of Canada's present constitutional situation that has created a serious and difficult circumstance for our country.
It did not have to be this way. Three years ago, we of the Official Opposition, offered a number of amendments, proposals regarding the constitutional accord of 1987, which, if they had been accepted, would have removed the concerns about that accord which had been expressed by many Canadians.
These amendments that we proposed were consistent with Quebec's five proposals, proposals which have been acceptable, generally, to parties in this House.
This Prime Minister and his government stubbornly rejected these proposals. They rejected, out of hand, these Liberal amendments. If they had been accepted, it is high likely the constitutional impasse that has worried Canadians for the past several months would not have occurred. This is one reason why I have to say it is because of this Prime Minister and his government's
mishandling of the constitutional situation that we have the current atmosphere of crisis and impasse.
We believe the Prime Minister showed a lack of essential leadership by waiting to try to resolve the constitutional impasse until after Premier McKenna had made his proposal for a companion resolution. It was clear from the time that proposal by Premier McKenna was made, and even before, that only the dynamic created by the Prime Minister and all the Premiers sitting and talking around the same table could lead to the development of a consensus for a solution to the constitutional impasse.
We know all too well how the Prime Minister absolutely refused to convene a meeting of First Ministers even though we of the Official Opposition Had been calling for just such a meeting for months for the reason I have just given.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister always answered our requests for such a meeting with basically the same argument. He said it would be premature to call a meeting of First Ministers and that Senator Murray was still out there somewhere, searching for common ground.
We now know and Canadians now know that was not the reason for the Prime Minister's delay or his refusal in convening a meeting of First Ministers. No, Mr. Speaker, that was not the reason at all.
On Monday, June 11, the day after the signing of the communique for the 1990 companion accord, after a week of discussions at the Conference Centre between himself and the provincial premiers, the Prime Minister gave an interview to The Globe and Mail of Toronto, and in that interview he said he had held a strategy meeting with his advisors and in talking about that meeting stated:
And so I decided after consultations with my colleagues, mostly with Senator (Lowell) Murray and Paul Tellier, Norman Spector, people like this, that-I remember when I told them, I called them right here, I asked them to come and see me, and I told them when this thing was going to take place. I told them a month ago when we were going to start meeting. It's like an election campaign, you've got to work backwards. You've got to pick your dates and you work backward from it. And that-and I said that's the day that I'm going to roll all the dice. It's the only way to handle it.
Q: And this was a month ago?
A: About a month ago.
Q: Roll of the dice, this was a conscious, obvious decision.
June 20, 1990

A: You had to roll all the-the only way that this could be done was
to roll all the dice.
Mr. Speaker, what a shocking admission. Is this the way to run a country, much less reach a decision on its constitution? Obviously, in the view of Canadians this is not the way to run a country or a constitution; it is not even the way to run a crap game.
The timing of the First Ministers' meeting had nothing to do with finding common ground among the First Ministers. But by the Prime Minister's own admission, it had everything to do with creating the crisis atmosphere which sometimes works in labour-management negotiations.
But as I have said before in this House, constitutional negotiations are not labour negotiations. They are matters of much greater consequence and much greater sensitivity. They should not, they must not be left to the last minute as the Prime Minister did, as a conscious and deliberate act. Also, the Prime Minister has no right to stake the future of this country on the roll of the dice. You do not roll the dice with the future of Canada as the stake.
The Prime Minister well knew that there was a time limit, a June 23 date. He well knew, or should have known, that Manitoba's legislature had a debating and a public hearing process it had to go through under its rules in order to deal with and make a decision on constitutional matters.
The Prime Minister well knew, or should have known, that in any legislative body, in any legislative process, there is a risk of procedural problems and procedural hang-ups. In the case of Manitoba, there was a requirement for public input and all of these things. The working out of the procedural problems, the requirement for public input could and would use up precious time, time that was all too short and limited.
Yet, by deliberately waiting until the last minute, the Prime Minister invited these problems, the very problems he was talking about in this House just a few minutes ago. He invited them himself. I could say that he created them through his delay and his devious manipulation of the constitutional discussions.
In the way he did it, he did not ensure there was adequate room, beyond all question, for the legislature of Manitoba to work its way through any possible constitutional problem or to have the hearing process
Government Orders
that the degree of public interest in that province would warrant and which its own legislature rules required. The Prime Minister and the Prime Minister alone, must bear the responsibility for the mess that has been made by him and his government of the constitutional situation. It is his mess and it is his responsibility. He cannot shift any blame or responsibility for that situation to anyone else. He should look at himself in the mirror and recognize that he is responsible for the difficult situation the country is in during this current constitutional impasse.
By his own admission he created this difficult situation and this mess in a deliberate way. He did so, as he told The Globe and Mail, in a way for which he has no apologies at all for the process he organized, one carried out in secret, one without participation of the public, one done in a crisis atmosphere and at the very last minute. For this, as he told The Globe and Mail he has absolutely no apologies.
He certainly owes an apology to Canadians for the mess he has made of Canada's constitutional situation. He owes Canadians more of an effort than he has been making up until now to try to clean up that mess.
I welcome, and we welcome, his announcement that he will speak to the Assembly of Newfoundland. But another of the major areas of concern is that of the aboriginal peoples of Canada. The Prime Minister sent Senator Murray to talk to the aboriginal leaders in Manitoba but they were not satisfied with what Senator Murray had to say. Yet the Prime Minister has for days refused to take the extra step we recommended, to go himself to meet and talk with the aboriginal leaders in Manitoba.
Today in his speech the Prime Minister spoke about the generous package which was offered at the last minute to the aboriginal leaders. But the Prime Minister has not explained why that generous package was not put forward to the provincial premiers and the aboriginal leaders during the week of discussions in the Conference Centre here in Ottawa. If that had been done, we might be in a very different situation today when it comes to whether or not the impasse will be broken and the accord will be adopted and proclaimed by June 23.
If he is going to meet and speak to the House of Assembly of Newfoundland, the least he could do is also

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
go and meet with the aboriginal leaders of Canada and talk to them about their concerns and what he and his government intend to do to respond to them in a meaningful way. This is an aspect of leadership, and if he expects to be looked upon as the leader of this country, he must take more meaningful action than he has done to resolve this difficult situation. Yet, we see he has left himself with almost no time to spare to work it out.

As I said on June 11 when I spoke in this House in response to the Prime Minister's statement in which he reported on the discussions that took place between him and the provincial premiers:
We understand the importance of the 1987 constitutional amendment, the purpose of which was to make Quebec a full member of the constitutional family. With Quebec back in, we can fully discuss all the constitutional changes being called for by groups and regions throughout our country.

We recognize there is much more still to be done in order to have a Constitution that responds to the needs and concerns of our aboriginal people, women, minority language groups, multicultural groups, the Territories and those who want a reformed Senate. As I said in the House last Monday, if we stay together as a country, then everything and anything is possible by way of constructive constitutional change, by way of working out how we can live together in a better, more secure and more constructive fashion. If we do not stay together as a country, then nothing is possible and everything that we have concerns about in regard to how we live together will be meaningless and irrelevant. Therefore, we must strive to maintain the unity of this country in spite of what I believe the Prime Minister and his government have done to weaken this unity and the strains they have put upon it.
The Prime Minister came into office pledging that he would bring about a new and greater national reconciliation. Yet, especially in the past three years under his Prime Ministership, we have had a great and troubling increase in the divisions and tensions between regions and groups and in expressions of disunity among some of the people in this country. It is now clear that the Prime Minister must take the blame and the responsibility for these divisions, tensions and disunity. It is now clear he created the conditions for it by the way he mishandled our constitutional situation through delay, manoeuvre and manipulation.
All of us must work to ensure the preservation and the strengthening of Canada, in spite of its present Prime Minister and government. We must work to ensure it stays united until and long after the people of Canada can and will exercise their judgment in an election and make the changes it is already clear that they want to create and to ensure a better and a more united Canada with a welcome place in it for all its people and all its regions.
On June 11, I said in this House we believe that the final communique setting out the accord of 1990, signed by the provincial premiers and the Prime Minister, during their week-long conference, can provide the basis for the successful resolution of that constitutional impasse. I went on to say that I hope the New Brunswick, Manitoba and Newfoundland legislatures will accept this agreement, this accord of 1990, and thereby will approve the 1987 constitutional amendment before June 23. New Brunswick has now done so. The Newfoundland House of Assembly will vote tomorrow or Friday, but the matter remains before the Legislature of Manitoba.
I want to say that, as far as I am concerned, in being asked to make a decision on the motion before us, we are being asked to deal with a motion which requests that the legislatures of Newfoundland and Manitoba take prompt decisions on the constitutional accord of 1987. This motion does not ask this House to pronounce itself again on the constitutional accord of 1987. This is something it has already done. Also, this motion, this resolution, does not ask this House to lecture or to instruct the members of the legislatures of Newfoundland and Manitoba on how to go about their business, how to cany out their responsibilities. It gives no instructions or advice on procedures they should follow.
I do not think that the members of the legislatures of Newfoundland and Manitoba need to be lectured by the Prime Minister or his ministers in this House. As I said on June 11, I am confident that the members of the legislature of Manitoba and the House of Assembly of Newfoundland are very much aware of their responsibilities for the future of Canada and I am sure they take these responsibilities very seriously.
June 20, 1990

In this connection, I want to remind the House of the words of Clyde Wells, the Premier of Newfoundland, to the House of Assembly of that province on the morning of June 11. He said: "I am confident that the members of this honourable House and, indeed, all Newfoundlanders and Labradorans will express their views on the basis of their own sincere convictions and with the future of Canada foremost in their minds and their hearts".
I say now as I said June 11 that calling upon us, the people of Newfoundland and in fact all the people of this country to keep the future of Canada foremost in our minds and in our hearts are wise and welcome words from the Premier of Newfoundland. They should serve as an example and a signal for all of us.
I believe it would be in the best interests of this country and its future, if the present impasse could be resolved by June 23. It would be better if the uncertainty created by the Prime Minister's mishandling of the constitutional situation could be, if not removed, at least lessened and not extended beyond June 23 if at all possible.
For these reasons, I support the motion before us, not because it is necessary in any constitutional or legal way to resolve the current impasse but because we Liberals want to send a strong message that Canada is worth preserving, that Canada must be preserved. We should all give priority to making sure it is preserved in the interests of all its people, all its regions, for our children and the future generations.

speechtext:
It is quite an incredible situation for all of us. Canadians will be the judge.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has been in a state of constitutional crisis for the past several weeks and even months. It is not the first time in our history that our young country is going through such a crisis. In fact, 25 years ago, the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Bicul-turalism, the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission, made public an interim report saying that Canada was facing the worst crisis in its history. Well, 25 years later, we are once again facing one of the worst crises in our history.
Between 1965 and 1990, the Canadian people have debated constitutional issues a number of times. In 1967, our centennial year, Ontario Premier John Robarts called a conference to discuss the future of the Canadian federation. In February 1968, Prime Minister Pearson called a constitutional conference to discuss findings contained in the report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. They talked about the formula for amending the Constitution, the Supreme Court of Canada and the possibility of involving provinces in the appointment of Supreme Court judges, which we find in the Meech Lake Accord that we want to see ratified in 1990. They also discussed linguistic rights and regional disparities, issues that are just as important today.
At the famous constitutional conference held in Victoria in 1971, they went back to the issues discussed in 1968 and reached a consensus on the condition that the First Ministers consult their respective legislatures within 12 days and return with their opinion.
We know today what happened after that constitutional conference, when Mr. Bourassa made an important decision and said on behalf of the Quebec people that he was not satisfied with what they were offering him.
We always think of the failure of 1971 when studying the Meech Lake Accord. In 1976, Mr. Trudeau proposed another constitutional initiative, based this time on the patriation of our Constitution. In fact, Mr. Trudeau was always true to himself: after 1976, every constitutional

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
initiative that he proposed had the patriation of our Constitution as its main objective.
At that time, he proposed three options for the patriation, but the provinces-and Mr. Lougheed from Alberta was their spokesperson-gave him the following answer: "There will be no patriation of our Constitution until we have the opportunity to discuss the roles, the jurisdictions and the powers of our provinces. We have to discuss the substance before we can discuss the form." The premier of Alberta said at that time-and it is interesting to note that today because, after all, we are talking about things that were said and written in 1976-that the provinces wanted more power, Mr. Speaker, in the area of immigration. Imagine, in the area of immigration!
What does the Meech Lake Accord do if not precisely respect the wish of the vast majority of provinces in 1976? At that time, Premier Lougheed told the Prime Minister of Canada that he wanted to discuss language rights and other powers. He also said, among other things, that he wished that a requirement to hold annual first ministers conferences on the economy be written into the Constitution.
That request, Mr. Speaker, was presented in 1976, not in 1987, not during the Meech Lake negotiations three years ago. That was the wish Premier Lougheed of Alberta expressed in 1976 on behalf of his colleagues, the other premiers.
In 1976, Mr. Speaker, the Parti Quebecois was elected. That election completely redefined the constitutional picture in Canada. In 1977, Mr. Trudeau reiterated his intent to patriate the Constitution, and he also put together a royal commission of inquiry, known as the Pepin-Robarts Commission. In 1965, we had the first interim report, by the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission and in 1977, the idea was revived by the Pepin-Robarts Commission.
In 1978, a White Paper was tabled. That White Paper, Mr. Speaker, prepared in 1978, stipulated that the Canadian Senate was to be replaced, or reformed by July 1st, 1979! The federal government intended to reform the Senate within a year. What was planned? A House of Federation House where half the senators would be appointed by the provinces, and half, by the federal government.
I refer to that, Mr. Speaker, for all those who are shocked today because the Meech Lake Accord gives the provinces a say in choosing senators. Can you believe that in some areas of Canada, people are shocked because the provinces will now be able to submit names-even if, as the Prime Minister pointed out, the final decision is still going to be made by the federal govemement- whereas in 1978, Mr. Trudeau was planning to let the provinces appoint half the members of the new Senate.
Nothing new there, Mr. Speaker. All this to tell you that there is not much that is new in the Meech Lake Accord. And this is only up to 1978. As well, in 1978, as in 1968-there seems to be a 10-year cycle here-the Supreme Court of Canada was an issue again. In 1978, Mr. Trudeau also proposed that the provinces play a role in the appointment of judges to the Supreme Court of Canada. This is not very surprising in a federation where the highest court of the land makes the final decisions and is the arbitrator between the provincial and federal jurisdictions. It is not surprising that we can expect the two levels of government to have their say in the appointment of those arbitrators. Don't you think that is only good common sense? In any case, I do. Mr. Trudeau thought so in 1978, Mr. Pearson thought so in 1968 and I believe Mr. Mulroney's opinion on the matter is the same in 1990 as it was in 1987-1988.
In 1980, Mr. Speaker, there was the referendum in Quebec. I do not wish to drag on on this subject. Suffice it to say that a commitment was taken, a commitment to a renewed federalism, a clear commitment, in any case, clear enough so that the vast majority of Quebecers could understand it as such. And several important politicians in this country went to campaign in Quebec, including our colleague from the House of Commons, the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is here today. He was among those who went to Quebec, with the Prime Minister of Canada, to make this commitment to Quebecers. But, unfortunately, for all sorts of reasons, it was not possible to respect fully the commitment made in 1980.
I do not want to go into detail; suffice it to say that two things happened in 1981-1982. First of all for the first time in its history, the Quebec National Assembly had its powers curtailed without its consent. That was the reality of the year 1981. We can look at it from every angle and
June 20, 1990

try to blame it on whoever we want, but it is a fact and no one can deny it. Second, that curtailment of powers was decided against the will of the province of Quebec and of the Quebec National Assembly which had passed a bipartite resolution agreed to by both the Parti Quebecois and the Quebec Liberal Party condemning these action of the federal government. It is in the history books and it is what we will remember about 1981-82 in the years to come.
In 1984, a new Federal government came to power, and in 1985 a new provincial government was elected in Quebec. Mr. Bourassa came into office and had his mind set on an important decision which was to be expressed in a speech delivered by his Minister of Intergovernmental Affairs, Mr. Remillard, in the spring of 1985 in which he stated the will of the governement of Quebec to get the province back again into the constitutional family. Indeed, Mr. Bourassa felt at the time that such an invitation was being extended to his province. And at that time, the Governement of Quebec did state the five demands to be laid on the table, that is the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society, some additionnal powers as regards immigration, which was part of the 1975 discussions, entrenchment in the Constitution of the three seats on the Supreme Court that Quebec holds today, another proposal that was discussed in 1968 and in 1978, certain conditions to the spending power of the federal government and also a veto power for the province of Quebec.
In August 1986, the provincial premiers, without the federal government, decided to go along with this and set as their top constitutional priority the return of Quebec to the Canadian fold, based on Quebec's five conditions. This was not much of a surprise. Later on, Mr. Speaker, there was in 1987 the Meech Lake Accord negotiation, the Langevin Accord negotiation on June 3, 1987, and sometime later, more specifically on June 23, 1987, the ratification of the Meech Lake Accord by the Quebec National Assembly, which brings us to June 23, 1990, because it must be said that the three-year time limit was not chosen by Brian Mulroney or anybody else, but by the rules set in the 1982 Constitution which provided that when a legislature adopts constitutional amendments, they must be dealt with within the next three years. There was, therefore, no discretion there.
Government Orders
Since then, the accord was ratified by the House of Commons not once but twice because, apparently, once was not enough, it had to be done twice. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, this accord has been widely debated in Canada ever since.
Since 1987, there were a number of parliamentary commissions. Were there three? No. Were there four? Do you think there were four, Mr. Speaker? You are not sure? Let me tell you how many. You can double this figure. There were altogether eight commissions! In British Columbia, the Meech Lake Accord was debated and adopted. In Alberta, it was debated and adopted. In Saskatchwewan, it was debated and adopted. In Ontario, there was a parliamentary commission; the accord was debated and adopted. In New Brunswick, a parliamentary committee held a very very long debate. The Meech Lake Accord was adopted there this week; it was also debated in the legislature. In Nova Scotia, it was debated and adopted. In Prince Edward Island, there was a parliamentary commission and the accord was adopted. In Quebec, there was a parliamentary commission and the accord was adopted. In Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker, I think there was a parliamentary commission, but I am not sure; the accord was unanimously adopted and later on almost rejected. It was rejected recently and now, it is debated for the third time.
This is the point we have reached in the debate on the Meech Lake Accord. In Manitoba, Mr. Speaker, there was a parliamentary debate, a committee, a task force, the so-called Manitoba Task Force on Meech Lake-I have the document here. What they heard, which is worth repeating, is what appeared on page 2 of the English version which read:

The hearings conducted in Manitoba were the most extensive held in Canada. Over 300 Manitobans made presentations before the task force. Over 40 individuals and organizations for Manitoba who did not appear before the task force submitted written briefs. All of the presentations of briefs are listed.
The Meech Lake Accord, the companion resolution, everything around this constitutional debate has been debated extensively for the last three years. In fact, by going through the chronology of events I have just gone through since 1968, most of the issues debated today in

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
the Meech Lake Accord have been debated in this country for close to the last 30 years.
There is no issue. I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no issue in this accord that is new to Canadians. There is no issue that has not been extensively debated, including the committee that I chaired that heard more than 160 witnesses. We received close to 900 briefs, travelled to Yellowknife, Whitehorse, Vancouver, spent three and a half days in Winnipeg, Manitoba, spent several days in the national capital region here, and spent two and a half days in St. John's, Newfoundland.
This debate and these accords have been extensively debated as well as all the issues that are found within them.
I think it is important today to remind ourselves of these debates, what they contain, and what we have said. The question put today before the House of Commons is extremely important. The House of Commons is in fact calling upon the legislatures of both Newfoundland and Labrador and the legislature of Manitoba to put this question and this issue before their legislatures for a vote.
That is what is most fundamental in our country and consistent with the commitment made by the premier of Manitoba, Mr. Filmon, on June 9, when he signed the agreement with the other premiers of this country and the Prime Minister of Canada. That is what is being asked by the House of Commons today of these two legislatures so that we can finally get over this debate.
One of the questions that has come up more recently is that we should extend the delay. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that that question has also been studied extensively and in fact the committee that I chaired studied that question very closely.
The first recommendation that we made in our own report published on May 17 says very clearly, and it is not by accident that it is the very first recommendation made, that your committee is of the opinion that June 23, 1990, is a political reality.
There is a reason for that, Mr. Speaker. This debate has gone on long enough. There have been eight parliamentary committees. The issues debated within these accords have been debated close to 30 years. The moment of truth has come. Legislatures must face up to that moment and put this accord to a vote.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I think there are some lessons we can learn from the present debate.

There are conclusions to be drawn from this debate, Mr. Speaker.
In any case, I drew my own conclusions, which bind no one. After chairing a committee that produced recommendations which were received with much emotion, mind you, I can tell you that I had a chance to think. One thing I observed is that the amending formula we used this time had its first test, because it is only eight years old, at the expense of the Meech Lake Accord. It is unfortunate, but that is a fact. The Meech Lake Accord paid the price of being the first test of an amending formula that we did not fully know or understand. That is the price. It means that next time, constitutional agreements will be negotiated differently, not in the same way.
The second thing I observed is that Canadians everywhere want to take an active part in developing and amending their Constitution. That is very clear from the experience we just went through. It came out clearly from the hearings we held.
The third thing I observed, and it is worth mentioning, although it may seem obvious to you, but some Canadians who have not yet realized it must be told that Canada is a land of regions, a vast country where people live differently from place to place. We do not always share the same experiences. We do not always perceive things, events and even documents in the same way. This means that Canada as a country is cut out for federalism.
Mr. Speaker, here is the fourth point: Although Quebec will not be reconciled constitutionally, in spite of my hopes, it will be reconciled in other ways. It will be reconciled in Canadian political circles. And this was made apparent in the experience the government of Quebec went through recently with the government of Canada which stood by Quebec on this constitutional issue till the end. Quebec also had unfailing ally in the person of the Premier of British Columbia, Mr. Vander Zalm, for whom it might have been relatively easy in political terms to oppose the Meech Lake Accord, in view of the upcoming elections in his province. There was also the Premier of Alberta, Mr. Getty, who was under pressure from his own party to oppose the accord following a convention held a few months ago. In spite of
June 20,1990

Government Orders
the pressures, he stood up for Canada and he stood up for Quebec too. That has to be pointed out.
Premier Devine of Saskatchewan, who will also run in a provincial election in the next few months, stood up for Quebec and for Canada. He went all the way, Mr. Speaker, on June 9 this year, as he had on June 3, 1987, in the Langevin Building. In Ontario, Quebec had Premier Peterson's unfailing support. I may not be Liberal, but such facts must nonetheless be recognized. There was also Mr. Rae, from the New Democratic Party, and Mr. Harris, a Conservative, for whom it might have been easy to object to the whole thing- But no, Mr. Speaker, they stood up for Quebec all the way, as did Premier Buchanan from Nova Scotia. Premier Ghiz, from Prince Edward Island, who is very articulate-I know that for a fact, having heard his testimony before our committee-took a passionate stand for Quebec. These things must be said. It is unfortunate that Quebecers can not be reminded of that enough. After all, they were not always there to witness those moments of passion and demonstration of commitment to Canada and Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I also came to the conclusion that our country is one of the few countries in the world, though I do not know them all, where the feeling of belonging to one's country is not the same from one area to the other. Let me explain that, Mr. Speaker. We must admit that a Quebecer will feel like a Canadian only inasmuch as he or she can be recognized as a Quebecer first and that is true for francophones and, in some cases, for anglophones.
The natives of our country offer another example of different feelings of belonging between individuals and between groups, Mr. Speaker. I think that we have come to realize in the last few days that a native will only feel he is a Canadian if he or she is recognized in our Constitution.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that my time is up. I really wanted to say that because we, as Canadians, are different from the Americans who, it appears, have a single allegiance to their country, their flag and their national anthem. We are only beginning to sense these great changes, these things which make us different.
