speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you and
others may remember, I was part of the 1983 debate when this House unanimously passed a resolution encouraging the Manitoba legislature to pass legislation on constitutional changes which would entrench French language services within that province.
Those motions, presented at two different times, were passed unanimously by this House. That was done in a non-partisan manner and with acceptance from all quarters of the House of Commons. That was done because we believed that the minority rights of the French speaking population in Manitoba must be protected.
It was not an easy task for many of us from the province of Manitoba. It was very obvious at that time that the resolution put forward by the Pawley government was not accepted by the majority of people in the province of Manitoba.
This House decided to intervene and passed the resolutions I spoke about. We could not have done anything more destructive. Not only did it not change the minds of the provincial Conservative MLAs in the legislature of Manitoba, because they continued to ring the bells and they continued to prevent the passage of that legislation, but it made it very difficult for those of us who were standing up for French language services in the province of Manitoba to explain our position within our own province.
I spoke after the present Prime Minister and after the present member for Winnipeg South Centre, the then member for Winnipeg-Fort Gariy. I thought we were doing the right thing at that time, but I can tell you that the two motions passed by the House of Commons at that time did not have the desired effect.
I can tell you, after spending a week in my riding, that if this motion were put to a vote tonight it would have exactly the same effect in the province of Manitoba this week. There are people in our province who would like to see Meech passed. There are others who have grave reservations about the Meech Lake Accord but are willing to accept it because they believe it might be the right thing to do to promote the unity and the strength of

June 20,1990
Government Orders
our nation. But the one thing they will not accept is the interference of the Prime Minister of Canada.
I say that in a non-partisan way. I listened to the leaders of all three parties in the Manitoba legislature when they spoke on national television earlier today and they were saying exactly the same thing.
People in Manitoba, for whatever reasons, feel they have been manipulated when it comes to Meech Lake. The member of the Conservative Party who spoke just before me said that we have already had public hearings in Manitoba. That is true. However, it was known by the Prime Minister and this House that the three provincial leaders in Manitoba had promised that there would be further hearings after the first ministers' meeting which took place two weeks ago. That was known. That was not a surprise. That was known before those people came to the week-long meetings at the Conference Centre. It is part of the written agreement signed by the premier of Manitoba. It was stated when those same three people left Ottawa to promote Meech Lake and the companion accord in the province of Manitoba.
The technical slip-up by the Attorney General of Manitoba, which resulted in longer and longer delays occurring in that province, does not give any one party or all three parties the right to cancel public meetings in the province of Manitoba. No attempt to rewrite history in advance is going to be acceptable. No attempt to cast the blame ahead of time is going to be acceptable to the province of Manitoba.
When I spoke in 1983 on the French language services issue I spoke with emotion. I said that the people of my province were not bigots. Certainly, some people may have opinions which we would not find acceptable. That is the state within our nation. People have different views. People have unacceptable views from time to time.
The vast majority of those people want to have Quebec stay within our Confederation. The vast majority of those people would make accommodations if they saw that happening, but they cannot be manipulated time after time and expected, as a result of the motion here on June 20, to pass major constitutional amendments within
the next three days. They cannot be expected to go against their word with regard to public hearings.
The Prime Minister, in his infamous countback from June 23, miscalculated. He made a technical mistake of his own. He made an error, and no bullying tactics by the House of Commons is going to do anything to help the public mood in the province of Manitoba.
As I said, in 1983 I spoke for French language rights in the province of Manitoba. That was not popular. I voted for Meech Lake in 1987. I spoke in favour of Meech Lake in 1988 during the election campaign. Those were not popular stands. I continue to believe that the Meech Lake Accord is the basis of a real accommodation for Quebec within our society. I believe it is an acceptable accommodation for Canadians, albeit at great emotional cost to many Canadians.
Some are concerned about the erosion of central powers by the federal government, a belief that the federal government has given up too much of its decision-making role to the provinces, especially in the area of social programs. There are others in our society who believe that there has been a loss of charter rights through the Meech Lake Accord. Those are valid opinions. I do not happen to share them, but they are valid opinions.
Those of multicultural and multi-ethic backgrounds in Canada feel excluded. They were ignored in Meech Lake, and they have been basically ignored in the three years since June 23, 1987.
However, as has been very evident over the last week and a half, it was the aboriginal Canadians who most severely and personally felt that they were being ignored. There is no one in this House who would ever deny that they are a distinct society. They are our first distinct society, and they should have been recognized. There should have been efforts to accommodate their concerns within Meech Lake within the last three years. A letter sent to Manitoba chiefs by the Prime Minister two days ago was not acceptable.
During the last three years those same aboriginal Canadians have felt threatened by this government. During Question Period today the government talked about its accomplishments in Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Government members talked about other of its accomplishments, but they did not talk about how
June 20, 1990

native people feel about this government. They did not talk about what is happening out there.
Let me give you an example. It is a personal example but it hits home very well. Last night I was speaking in Thompson, Manitoba, at a gathering of students in the Access and NTEP programs, two programs that will lose their funding this fall. This program has existed in a number of forms over the last ten years. It has promoted and helped to educate native people as teachers, nurses and social workers. Last year that joint federal-provincial program was dismantled by the federal government. There was one year of extended funding. Some students in that program do not know where their funding will come from as of August 1 of this year, one month from now. Because of the federal government's cutbacks, there will be no new students accepted in those programs as of this fall.
We have a shortage of native teachers, native nurses and native social workers. We need more natives in engineering and other technical areas. How do you expect those people to take the great leap of faith to sign Meech Lake on the basis of some future goodwill by this Prime Minister when those same people are being denied their educational potential this coming fall? The government has made many other such cutbacks which have hardened the resolve of native people in this country.
Elijah Harper is one of my MLAs and I am very proud of the stand he took last week. He and I have both spoken in the past about the need to accommodate Quebec. He and I have both spoken about the need to protect native rights. We have said that those are joint common causes that should be worked on together by our nation. Elijah Harper, by the way, was one of those people who spoke in favour of the entrenchment of French language services. He did that in a riding which is 90 per cent Saulteaux and Cree. He spoke out about the need to defend the French minority and let that message go home to the province of Quebec.
For the last three years many native Canadians have been willing to accept the Meech Lake Accord. They had hoped that in that time the Prime Minister and others would take the necessary steps to show good faith. That did not happen.
Government Orders
The manipulative way that the province of Manitoba has been treated, the way that the native people feel they have been treated over the past three years, has made it very difficult to pass the Meech Lake Accord in the province of Manitoba in the next three days. I do not believe it will happen.
It will be a sad day for our nation. I am very concerned about what will happen on June 24, 25, and afterwards, because we do need to show goodwill. We do need to show faith. We do need to show a desire to bring this country together. But, unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the last three years were wasted.
Many people spoke out. Many people kept their own personal concerns to themselves. But there was not enough goodwill, not enough work, not enough honesty by the Government of Canada and it will have to accept the blame for the failure.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin, if I may, with the words uttered by my friend from Churchill as he concluded. He is, as he knows, a member whom I respect in the House. He said that the work of the last three years has been wasted. I think that is precisely the question that we are debating here tonight, whether or not the work of the last three years has been wasted. I think that there is a genuine feeling throughout this House that it would not just be a shame, it could almost be a tragedy if that work were wasted.
There has been talk here, rather to my surprise, of bullying and of blame. As someone who has been involved in these discussions and these negotiations, and who is not myself blameless, I can certainly say that if blame were our purpose I could give you a list as thick as the Toronto telephone directory of people to whom blame can be ascribed.
But surely that is not our purpose because that takes us nowhere. What we want to do now in these last hours of this debate is find some way in which we can bring Canadians together to achieve, not an end, but to achieve a beginning, first, of constitutional renewal but then, and I think this is a much larger question, the beginning of a process of national renewal because none of us who has lived these last months can doubt that there are profound problems in this country that go

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
beyond disagreements that arose in a particular negotiation among First Ministers.
These are the last hours of this debate. It is a question that is of fundamental importance to the whole country. By the turn of events the last debate will occur not in this Parliament but in the legislatures of Manitoba and Newfoundland and Labrador. I certainly do not take my place in this Chamber to try to lecture the elected members of those two legislatures. I know better than that. I tend to share something of the view of my colleague from Churchill with regard to the counterproductivity of one legislature trying to lecture another legislature. It is not any more helpful in politics than it is in other aspects of life for people to undertake that sort of conduct.
But, Sir, I think it is, on this question that is so fundamental to the country, legitimate that we express our views in these final hours in the hope that our views might be useful to the individual members of the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba and the individual members of the House of Assembly of Newfoundland and Labrador who have this final decision to take.
Let me begin with four propositions which inform my approach to this crisis in our national life. First, I believe that we are the luckiest country, the luckiest people in this world. Some of that good fortune we have earned ourselves. Some of it was given by God or was earned by others before us who surely have a right to expect that we would treasure and respect what it was that we inherited.
Second, there is an anger and a distemper in Canada that is more widespread that I can ever remember before. Hatred, Sir, is not too strong a word for some of the emotions that I have seen and heard. Obviously, anger that strong reveals a frustration that is profound and that is personal and we must all ask ourselves seriously why people are so angry and what we need to do to rebuild the basic bonds of goodwill that any community needs to hold itself together. We cannot repair anger by blaming others for it, but if we do not repair that anger it will feed, it will grow and it will tear this country apart.
Third, Meech Lake has become far more than a document signed by First Ministers. It is a symbol. More accurately, it is several symbols. For Canadians who
oppose it, it is a symbol of something they dislike-a process, a government, a perceived unfairness; for some, unfortunately, a people.
For the wider world it is a symbol of the stability of Canada, whether we are a country the world can count on or a risk. For many Quebecers the symbol is direct and it is personal. Acceptance or rejection of Meech Lake is seen as acceptance or rejection of Quebec; not Quebec as the author of five conditions, not Quebec as a participant in an amending process, but Quebec as a partner in this country.
I have heard opponents of Meech Lake tell me that if Meech Lake is rejected Quebecers would be angry for a while and then would forget. Well, Sir, I do not believe that. Of course, I can be wrong, as we all can. But I have spent three decades in national affairs trying to understand what makes our different communities work and work together. All of that experience tells me that this rejection of Quebec as a partner in Canada would damage this country permanently.
I have no right to decide for others, but I pray that Canadians whose decisions might affect Meech lake would consider my view and would consider the consequences if I happen to be right.
The fourth proposition concerns aboriginal rights which appears to be the issue which was causing people to urge Elijah Harper to stop constitutional reform. I have some history on the question of aboriginal rights.
In 1973, Flora MacDonald, Frank Howard and I moved a motion that caused the first acceptance by a parliamentary committee of the concept of the legitimacy of aboriginal title. I have been involved throughout my public life with native people. I simply cannot understand the logic which says Meech Lake must be killed in order to advance aboriginal rights. Killing Meech Lake has the opposite effect. It makes action on aboriginal rights more difficult to achieve.
Aboriginal interests are, by definition, constitutional interests. If there is a constitutional impasse, nothing will be done on aboriginal rights. That is not theory, that is history, that is recent history. That is what happened when we tried to deal with aboriginal rights in 1985 and did not have the votes because Quebec, which would have voted for change, was not a part of the Constitution.
June 20, 1990

The only way to make progress on aboriginal rights, on Senate reform or on the other priorities agreed to by the 11 First Ministers is to start with what we have. To reject Meech Lake is to reject progress on aboriginal rights. Anyone who takes that action should be fully aware of the consequences.
Sir, I can fully understand why the National Citizens Coalition would act against aboriginal interests, but I cannot understand why Indian leaders themselves would do that.

Mr. Speaker, the situation is critical. There is not much time left. But there is still time to succeed if we really want to. Meech can still be signed by Manitoba and by Newfoundland and Labrador. It is not over yet.
In the last three years, many have said that Meech was dead. Yet, it made it to this day. Maybe there are still some nice surprises left in Meech, one last time! I wish it were so with all my heart, for our greater benefit and for the benefit of our country, Canada.
Mr. Speaker, all of us watched, some of took part in that long discussion of seven days and seven nights. The most poignant moment on that ninth of June was when the pen passed to premiers whose earlier positions had put the Meech Lake Accord in doubt. Those premiers, Mr. McKenna, Mr. Filmon and Mr. Wells put their pen to paper at the end of the day, and in so doing demonstrated the best of Canadian qualities.
They had travelled far, they had strong views, principled positions and deep concerns. But in the overriding interests of keeping this country together-and I trust that is the overriding interest of all members of this House-they compromised, and all First Ministers compromised. They vowed to take Meech Lake back home, to put it to the representatives of their peoples and to let democracy take its course.
Other societies and other countries do it differently. They deny legitimacy to the concept of compromise. They do not accept that different parts of their societies can hold different things to be true. They prefer to
Government Orders
resolve their differences through fiat or through fighting. That is not Canada. That is not the unique achievement which is admired around the world without reservation or without caveat. That has not been our experience, and it never can be if we wish Canada to continue.
Eleven days ago, eleven First Ministers made a solemn pledge to each other, to the Canadian people and to future generations. The three Canadian premiers who had travelled so far promised to use every means at then-disposal to allow their people to decide on their Constitution. That was eleven days ago. Three days from today, Meech Lake will pass into history. It will either pass into history as a moment when Canada came to terms with itself and decided to move forward, recognizing that, of course, all was not perfect, but the perfection could not be approached until the country was whole once again. Or it will pass into history as a serious step backward for our country.
As was indicated in debate earlier today, and as I believe Premier Wells has now indicated, Newfoundland will vote, either tomorrow or on Friday in the House of Assembly. As the House knows, debate has now begun in the Legislature of Manitoba. That debate was delayed longer than anyone anticipated by procedural difficulties. The fact of that unanticipated and procedural delay has created a special situation that nobody anticipated. There was a commitment to make every effort to ensure that the agreement reached, after careful compromise and discussion in the best Canadian tradition, would be moved through the legislatures of the respective provinces. It is clear that the country is counting on that.
Just as procedural moves delayed debate in Manitoba, so surely procedural ways can be found to move debate forward so that the word of the three leaders of Manitoba can be honoured and so that the country can move forward to other priorities, whether those priorities are constitutional or whatever they are.
Just prior to the conclusion of the last conference on the Constitution in Ottawa, I spent two days in Europe in separate meetings with the foreign ministers of NATO and of the Helsinki process. Naturally, whatever point I tried to make in advancing the foreign polity of Canada, I was asked about Canada's problems at home. I was asked by incredulous ministers from Hungary, Germany, the United States, United Kingdom, and Yugoslavia.

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
They could not believe that a country as envied and respected as Canada would put itself at risk, and particularly, that we would put ourselves at risk over the question of how we deal with different cultures. Because that is the signature of Canada, that is the success that is admired around the world, the success the new governments in Czechoslovakia, a united Germany, and a new South Africa, will want to copy.
Nelson Mandela left Canada this morning. I had the privilege of bidding him bon voyage. He spoke to this House and to the people of Canada of his hopes for his people. He spoke of a country which would discover tolerance and compromise, which could learn to live in unity, which could consecrate itself anew as a nation among the leading democracies of the world. He spoke of the bitterness, the intolerance, the hatred and the prejudice which have governed South Africa. He spoke of Canada as a society to be admired, a concept which inspired him as he faced the enormous challenges which lie ahead.
Nelson Mandela was right. What we have achieved here has been achieved nowhere else on this earth. We are a society of many cultures, many regions, many races. It is a society that has always said yes to compromise and no to intolerance. It is a society which says that different cultures, different regions and different races can more than co-exist; they can thrive and prosper in community with diversity.
The history of this remarkable land has been a continuous act of affirmation. We can never forget that the existence of this country was not a given, that the building of Canada has been a task accomplished against the greatest odds; geographic, economic and demographic. Tending the community that is Canada requires great care. How ironic it would be, how wasteful if, at a time when the rest of the world was thrusting forward with vision, the people of this country were to turn away from our strength and our future.
The Parliament of Canada has spoken. The Parliaments of eight provinces of Canada have spoken. The premiers of all provinces are committed to letting their people speak. Let that process proceed. Let history judge the results. Let us all pray for Canada. Then, together we must define new shared goals for Canada which reflect the new realities of this new world in which we live.
Everywhere in this world, there are dramatic changes that shake old conceptions and raise new hopes. People everywhere are hoping to become what we are. That is the reality.
There are serious differences in this country. There are serious issues to resolve. We have to find ways to define this country that make sense to all of its people. We have not yet succeeded in doing that. That is what the bitterness of these recent months has demonstrated. In doing that, if we succeed we can preserve one of the most respected nations in the world. That is the issue now.
This is the challenge that faces us, the legislature of Manitoba and the House of Assembly of Newfoundland and Labrador who have the right of the final vote to decide the future of this accord, of this process, in many ways perhaps of this country. The next step is for them. I say this as only one member with some experience here; the work is not over for us. Then the challenge to all of us is to recognize that this country is not as united as it needs to be, that the goals we have set for ourselves are not as contemporary as they need to be, that the definition of this nation does not mean as much as it should to people in different parts of the country.
This is not something which should not cause us to lay blame or to distribute retribution. It should be a challenge to us all, to get on with the redefinition of this extraordinary country. But I fear deeply that, if we fail in the challenge that is before us now, we will not have the opportunity to move to that new agenda.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I appreciate the viewpoints expressed by my colleague and I appreciate many of the things that he said.
I have a couple of questions about some of the phrases that he used in terms of anger and intolerance, that he sees across the country and I have certainly have seen that, as well, in our home province of Alberta.
The hon. member used the words bitterness and intolerance. He stated that Nelson Mandela and he talked about where we say in this country yes to compromise and no to intolerance and that we should be proud of community with diversity.
June 20, 1990

In his wide experience with people from these countries where they are experiencing pain and are undergoing reform situations, as Nelson Mandela in South Africa, as well as in eastern Europe, what do they see as an example of democracy in Canada? We are seeing that the government cannot handle community with diversity, when people feel that they should represent their constituents and they were excommunicated from the caucus within a matter of 12 or 14 hours. Also, what do they see when the Prime Minister says he rolled the dice as we have heard about so much.
When the First Ministers were brought to Ottawa they were physically beaten down with tiredness. After seven days and seven nights-we all saw it on TV-those of us who were not allowed to witness those meetings, saw those men were so physically exhausted that you could almost see them at the point of saying, I'll sign anything, I'll do anything, just let me go home to bed, please. What do these other countries feel and think when they see such things in our country?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have one or two comments that I would like to make in response to that question.
The first is, I think the hon. member will admit that she exaggerates and she, perhaps unwittingly, makes comments that are insulting and demeaning to the Premiers of the country. They are elected leaders of their provinces. They are accustomed to pressure. If she stays here longer, she will grow more accustomed to pressure too. They are accustomed to pressure and they are accustomed to making decisions under that kind of pressure. They did that. Theirs is not a leisurely life. Nor is the procedure of making decisions at federal-provincial conferences in private, a new procedure. It is the procedure that has, in fact, prevailed for some veiy long time.
The second comment that I would make responds directly to the question that she asked. I cannot answer for Nelson Mandela but let me quote a leading Canadian, Paul Desmarais, who has had experience not only in this country, but around the world. I do not always quote him with approval, but he said, the other day, that he wished the citizens of Canada would show the same respect for this nation that foreigners do.
Government Orders
Yes, it is true that there are imperfections in this country. It is true that there are faults in the way this House of Commons works. It is true that our democracy works imperfectly. It is true that we need to have changes. It is also true that the system here is better than what it was. It is not what it should be but it is better than what it was. It is true that there is a serious problem in the country, a serious lack of a national will that can bring people together. In part, that is because people define their constituencies too narrowly. In part, that is because people who come from one part of Canada speak only for that part of Canada and not for the whole nation. In part, it is because we are too focused upon narrow interests and not enough upon the larger interests.
My part of Canada and hers would not be as strong as it wants to be without the context of the whole country. Special interests that too often define and narrow debate in this country, would not be preserved as much as they need to be, without a whole nation that is marked by tolerance and by growth. Those are some of the questions that are at issue. She and I will disagree about particular instruments that might be used. We do not disagree about the fact that there is a distemper in the country that must be addressed. I hope that she will try, as I will try, to rise above party affiliations, to rise above particular commitments that we might think we have, to look at the whole country. That is what I ask the members of the House of Assembly of Newfoundland and Labrador and Manitoba to do tonight.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
I would simply like to say to the right honourable minister that his experience and reputation with regard to national unity are already well established. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is the one who has listened to and understood for the longest time the wishes of official language minority groups. He established in 1979 the House Committee on Official Languages, and I would like to thank him for that and tell him how useful this committee has been to advance the cause of linguistic minorities. I would also like to tell him that his speech deeply moved me. With regard to the exercise we are or will be completing within a few days, it is for us Canadians the first time we are going through the exercise of amending our Constitution. This is the first

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
time since its patriation in 1982 that Canadians are called to amend substantially the Constitution of this country. Like him, I regret very much that in 1982 the process was flawed and that Quebec did not feel welcome.
Today, we have a provision inviting Quebec to join the Canadian family by signing this resolution or constitutional amendment. Since I am deeply concerned as he is that we might be living the last hours of a very important and misunderstood process, I would like to ask him here in this House how he sees the Canada of tomorrow. I know it is not easy, but is he seeing a united Canada on June 24 and 25? Is he seeing a Canada whose elements stick together, a Canada respectful of minority groups, a Canada without resentment nor hate towards anyone? If Meech lake fails, does he think that Canada will say on June 24 or 25: This is how it happened, there is nothing we can do about it! Or, is he, like me, preoccupied by the seriousness of the matter and does he try, as I know he does, to explain to all Canadians that this is a critical time for Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the tone and substance of my honorable friend's remarks. The answer depends on the results of the vote in Newfoundland, Labrador, and Manitoba. I hope it will be a success, I believe it will be a success. But it is not the end of all things. Among the things we have experienced and discovered these last few months, there is, in the first place, the fact that some of our achievements are not shared strongly enough throughout the country. I think, and I am not speaking as a minister but for myself, we must reexamine our own ideas on the country. We must do it in a really open way. It is time to speak again of national objectives for Canada, of objectives which can reunify all Canadians, but we have to do it in the context of the profound changes which await us in our country and internationally.
I remember, if I may be allowed a partisan recollection, a time in the life of the party in which I have worked my life when just after the debate on the flag when my party was deeply divided, when it risked becoming a captive of the past. Leaders in the party at that time had
the sense to draw our membership together to focus on what was then called a national conference on Canadian goals, not to talk about what we had been, but to talk about what we could become.
The party of the hon. member underwent a similar experience in Kingston after the election of 1958. It may be in this time of such disrespect for our political parties there is a lesson that the country can learn from them. It may be that it is time for us now, together and without agendas written in advance, without too many assumptions, to try together in this country to define what the national goals of this country as we enter the next century should be.
As the hon. member will know, whatever doubts one might have in Canada about our good fortune, those doubts are not held elsewhere in the world. Our imperfections are known. If they are not known, my friend from Spadina will raise them in the House of Commons and others will, which is part of our democracy. Our faults are known. Our weaknesses are known. But there is no question that we have both the responsibility to establish leadership in the world and an extraordinary opportunity to demonstrate that people of differences and people of genius can build things together.
I think that is a goal that is worthy of the next century of Canadians. I believe that that is a goal that Canadians in this House of Commons of all parties would want to pursue. I do not see the Meech Lake debate as ending things. I do not see this, in fact, as a constitutional question. I think this is a question that has to do with the purpose and the nature of the country.
While these months have been terribly difficult for all of us, I think that they may well have driven us more quickly than we might otherwise have arrived to face that reality and to undertake that kind of searching of the soul of this country, that attempt to define what it is we want to become that is overdue.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which is before us tonight urges the legislative assemblies of Manitoba and Newfoundland, and I quote from the motion, to:
- exert efforts to bring about full ratification of the Constitution Amendment, 1987 -
That is the Meech accord.
-by June 23, 1990 -
June 20, 1990

In this motion we are not discussing once more the value of the Meech accord. We will not be voting on an approval or disapproval of the Meech accord, nor will we be discussing or debating the value of the new accords reached on June 9 after a long week of discussion by the First Ministers of this country. No, we are not discussing those new accords either.
What we are discussing here today is a plea from this House to the legislative assemblies of Manitoba and Newfoundland that they pass as quickly as possible the Meech accord.
Why is such a motion necessary before this House? Does the government doubt the good intentions of the political leaders in Manitoba and Newfoundland? Why is this motion necessary?
Mr. Speaker, to fully understand this motion I think we have to look at it in conjunction with, first of all, Senator Murray's expedition to Manitoba on Monday when he preached to the aboriginal leaders of that province and to the legislators in their provincial assembly.
We also have to look at this motion in conjunction with the answers that the Prime Minister gave to questions in this House yesterday when he also put the blame for the situation which the country is in on the backs of the political leaders of Manitoba. As far as I can determine, the purpose of this motion is an attempt by the Prime Minister to re-establish his credibility because of the mess we are in, the fact that he caused a lot of that mess, and to shift the burden to other individuals.
If there is a constitutional crisis in this country today, and I believe there is one, it is principally due to the cynical and scheming actions of the Prime Minister.
According to the interview that he gave to The Globe and Mail on June 11, he admitted that he deliberately delayed the calling of a First Ministers' Conference in what appears to be an attempt to create a pressure cooker atmosphere. It worked to a certain extent. It certainly worked to the extent that he was able to get an agreement on the night of June 9, an agreement that all premiers signed, some of them conditionally. We now see that that agreement was fraught with great difficulties, in particular the procedures required in several of the provincial legislatures.
Government Orders
Here we have a Prime Minister who waited to the last possible moment to call the First Ministers together. Despite repeated calls from members of the opposition parties in this House and from the Premiers of several provinces, including Manitoba and Newfoundland, who said to the Prime Minister that they needed time to steer corrective or add-on resolutions through their legislatures. But no, the Prime Minister took a casual approach. He said that all was well, that the three legislatures in Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Manitoba would pass the accord as it was, that no change was necessary, that no First Ministers' Conference was necessary. It is now clear that he was wrong.
I hope that the accord will still be passed, but the crisis we are now in was not necessary. If the Prime Minister had called the First Ministers together last year when many of these issues were known, or at the latest in January, February or even March of this year, rather than on June 3, there would have been time to work out the difficulties that we see today, difficulties with respect to aboriginal peoples, with respect to women, and with respect to the Charter of Rights.
The Prime Minister, until Premier McKenna, made his proposals in March, was totally inflexible and arrogant. Worse still, we now find that he almost plotted and planned the delay in calling the First Ministers together, as he said, to roll the dice on the right day, all of which is set out in the article in The Globe and Mail of June 11.
There is also in the attitude shown by Senator Murray, the Prime Minister, and some other members of the government, an attitude that parliaments and legislators do not really count. What really counts is the executive side of the government. In other words, if the premier signs, that is it, it should be done, that there should not be time for adequate debate and discussion, that rules in parliamentary systems are not really necessary. If it is necessary, you suspend them. Well, we know that this government is probably the worst for that sort of thing in the history of Canada. According to my records, this government has imposed closure 34 times since 1984, which is more than any other government prior to 1984 going back to Confederation.
This government also day after day suspends the rules. If they feel they do not want to listen to petitions from hon. members, they just suspend the rules and move that we go right past them into other business. Senator Murray is up in that other place, but he was preaching to the people in Manitoba the other day. They have this attitude that procedures, rules, traditions, parliaments, and legislative assemblies are not really important.

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
Those rules and procedures are there to protect the liberties of members of the House of Commons, in particular members of opposition parties and independent members. There is a reason for those rules, and you do not suspend them without reason.
When we go back to the beginning, we see that after he was elected to office Premier Bourassa of Quebec made five proposals, five demands which he thought were necessary for Quebec to sign the Constitution of 1982, and all parties in this House agreed to those five proposals. I agreed. My political party agreed. We all agreed. Those proposals, of course, then were agreed to at the first Meech Lake conference by all the provincial premiers, and they signed a document to that effect.
It was only after the document was written up in legal language, when those five proposals agreed to were put into legal language, that some objections began to arise. Objections arose because while people agreed to the five proposals they saw impacts that the document made on other areas of Canadian life and on other Canadians that were not expected, and they did not want those sort of impacts. While they agreed to the five proposals, they did not want any other rights or traditions reduced.
There was also objection because many Canadians, and especially the aboriginal Canadians, felt that things were left out that should have been put in. Canadians who came here from other countries, other than Britain and France, thought that they should be recognized in some way or other. There were objections to the way in which the Meech Lake Accord was drafted and the way it impacted on other things and what was left out.
This is the sad part of this whole debate: individuals, parliamentarians, and legislators objected from time to time to the Meech Lake Accord, but it never meant that they were against Quebec, or against the legitimate aspirations of Quebec, or that they were against Quebec as a distinct society. No, they supported those things, but they wanted their own rights, their own qualities, and
their own expressions protected in the Constitution as well.
During the debate in 1987 the Liberal Party put forward nine amendments to the accord. They were all defeated by the government. They were not even listened to seriously. They were defeated. They were tried once again in the Senate. They were defeated once more. For most of us in the Liberal Party-and this was the official position of this party-despite the flaws, despite the inadequacies in the Meech Lake Accord, we thought it was best to vote for it for the greater good of this country and for the unity of the country. I was one of those who voted for it. I felt that what I did was right then and I support my position, although I still feel that the accord has flaws.
Once the debate was over in this House and the accord was passed by eight of the ten provincial legislatures, the discussion went on. It went on in New Brunswick. It went on in Manitoba. It went on among Canadians throughout the country, many of whom were not satisfied with the accord, continued to campaign against it, and wanted amendments.
Despite the fact that questions were raised in this House, demands were made of the Prime Minister and of other ministers to do something about the impasse that was continuing in Manitoba, in New Brunswick, and later in Newfoundland because Newfoundland rescinded its agreement to the accord. There were continuous demands of the Prime Minister to go out there, to call the premiers together, to do something to break the impasse, to consider some amendments, to be flexible, and to make some changes that would meet the aspirations and the requirements of other communities in Canada. Nothing was done.
Time went by, month after month, until March of this year when Premier McKenna tabled a resolution in his own House to provide for a companion accord. He proposed that we accept the Meech Lake Accord fully as it was, but he put forward another accord which would add on other provisions to satisfy the criticisms that were being made by certain Canadians.
Following that, the Prime Minister set up the Charest committee which studied Mr. McKenna's proposals and other alternatives. The blockage started to come undone and everybody was happy. Those of us who wanted to see
June 20, 1990

the country united were quite happy and pleased with some movement forward, all of a sudden, to save the accord, to save the country, and to meet the aspirations of Canadians who were not happy with the accord.
What seemed to make many of us in this party happy was that the recommendations of the Charest committee of this House contained many of the proposals that we had in our amendments of 1987. Many of the things that we said were necessary in 1987 were recognized in April 1990 as being essential to get the Meech Lake Accord through.
We know the history. Finally the Prime Minister calls the First Ministers to supper on June 3. They sit in a pressure cooker atmosphere for one week, in private, with most Canadians not knowing what was being proposed and counterproposed. They came up with the two companion accords of June 9.
We in the Liberal Party feel vindicated to a certain extent, because once again many of the provisions in these companion accords were similar to the amendments we made in 1987.
Once again those of us who loved this country and wanted it to stay united were quite pleased with the results. We did not like the process. We did not like the way it was done, but we were happy to see all the provincial premiers and the Government of Canada agreeing on how to resolve the crisis.
As I said, now we are faced with the procedures in the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba. We see that we have only three days left to meet the deadline. The Prime Minister is putting pressure, and it seems putting the blame for that situation, on the leaders of Manitoba and the leaders of Newfoundland. I think that is wrong.
The fact of the matter is that one year, two years, two and a half years went by when something could be done to resolve the differences and to resolve the pleas of many Canadians with respect to the accord. Nothing was done. Unfortunately, it was left to the last minute. I think the Prime Minister and the government must take responsibility for that. If the Prime Minister had not been so inflexible, the process which led to the Charest committee and to the companion accords of June 9 could have been done at an earlier date.
Government Orders
Then again we have the situation with our aboriginal people. As I said, the other day Senator Murray rushed to Manitoba with a six-point program. As a former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, I examined that program. It looks very good to me, but to expect our aboriginal people to be presented with six proposals in the morning and to give an answer at the end of that day, or even the next day, is totally unacceptable.
Our aboriginal peoples have been betrayed over and over again by governments in Canada, both federal and provincial. Even when we have put our signatures to paper on treaties and other documents, we have done the very opposite of what we said we were going to do. One can easily understand how our aboriginal people could look on those six points put forward by Senator Murray on Monday as something of a Trojan horse.
Their experience has led them to believe that they cannot trust us. They are suspicious of every sort of proposal that we make to them. Even when it looks as good as a Trojan horse, they do not want to accept it right away. They want to look at it over and over again. They want to discuss it with their own people. They want to know what it will really do for them. Why at the last minute are those proposals, as good as they might be, being put forward to the aboriginal people of this country?
Even in the companion accords of June 9, all that was given to the aboriginal people was the right to have more First Ministers' Conferences with respect to their issues. On June 9, the aboriginal people only got promises of more constitutional conferences. On June 18, they got a six-point program but no time to consider it as a people should be able to do. We have to remember that most of the associations and tribal councils in this country do not have the resources behind them that the Government of Canada has. The do not have the lawyers, the accountants, and the specialists to examine and look at those things in the same way the Government has, so when they are up against the government of Canada they react with suspicion and with doubt.
Another area where the Prime Minister bears a lot of responsibility with respect to the situation we are in is the way he went about this country promoting a disaster scenario with respect to the Meech accord.

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
How many times have I heard the Prime Minister say to those who in good faith put forward or suggested amendments to the accord: "Why are you against the province of Quebec? If you defeat this accord as it is, you will drive Quebec out of Confederation" or words to that effect.
Either you do it this way or there will be a constitutional crisis; therefore you had better do it this way and no change is possible. By repeating that over and over again-and some of his ministers did the same thing-it led Quebecers to believe that the Meech accord was absolutely essential for them, that if they did not get it their province would be in ruin, and that it would be an insult to their province.
I have spoken to many Quebecers. They have not read the accord, but the accord has become a symbol for something much greater than the contents of the accord itself. It is like a flag. It represents the following for many Quebecers: if you are for the accord you are for Quebec; if you are against it you are against Quebec. There is no consideration for the fact that most of the provisions in the accord apply to all the provinces, not just to Quebec.
The Prime Minister by his rhetoric over the last three years in trying to get provinces and individuals to support the accord went so far that he created this disaster scenario. Now we are faced with a disaster because it is not being approved in the manner which he would like and which I would like.
He threatened those who opposed. Those who questioned and wanted amendments he accused of rejecting Quebec.
I want to make it very clear that many people who accepted the five proposals of Premier Bourassa, including the distinct society, were quite ready to agree to most of the Meech accord but simply wanted changes that would take into account their own special place in Canada.
As an anglophone Quebecer, if I can call myself that, I have never had any problem with the distinct society. I accept totally that Quebec is a distinct society. It is the only jurisdiction in all of North America with a majority of French speaking people. We have the civil law. In Canada we collect our own income tax. We do not use
the RCMP, nor does Ontario, as a provincial police force. There are many other distinctive qualities. This goes back to 1774 in the Quebec Act when the British recognized Quebec in a very distinctive way as opposed to other colonies in their colonial empire.
There is a long tradition of recognizing distinctive features about Quebec. Some Canadians say: "Well, other provinces have distinctive traits as well." That is true, but some people are not anxious that their distinctiveness be recognized and others are not anxious that-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us is about nothing less than the fate of our country. No one should underestimate the seriousness and urgency of our situation.
One thing I heard consistently as I crossed this country was the clear, unequivocal statement by all Canadians of how important it is for us to stay together, to stay whole, to stay unified. How good we feel as Canadians, how proud we are, how respectful we are of the kind of nation we have become, the nation of freedom and opportunity.
Mr. Speaker, through this very difficult period that many of us have lived one thing was very clear. The situation had to be addressed and addressed with a great degree of urgency. The time for healing had really come upon us. We really had to start coming back together in a very important manner. This is not a time for procrastination, it is a time for decision. The Fathers of Confederation faced the same challenge 123 years ago when the very idea of Canada was tested.

Different leaders, different parties and different provinces, but they all understood that the great nation they were looking for simply could not be unless there was a will to compromise.

Our greatest successes have been achieved when we put Canada first. . .first in our hearts. No obligation is more compelling than the duty we have to this great nation of ours. Canada is a precious land of boundless energy and promise.
June 20,1990

My family came to Canada and made Montreal their home. They raised me to value my heritage, to seize the promise of Canada and to cherish Quebec. I am an anglophone Quebecer. I have lived all my life in Quebec. I have seen all the changes that have occurred in that time, along with the emergence of a new Quebec. I have also lived through the moments of tension and crisis. I cannot forget the presence of troops on the streets just 20 years ago. These memories are etched in my memory forever. I cannot speak for all Quebecers, but if you ask me if Quebec should be called a "distinct society", how can I answer anything but yes. Quebec is a "distinct society". It is a fact and an integral part of that distinctiveness is, as the Meech Lake agreement makes absolutely clear, the anglophone Quebecer.
My riding of Pierrefonds-Dollard is a microcosm of Canada. My neighbourhood, half English-speaking and half French speaking, with people of origins from all over the world, ask me to send their message to the legislators and the people of Manitoba, Newfoundland and Labrador. They say: Put Canada first, protect and defend this glorious and magnificent country of ours.

Canadians everywhere convey the same message and keep saying: Together, we will go far!
Mr. Speaker, constitutional speeches may help promote unity, but it cannot be achieved unless people have confidence.
Quebecers sought our confidence when they said no to independence and yes to renewed federalism. With the Meech Lake Accord we wanted to express that confidence to honour Quebec and Quebecers, and to enable them to regain their dignity and their place in Confederation.
But this promise has yet to be fulfilled and time is running short.

Now, more than at any other moment in our history, we must keep our faith with each other. Only then, can we go forward to build a new, vital and dynamic Canada of the 21st century. The world is watching us. They witnessed our evolution as a nation, one that stands firmly on the side of justice, fairness and of freedom. Nelson Mandela appreciated this and so should we all. We cannot throw away all that we have built and all that we can be. We must not fail our own ideals. We must not
Government Orders
compromise ourselves by pursuing anything less than the excellence which only a strong united Canada can achieve. Across the continents and around the world, the gentle breeze of liberty is blowing. Old walls, old barriers and prejudices are being dismantled, not by powerful dictators and their armies, but by ordinary people. This is the world of Lech Walesa, Vaclav Havel and Nelson Mandela. In this dawning of a new era, hope lives. Today, civilization cries out, not for a narrow, limited view, but for generosity, understanding and true vision.
We are at a crossroads. Down one road, the high road, lie unity, prosperity and greatness. Down the other, the narrow road, we and our children face division, intolerance and despair. That high road is beckoning us now. It is the only choice we can make.
We have so much to offer each other. Together we can continue to build a strong foundation of courage and hope for all Canadians. We can continue to free our society from the shackles of bigotry and racism and advance the noble cause of equality. Is it possible that we have forgotten all that unites us? Have we forgotten what makes us unique among all the nations of the world; our two official languages, our aboriginal heritage, our multicultural fabric, our dedication to peace and human rights, and our caring and tolerant traditions. These are among our proudest achievements, achievements which set us apart and which can lead us to excellence. They are what make our Canadian citizenship among the most sought after in all the world.
The Prime Minister told this House a few days ago what is at stake. He said: "There is a new world to be won. Canada needs to turn the page, at last, on a long, controversial and crucial period-we need to recapture the sense of tolerance and common interest and common purpose that lies at the root of our success as a nation".
For me, our greatest duty as Canadians now is to truly know and accept each other better. Wherever we live, wherever we come from, we are all Canadians. We have worked to build a house of freedom and compassion, with a strong foundation to support newcomers from all over the world. Ours is an "open house", to every culture and every origin, where equality and justice are a promise made to each other. Erecting barriers of ignorance or fear is not the Canadian way. Instead, we build bridges to truth and understanding. Our tradition is to heal wounds, to correct injustices and to right wrongs.

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
There is only one way to dispel fears and misconceptions in a democratic society. It is to reach out to individual Canadians of good faith. It is to stand up and be counted and not to yield to lesser obstacles. Canada is more than earth and mountain and stone. Canada is a state of mind, a quality of life.

Mr. Speaker, the motion now before the House is a strong appeal to the two legislatures to maintain confidence in Canadian unity.

We respect those legislatures and the people they represent. We acknowledge legitimate concerns and aspirations. We have pledged that they will be addressed fairly and resolved speedily. Once again, as has been the Canadian way, we ask that trust be exchanged for trust.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier called Canadians to that duty a century ago. Speaking in Quebec City, he said, and I quote:
What this countty needs above all is peace, concord and union between all the elements composing its population. Let us show to the world that if we reverence the past, we also have regard for the future. Let us show to the world that unity does not mean absorption, and that autonomy does not mean antagonism.. .and in all the vicissitudes of our situation, let us always remember that love is better than hatred and faith better than doubt, and let hope in our future destinies be the pillar of fire to guide us in our career.
Let us all be faithful to that duty in the hours to come. That is our answer, our only real choice.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue we are discussing today is among the most difficult that Canadians can face or that Parliamentarians can ever have to deal with. It is an issue which must be beyond partisan politics, because it is an issue which divides parties. It divides families. Canadians are not united on the issue about which we speak.
The Constitution is probably one of the most difficult of all issues we have had to face throughout our history and, indeed, our Constitution has been an issue that has been with us since before Confederation and will be with us for many years to come.
Let us look, however, just at the recent history, the past decade. I was there, as were many many members of this House, when the referendum of 1980 was being decided. I went to Quebec at that time to fight to keep Quebec in Canada. Part of the promise delivered by those who voted against separation, the promise of those who were fighting to keep Canada united, was that Quebec would have a renewed federalism. This manifested itself in the Constitution accord which a separatist premier of Quebec refused to sign. It manifested itself in the Meech Lake Accord, which all 10 premiers and the federal government signed. Then it manifested itself in the companion agreement signed just recently.
This companion accord made changes to the Meech Lake Accord in an effort to deal with some of the problems contained in it. Canadians had many concerns about Meech Lake, and the First Ministers, having heard these concerns, met. All of those concerns were represented at the table. This is why the companion accord was signed, dealing with these issues in a way that Mrs. Carstairs, Mr. Doer and Mr. McKenna, who had previously been opposed to Meech Lake, were able to give their support to the package.
We recognize, on all sides of this House, that this may not be the perfect package. It does not have all the answers to all of our constitutional problems, but is merely one step in a process of constitutional reform.
Probably, most of the debate over Meech Lake has focused on the so-called distinct society clause for Quebec. It is simply a recognition of Quebec's unique problems as the home in Canada of the largest portion of Canada's francophones, francophones who are still in a minority in Canada. It is a recognition that they have different cultures and different institutions which have been part of the Confederation agreement for more than 123 years.
But this distinct society clause has caused much anguish. I believe that the companion accord has dealt with it in a responsible manner. They have attached a legal opinion from some of the best jurisprudential minds in Canada saying that the distinct society clause does not overrule individual charter rights.
June 20,1990

I may be accused of some bias, Mr. Speaker, but I could not help but be impressed by the words this morning of the Premier of Ontario when he spoke to Newfoundland.
He indicated there that even if this legal opinion were wrong and at some point in our future it were held that it could be used to impinge on certain individual rights, it could only be done in the province of Quebec. It would only be Quebec legislation which, in furtherance of protecting its unique and distinct status, might be able to overrule certain charter rights at a certain point.
Quebec is a province that wants the distinct society. The distinct clause is also supported by the major leading women's group in Quebec, so who are we to say that even if our legal opinion were wrong, that Quebec should not be able to determine certain rights to protect its own distinct francophone status.
A lot has happened that is causing us dismay. Bill 178 and the use of the notwithstanding clause were not appreciated by the rest of Canada. There is some evidence that some Canadians want to get even. Even the Premier of Manitoba changed his mind about Meech Lake after Bill 178 was passed.
Maybe we can criticize Quebec, but surely let us look at the signals we have been giving to Quebec: tramping on the flag in Brockville; Ontario municipalities passing English only by-laws. What signal does this send to a people who are Canadian, who are our brothers and sisters?
Quebec has said yes to Canada three times in this decade: once at the time of the referendum, once at Meech Lake, and once on the companion accord. How many more times is Quebec going to say yes to Canada if Canada says no to Quebec?
The political reality is that if there were an election in Quebec and Mr. Parizeau were elected, Quebec would be leaving Canada. He has said that he is there not to keep Canada united, but to break up Canada.
There is a symbolic mythology, apart from its meaning, which pervades the whole Meech question. It has come to be a symbol of whether we want Canada to stay together, whether we are prepared to say yes to Quebec after it has said yes to Canada three times in this decade.
Government Orders
Do we know with certainty whether Quebec voters will reject a separatist alternative? Can we say for certain that they will come back to the table? Can we afford as a nation to start this process all over again? Should we not be getting on with other issues as well, not only the companion accords and further enhancements to our constitutional process, but dealing with the severe economic challenges we face?
We have so much to do. Perhaps in the past we have said that in Canada our unity was founded on the rail from coast to coast. But perhaps we have put too much stake in ribbons of wood and steel and not enough in the great human spirit of humanity, sharing and caring about our nation. Together we can be strong.
The risk of not standing up for this accord is enormous.
