speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a certain emotion that I am addressing this House tonight. So far I am the only francophone outside Quebec who has had the opportunity to take part in this debate.
I listened carefully to the speeches made by some of my colleagues, the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Secretary of State who, as usual, has enriched this House with his eloquence. I must say that I share many of his feelings. It is perhaps unusual for us to talk this way about our colleagues opposite but that is what is called for today, I think.
Mr. Speaker, ever since I was a kid, I have been hearing about our national unity and how it is threatened. I remember very well the October crisis of 1970, the election of the Parti Quebecois in 1976 and the fears it gave rise to, the 1980 referendum on the future of Quebec and all of Canada and, let us not forget this component of the referendum, the patriation of the Canadian Constitution in 1982, that I had hoped for and agreed with, and finally the defeat of the Parti Quebecois in Quebec and the renewed interest in national unity not only in Quebec but throughout Canada.

June 20, 1990
Government Orders

We in this Parliament did not invent the subject of discussing our Constitution. Canada has had 24 constitutional documents, Orders in Council, Acts of the British Parliament, Acts of our Parliament. I want to take a moment and describe perhaps a component of one of these acts, namely, the Statute of Westminster of 1931, which, after all, is the law that gave this country its independence over foreign affairs and its independence generally.
At that time Canada, New Zealand and Australia were granted this independence. We in this country, of course, could not take advantage of all that was given to us and all that we had earned at that time. We could not do it because we had not yet resolved a difficulty within our own country as to how it was that we would amend our Constitution in the future and how we would deal with such issues as constitutional amendments. So our constitution stayed in Britain.
I suppose in typical Canadian form of compromise and sometimes delay, 51 years later it finally came home. That was a very historic day, April 17, 1982. I was a member of the Ontario legislature at that time, a brand new member, and I had the privilege of viewing, like many other Canadians, what was happening before us on that great historical day. Of course, many of us said at that time that it was not over, and it certainly was not. We were back almost immediately talking about constitutions again.
On April 30, 1987, the First Ministers of our country, the Prime Minister and his provincial colleagues signed the Meech Lake Accord. I was watching television that night when I heard of the signing of the accord. I was really taken by the fact that, at last, we would see an end to some of the disagreements that we had had. I was so optimistic and so pleased, not only for myself but for my family, for my children and for my country.
Within a few days things looked as though they were unravelling again, but finally they got back on track and on June 3, the Langevin document was signed, if that is what we call that document. Let us call it that for the purposes of this discussion.
Then I became very optimistic again, as I think all Canadians were, about the process and the possibility of
putting this national unity issue finally behind us and working towards the great potential that we have as a nation.
We in this House, after much debate and some difficulty-difficulty within my own political party and all political parties and I do not think that we were the only ones who had difficulty-adopted this accord. It was adopted in the other place and then finally it had to be adopted again by this House. It was adopted by legislatures right across the country save and except two. Then there was the subsequent withdrawal of a ratification. We got to a point that was what I would call very close to that eleventh hour. The concern then heightened.
Constituents of mine in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell a few weeks ago were having very serious reflections on just where we were and where we were going.

My constituents, Mr. Speaker-and I know I have the privilege of representing a special riding, almost surrounded by Quebec, but still an Ontario riding where French-speaking people are in a majority-worried about their future, the future of Quebec and the future of the whole of Canada.

The electors I represent understood one point very well. Perhaps not all of us in this House and in other legislatures, or even some Canadians understood the following point. Heaven forbid that this country were ever to become divided by the withdrawal of one of the provinces, namely Quebec. It would not only be Quebec withdrawing from the rest of the country, but a big component of the country would not be there. There is no question Canada would not be a member of the G-7 group of nations without 25 per cent of its population, a great proportion of its riches and everything else that would be gone if that were to happen.
It is not just one part of the country that loses, Mr. Speaker. The whole country would lose were that to happen. It is you and I and everyone out there listening to the House of Commons debates tonight, all Canadians. Perhaps some regions of the country would suffer financially more than others. I do not know. But very few, if any, would ever gain from that kind of proposition and disunity.
June 20,1990



Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not saying either that if the accord is not ratified this is the end of it all. This would be irresponsible on my part. What we have to do is try our best to ratify, and encourage others to ratify the Meech Lake Accord. As far as we are concerned, in this House, it is done. We are not being asked, tonight, to ratify the accord, but simply to urge others to do it, as agreed between the various government leaders.
Mr. Speaker, if all Canadians do this kind of soul searching about our future, I am convinced they will realize, as I did, not that the agreement is perfect, it is not-however, the previous one was not perfect either, nor the one before it-they will realize that having amended our Constitution so often, having had that kind of debate in the past, we will continue to do so in the future.

In conclusion, let us remember that this accord is not the end of constitutional discussion, it is merely a component of the continuing process. We have had discussions in the past.
Let us pass this accord. I hope that it passes. If it does not, I do not want to pretend that it will be the end of the world. That would be irresponsible. We will all have to work together after June 23, pick up the pieces and try to build again. I am sure that we would. I am confident that we would. But why at this point would we want to risk it. This is no time to play Russian roulette with the future of our country.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today with a very grave concern in my heart about the future of Canada, the future of this country. I have heard people say that those of us who have that concern are fearmongering. I cannot believe that anybody could characterize the concern that all of us feel here in this House and across this great nation as fearmongering because there is ample reason for that concern.
I believe that those who raise the spectre that fearmongering by raising concerns is counterproductive to this process are putting their heads in the sand and misunderstand the very deep feelings in Quebec and the gravity of the situation with which we are faced. Those who would say that our concern is fearmongering are doing a disservice to this country.
Government Orders
I believe that we in Canada right now are at a crossroads of choice. Either we can open our minds and our hearts and generously embrace our future as one Canada, one single country, one entity, a Canada that is rich in diversity but bound by a common determination to survive against sometimes incredible odds or we can continue to pursue a debate that will only lead us to a mean and bitter end, an end not worthy of the country that we have come to expect Canada will be in the future and has been in the past.
During the recent discussions at the Congress Centre in Ottawa, some wise soul in the audience made a sign which read very simply: "Nine plus one equals ten. Ten minus one equals zero". No more words need to be said because I believe with all my heart that that is so. We cannot have a Canada that lacks a great and vast geographic part of our country and still have a Canada that is a Canada at all.
In Manitoba, where I come from, the skies are clear and wide, bright and blue and to me they symbolize the spirit of the people of Manitoba. I believe that Manitobans are warm. I know that Manitobans are generous. I have watched as Manitobans over the years have embraced new ideas and other cultures with gladness and with joy. Manitobans, I also know, love this country with a great profundity and they want to see it stay together more than anything else in the world. I also believe that Newfoundlanders want the same and have the same warmth and generosity of spirit in their hearts.
So what are we to do about this awful pickle that we are in? How are we going to solve the dilemma that we find ourselves faced with? I do not believe that the way to do it is by attributing blame. History will take care of that, if there is any blame to be attributed.
Instead, we have to search actively for answers, for solutions that will keep this country together. That is our job as leaders and we cannot rely on process to substitute for that responsibility either.
We must exercise the leadership that has been vested in us by the people of Canada, be it at the federal level or at the provincial level, or wherever it might be. If it is only the leadership of a group or a society, we must

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
exercise that leadership, too, to find a way out of this dilemma that we are in.
There comes a time when personal political fortunes and personal political dreams become very insignificant in the greater scheme of things when we are faced with something like this. There also comes a time when heavy though the mantle of leadership might be, it must be borne bravely, or it must be cast aside and left for others to pick up and carry on.
The Meech Lake Accord is a simple document. There is nothing terribly complex about it. It is an affirmative document. It is a positive document. It says yes in almost every line. It says yes to the aspirations of seven million Canadians first of all. It says yes to the federal government in the matter of the spending power. It also says yes to the provinces and it respects our diversity and our differences in the same manner. It says yes to the provinces on the question of immigration. It says yes to the provinces in the matter of having a veto. It says yes to the provinces on the matter of appointing judges and senators.
I cannot think of a single thing in the accord that says no to anyone in this country. In fact, the accord even says yes to those who are not mentioned in the Constitution at this time. It says yes to those who have constitutional aspirations for the future because it is only by completing the unfinished business of 1982 and by embracing Quebec and bringing Quebec back into the circle of Confederation that other reforms can be initiated; other reforms that will allow Canada to say yes to those who have constitutional aspirations.
It is a simple fact that we cannot undertake any other constitutional reform until Quebec is brought back into the circle of Confederation.
Aboriginal concerns about constitutional recognition cannot take place without ratification of the accord. The addition of other recognitions must also wait until the accord is ratified. We cannot deal with things like Senate reform, if we determine in the future that that is what we want to do, until Quebec is back in the Constitution.
So why would we not want to do everything that is humanly possible to achieve that simple goal, to bring our country back together, to knit it into one 10-province family with two territories waiting in the wings, looking for a future that they will develop and be able to reach
and aspire to in a whole and complete Canada. Why would we not want to do everything within our means, within our reach, to ultimately accomplish that goal?
If the accord is the affirmative statement that I really believe it to be, why would we ever want to turn it down? Why would we not want to say yes immediately, openly, freely, and hold out our arms and embrace the opportunity that is afforded to us here today.
I cannot believe that we are so narrow and so warped in some sort of selfish dissatisfaction-maybe we are overfed, maybe we are over rich, or maybe we are over lucky, but I do not believe that we are so steeped in that kind of narrowness that we cannot endorse a document that I understand most deeply to be a confirmation of everything that we hold dear as Canadians. It is confirmation of all those things that we like to think of ourselves as being: open-hearted, generous, warm, kind, tolerant. Canadians have a conceit that we are all those things, and I have that conceit as well. But if they are true, if indeed that is what we are and that is how we see ourselves, and if that is what our identity is, then how can we turn down this opportunity to use that character to embrace the very simple aspirations of Quebec and get on with running the country?
I believe in my deepest heart that we are all those things. So it is with the utmost astonishment that I have watched the debate these past 16 months over something that is so generous-spirited as the inclusion of the distinct society designation for the one province that by its very existence lends so much to the roots of that Canadian character that I just spoke of. It is because of Quebec, because of the fact that a country had to learn to live with differences at a very early stage in its development that we have that conceit of being tolerant, open, generous and kind.
Oddly enough, nobody else seems to disagree that Quebec is indeed a distinct society. As a matter of fact, I have listened one after another to provincial leaders across this country tell us that Quebec is a distinct society, and that they agree that is so. That includes premiers who are having difficulties right at this moment.
What appears to bother us is the fact that somebody wants to write it down. We want to write the words "distinct society" and to us in English Canada that sends
June 20, 1990

a thrill of fear to the very core of our being and we believe that will have some negative impact on us.
This might be understandable. In the weeks that I spent travelling across the country with the Charest committee, I came to understand something about us in Canada that I did not understand before. This discussion about two Canadas, the two solitudes, two nations, is not only steeped in language, although we often point to language as being the one to blame, it also is based on the fact that we have two very distinct approaches to the way we do business in our provinces and the way we deal with the business of writing laws and rules.
English Canada lives by the common law, the unwritten law, the rule of the understatement. We have a profound and deep understanding that what is not written down sometimes means more than what is.
French Canada lives by the civil law, the written law, which demands that things be written down, because if they are not in writing they have no legal meaning. Those people are steeped in that cultural understanding. It goes very deep.
It seems to me that these two ideas are at the veiy centre of the discussion about the distinct society and they come into conflict time after time after time.
I believe that this is what was at the root of the western premier's insistence in 1982 on the inclusion of the very much maligned notwithstanding clause. It seems to me that Mr. Lyon and Mr. Lougheed were also steeped in their very deep understanding of the unwritten law and they feared being hemmed in by the words in the Charter of Rights.
In fact, is there anything to fear from the words "distinct society"? I have every profound belief that there is nothing to fear in those words.
In fact, at this very moment, if the Supreme Court were to be studying a matter of the Constitution, they would take into consideration the fact that Quebec is a distinct society in making a judgment. They did so when they handed down their decision about the signage law in Quebec. The words "distinct society" were written into their decision when they said that while both languages must be placed on the signs, French could take precedence and English could appear in smaller type.
Government Orders
People also seem to worry that the distinct society will give Quebec an advantage over other provinces. That simply is not true.
It states what is a fact: Quebec is distinct. For purposes of the law in Quebec that is a very important fact. Something many women's groups have said is that somehow the words "distinct society" will affect their rights under the charter. I do not know how that could be when the distinct society clause affects only the people in Quebec and the women of Quebec are not worried about the inclusion of that clause.
I really have no understanding of where those fears come from. We must put them aside and come to the understanding that the words "distinct society" do nothing at all to hurt, abrogate, or denigrate anyone else in Canada. They are a statement of fact and they are necessary to the people in Quebec in order to interpret their law.
If in some comers of the country we are going to ask any question at all, and if we are still confused about whether we should pass the Meech Lake Accord, in my opinion there is only one question that we should be asking: Is there anything at all in the Meech Lake Accord that hurts anyone in Canada? I have to say: "No, there is nothing. There is not a word that hurts anyone in Canada."
That is the question that the people and the leaders of Newfoundland and Labrador must ask themselves: Is there anything in the Meech Lake Accord that hurts the people of Newfoundland or Labrador? The answer is no, there is nothing that hurts the people of Newfoundland or Labrador in the Meech Lake Accord.
The people in Manitoba must ask themselves: Is there anything at all in the Meech Lake Accord that hurts Manitobans? The answer is no, there is nothing in the Meech Lake Accord that hurts the people of Manitoba in any way.
There is something that does have the possibility of hurting the people of Labrador, Manitoba, Newfoundland, Quebec, and all the rest of Canada. That is the lethargy, the lack of positive will, the inability to grasp this opportunity and take the responsibility to pass the Meech Lake Accord, to say yes, to take affirmative action, and to overcome whatever processes, problems or

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
barriers which might seem to be in the way. If that is not done, it could have a very profound effect on all of us.
In closing I want to say that I know that all the leaders of Newfoundland and Labrador, all the leaders of Manitoba understand this issue very well. I feel very strongly for the terrible trauma they are going through and for the dilemma they are in. Even at this moment I know that they are wrestling with these very heavy questions and the tremendous burden of responsibility that they bear for the future of this country.
I believe, with all my heart, that they will come up with the right answers and that they will find the solutions we all seek. My appeal this evening is not to those leaders. My appeal tonight is to the people of Manitoba and to the people of Newfoundland and Labrador to support their premiers and to support their representatives in doing whatever it is they must do in order to pass the accord so that we can get on with the business of building this wonderful nation.
My appeal is to the warm, generous, tolerant people of those two provinces and the rest of this country to support our provincial leaders in their search for solutions, to say "yes" to Quebec and to say "yes" to Canada.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for her remarks.
The hon. member closed her remarks by saying that she is appealing to the people of the provinces of Manitoba, Newfoundland, and Labrador. Unfortunately the people are the ones who have been left out of it because of this heavy-handed, top down approach. It is up to the politicians now to decide what will happen. We see quite clearly that the fundamental flaw of the Meech Lake Accord is that the people themselves have had veiy little to do with it.
The hon. member also mentioned in her speech the rhetorical question: is there anything in the Meech Lake Accord that hurts Manitoba or Newfoundland and Labrador? Possibly, at this point, it would be academic to say no, there isn't really anything wrong with it because once we bring Quebec into the constitutional family all will be well.
I would argue, being one member of the family of Canada and certainly a western Canadian, that I am a brother or a sister in the family of Canada, that Quebec
is in the Constitution, that it is in the family of Canada and always has been, quite clearly, legally, and constitutionally since 1867.
Maybe nothing now will hurt Manitoba or Newfoundland and Labrador, but I would like to ask a short question about the comments made that the Meech Lake Accord says yes to everybody and everything. I would just like the hon. member to make a couple of comments regarding whether there is anything in the Meech Lake Accord that should hurt these other two provinces if Meech Lake is not ratified?
Yes to Senate reform, is that a possibility with the unanimity clause as it stands right now? Are we saying yes to a person like Elijah Harper who is exercising his constitutional right to do what he is doing now because he believes in it, whether we agree or disagree with it? Are we saying yes to Elijah Harper's constitutional right? Are we saying yes to this because of vetoes to all linguistic groups in Canada of whom we should be proud rather than only saying yes to the main two linguistic groups?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her questions. I know she wants to understand the accord. I think her questions were searching and appropriate.
I am pleased to answer again-and I do not want to sound repetitive-that the answer to your question is yes. In fact the Meech Lake Accord and ratification of the Meech Lake Accord allow us to proceed with Senate reform. Yes, ratification of the Meech Lake Accord allows us to proceed with responding to the needs and the constitutional aspirations of the aboriginal people. Yes, ratification of the Meech Lake Accord allows us also to proceed with the constitutional aspirations of other minority groups in Canada who may want to be included in the future.
Until constitutionally we bring Quebec's signature to the document, we cannot proceed with any of these reforms. In the interests of this country and in the interests of all the people I know the hon. member represents so well and so whole-heartedly, I know she would want also to help us make that appeal to the people of Canada, the people of Manitoba, Newfoundland and Labrador, to support their leaders in searching for answers and solutions, to say yes to. . . Quebec, and
June 20, 1990

to say yes to Canada so that we can get on with the rest of the business of the country.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank all members who have participated in this debate for a very positive and progressive debate. The feelings communicated to the people of this House and to the people of Canada were strongly held on the part of those members, sincerely and honestly held on the part of those members.
I have always been a supporter of the Meech Lake Accord, as have many members in my party, but I have always had a number of concerns about the process, about what was included in the accord, and about what was excluded from it.
I do not think any constitutional document, no matter where you look in the world or even the constitutional documents of this country, can fully address the aspirations of the people of Canada. It is widely recognized that these are imperfect documents, but they are vital documents as well, documents always being corrected and improved upon.
The process in Canada is always a little difficult, but as we move toward protection over the hundreds of years we have been in existence more and more we will see the Constitution reflect the aspirations of the people of this country.
I also recognize the importance of Quebec becoming a full participant in the Constitution, a signatory to the Constitution, and a full participant in future constitutional discussions and developments. It is extremely important for this country to claim to exist as a national state when 25 per cent of its population has not agreed to the fundamental law of the country and does not make any sense at all. We have to strive to make sure that Quebec is a signatory and is a full participant.
I also argued over the months since the accord was signed that there is really nothing in the Meech Lake Accord that is inconsistent with Canada's constitutional tradition dating back, not only to the Treaty of Paris in 1763 or the Proclamation of 1763, but even to the edicts of the military government that took over Quebec after 1759. Those military governments recognized, in order to maintain the security of Quebec and North America, that the right of Quebec to its religion, its civil law, and
Government Orders
its language, were critical elements. Back then even the successors in terms of military government to General Wolfe, recognized the distinct society in Quebec and the importance of that society to the continuation of British North America.
I think there has been a problem and I think there is some blame that has to be laid. After the signing of the Meech Lake Accord and the endorsement of the accord by the eight provinces and by the Parliament of Canada, I think there was an obligation on the part of the federal government or an obligation on the part of the government that sits opposite to cross Canada and to explain to the people of Canada exactly what that accord was all about. This is where the initial failure of leadership took place.
I can say as a person who represents the most western province, British Columbia that there was an absence of any government representatives in that province to explain to people exactly what the Meech Lake Accord was about, why it was a good thing for Canada, why it was a good thing to recognize the distinctiveness of Quebec society within the accord, and why the accord should be adopted, not simply by every legislature and the Parliament of Canada but also by the citizens of Canada who could take up that document and that Constitution as their own, be proud of it, and have nothing to fear from it.
That is where the initial failure of leadership came because the Prime Minister of this country did not go around and talk to the people of Canada, explain what was in the document, and explain the advantages of that document to Canada: the advantage of bringing Quebec back into the constitutional family and the advantages which would proceed in the future in terms of addressing other constitutional requirements if this constitutional amendment were passed in the time set out for it to be passed.
That is when the debate was hijacked by western extremists, by people like APEC. People who wormed their way into the debate eventually took the leadership of the debate and turned this document, in western Canada at any rate, into something that the people of that region feared, loathed, and wanted to see defeated.
Also I think some people had the worst intentions in mind. They wanted to attack the French speaking people of this country, were intolerant, and wanted to use the

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
intolerance that was growing in Canada at that time as a vehicle to defeat the Meech Lake Accord and to defeat the constitutional amendment. I think the blame for that hijacking of the debate around the Meech Lake Accord by extremists on the language issue and by extremists who wanted to force Quebec out of Canada can be put squarely at the door of the Prime Minister of this country.
As one Liberal member suggested, rather than going around the country and saying "you must accept this" and "not to accept this is to be anti-Quebec" was not the argument that registered well with the people of Canada.
My finding, when explaining this document to the people in my constituency, was that many of them had not even read it. Many of them had not seen the document. Many of them who had scanned the document did not understand it and needed some explanation. They needed the authorities there that they could consult, trust, and rely on to explain the document to them.
Who did they have? They had Preston Manning, they had the Reform Party, they had APEC, and they had a whole series of people who wanted to use that document for their own purposes, whether political or whether to increase the intolerance between groups in this country. I think it was a shame that those people were allowed to hijack the debate because of the failure of the leadership on the part of the Prime Minister of this country.
Mr. Speaker, there are other things that have contributed to the disunity of Canada. I think that those contributions to the disunity of this country, again, rest squarely on the shoulders of the Conservative Party opposite and the Conservative government opposite.
My family has been in this country since before it was a country. They moved to Canada east in 1819 from Ireland. They did not consider themselves English Canadians because Irish was the language that was taken away from them by the English in Ireland and they did not see themselves as English Canadians. But they did see themselves as Canadians nevertheless.
They have been here since 1819. They drilled in the Rebellion of 1837, on the side of Canada. They fought in wars, both in western Canada and in Europe on the side of Canada. My family, over the five generations that they have been here, have committed themselves to Canada
and we hope will be able to commit ourselves to Canada in the future. That is certainly my commitment and I know the commitment of one other Skelly in this particular House.
We are concerned about what is happening with this country because this country was put together contrary to all the predictions of the experts on how a country should be put together. The geographers told us that the natural lines of trade are north and south with the various regions of the United States and that you could not pull a country as large and diverse as distant from shore to shore as Canada, together. Yet, Canadians and Canadian governments over the years, through the active involvement of government in the process, managed to turn this country into the nation that everybody predicted could not exist and would ultimately fall into the jaws of the United States.
The fathers and mothers of Confederation actually put this country together and it is always a problem keeping this country together. It is a problem that those of us who enter public life, whether at the provincial, municipal or federal level, always must address ourselves to. We know if we neglect this country at any particular time or neglect the sinews and glue that hold this country together, then it is going to spring apart. We have to take good care of the sinews and glue that hold this country together.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs talked about Canadians as being some of the most fortunate and luckiest people in the world. To some extent, some of us are the luckiest people in the world. Some of us are, but not all of us are.
I think that some of the policies of this government, over the last few years, have contributed in a very dangerous way to disunity in this country and contributed to disunity in such a way that the country is being pulled apart to the point where it is not willing to accept the Meech Lake Accord.
I look at this government's action in destroying the VIA Rail system. It was that railway that pulled this country together from sea to sea and Canadians are proud of that railway. It is a railway that served virtually every region of the country and a railway that could have been held together by government not simply dismissed and destroyed. That railway was perceived as being a symbol of Canada, and an important symbol that pulled
June 20, 1990

the people of this country together in recognition of this country, Canada.
This government has attacked senior citizens through the clawback program. The one thing that this country stood for was that pensions would be the same, whether you lived in Nova Scotia, Newfoundland or on the coast of British Columbia. The value of universal programs in this country was to maintain this country and to maintain social programs at a certain standard in every region of the country. By undermining the universality of those programs, the government again has removed some of the sinews and glue that keeps this country together and keeps us thinking as Canadians. Some people suffered as a result of that. Other people did not suffer.
Another example of what the government has done is the unemployment insurance legislation. Some people in Canada are going to be paying a greater penalty than others as a result of what that legislation will do. You cannot have a country where everybody pulls together, where everybody considers themselves fortunate, where everybody contributes and has the same aspirations for the future when some people pay greater penalties for being a Canadian than others. That is a serious problem which is a result of the policies that this government has brought down.
If this government had been more sensitive to the need to maintain programs in Canada, to maintain the symbols of what this country is all about, then I think there would be stronger support for this government and for the Meech Lake Accord and for keeping this country together. I do not think we would find ourselves in this House of Commons, at the eleventh hour, trying to talk two legislatures into approving something which on the one hand they see as against their best interests but, on the other hand, feel they are forced to accept in order to keep the country together.
I think that the Prime Minister and the government in the last two years have contributed, to a great extent, to the disunity of this country. As a result, Meech Lake tends to fall on deaf ears, especially for the people who are paying a higher penalty for being Canadians than others because of the inequality in the legislation that has come down as a result of this government.
Government Orders
I do not think there has been any more important group that has been hit by this than the aboriginal people of this country. In the February budget these people were the hardest hit by the budget reductions. Why did the government focus its attack in the budget on the native people of Canada? The government cut back native print media so that newspapers used by native organizations and tribal councils are now being forced to shut down. Newspapers like the Micmac News that first brought to the attention of this House and to the Nova Scotia Legislature the injustice practised by the Nova Scotia justice system against Donald Marshall; newspapers that in the north and in western Canada are agents for providing literacy training and providing retention of native languages were totally eliminated because their budgets were cut 100 per cent. Many of them will be gone by the time this summer is over. Why were aboriginal people singled out by this government, by the vicious Thatcherite kind of budget that this government imposed on native Indians?
Native broadcasting was cut by 15 per cent. Native people, with an oral language tradition, relied on native broadcasting, both radio and television broadcasting, again to preserve their traditions, to preserve their languages. Yet this vehicle for preserving the language of native people in this country and for keeping their traditions intact was cut by the government. Natives do not see this government and its proposals as supporting their aspirations. They see themselves as being singled out for an attack by Canada. How can Canada now expect native people to want to support the Constitution of a country that they feel does nothing but marginalize them, force them to the outside of society, both in economic and social terms. Now they want native people to endorse the Constitution?
I think it would be a matter of good faith on the part of this government to reverse those cuts, to say they were wrong because they were an attack on native people. I think that would be absolutely necessary in order to get the native people on side, because right now they feel the most attacked of any group in our society.
The Prime Minister sent his agent, Senator Lowell Murray, to talk to the native people and to MLA Elijah Harper out in Manitoba and made them a whole series of offers about involvement in the first ministers process, so that they could be involved in the first ministers process. Why did the Prime Minister not make that offer

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
before? The Prime Minister went to Manitoba and offered a royal commission into aboriginal issues, a royal commission that would be the equivalent to the bicultur-alism and bilingualism commission of years ago.
The natives have specifically asked not to have a royal commission. The Prime Minister has offered any number of things. Native people remember when this Prime Minister made promises to them coming out of First Ministers' conferences. Those promises simply were not kept.
This is a release by the Prime Minister of Canada in 1985. He promised after a First Ministers conference in 1985:
My policies and those of my government are based on certain
principles:
-the special relationship between Canada and the aboriginal peoples should be strengthened;
How? By cutting their budgets? By making it more impossible for them to operate their media and their representative organizations? Is that how the Prime Minister is going to strengthen the relationship between aboriginal people and the Government of Canada? In fact, this promise was not kept and the native people in this country are suspicious of this Prime Minister keeping any of his promises to them at all.
Aboriginal rights, especially the right of self-government, should have constitutional protections. In the land claims settlements just discussed by the Prime Minister in the House today, the rights of self-government were not, specifically not, constitutionally protected.
Current funding levels of programs designed to correct the serious inequities which exist for native people and native communities will be maintained. In fact, the inequities have grown as a result of cut-backs in funding for native people from the Secretary of State's department. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development says the funding for Indian Affairs is increased. In fact, for certain native programs it has been capped.
Because of the growing population of native people, the amount of money going to native people in this country per capita has been going down. How can the Prime Minister expect the native people of this country to believe him when he has certainly not kept the
promises he has made in document after document after document. They are tired of listening to promises that are not going to be kept.
If the Meech Lake Accord is to pass and be accepted by Canadians, we must have some kind of change in the kind of leadership that has been shown by this government. We have to see policies brought down in this House that do not protect some Canadians and punish others and then expect to see those Canadians pull together at a time of need for national unity.
If we are going to see the Meech Lake Accord passed and accepted by Canadians in the future, we will have to see a government that embarks on policies that brings this country together and holds this country together and treats some people much better than this government has.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say, first of all, that I am not particularly joyful as I rise in the House this evening, at the eleventh hour of a great constitutional debate, to speak to the motion before the House, a motion that urges the Manitoba and Newfoundland Legislative Assemblies to ratify the Constitution Amendment, 1987. Nevertheless, I am optimistic, and I am convinced that the accord, as negotiated, will be ratified on time.
Mr. Speaker, today we are discussing, as we have been for the past three years, a constitutional document, but we are also talking about the future of our country. As a Quebecer, I want to be a full participant in Canadian society. As a Canadian, I want a united country from coast to coast.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, in politics we must have a number of goals. The question that often arises is the following: What do we, as leaders of a country, want to leave to future generations, to our children and grandchildren? My list is not very long, but I think it will meet with the approval of all members of this House. We want to leave a country that is strong and united. We want to pass on a prosperous country; we want to pass on a country which is fair; we want to pass on a country where every citizen, man or woman, can find respect. And we want to pass on a country which gives its citizens the opportunity to realize their potential.
June 20, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I think that Canada, on those five scores, is showing a rather impressive record, but still incomplete, a record that the accord we are discussing today could enable us to improve in a major way, while enabling us to realize in a more concrete way the goals we had set for ourselves. Of course it has to be done by welcoming Quebec in the great Canadian constitutional family, and this will enable us to go forward to realize some of the goals that we had set for ourselves and that still need more improvement.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I rise today not as a minister, but as an ordinaiy member of this House, as an ordinary citizen, as a French-speaking resident of Ontario whose ancestors came from Quebec. Throughout my life, Mr. Speaker, I was given several opportunities. First, when I was very young, I had the opportunity to learn both official languages of Canada. I was given the choice, and I made a decision. I can say today that I have no regret.
I also had the opportunity to study in Ontario and in Quebec, and I still consider myself fortunate today. Afterwards, I had the opportunity to study in the United States with the assistance of two institutions, Hydro-Quebec and the Arts Council. The two levels of government helped a young student to develop and reach his goals.
After graduating in the States, Mr. Speaker, I had the choice either to stay south of the border, or to come back to Quebec, and to Canada. I decided then to come back to my country, because of the values we share here, the tolerance, the openness of mind, the faith in our future, the willingness to build a country, to assert ourselves, all of which I could not find anywhere else. I willingly made those choices, Mr. Speaker, I made those decisions, I said yes to Canada.
Nowadays, we are discussing a constitutional agreement, one in a series of several such accords. It is not the first of its kind, nor the last, Mr. Speaker. We have to realize that a Constitution is a dynamic, living instrument, one that reflects our society.
Today, we are discussing a document approved by all the First Ministers of the country, a document which would allow us to pursue our constitutional evolution. The requests dealt within the document-I will not read them to you because they are quite well known by now-were the minimum demands of a people, one part
Government Orders
of our country which had been excluded from the constitutional agreement of 1982. By ratifying the accord, we could proceed to a new round of constitutional review.
Then, as Canadians, the question we should ask, and probably the question many people outside of the country are asking themselves, is what will happen if the accord is ratified and what will happen if it is not? Where will we go after the signing of the accord? How can a single piece of paper take such a vital importance for the future of our country?
Mr. Speaker, all of us Canadians have made tremendous progress in dealing with many problems to make Canada more competitive and put the country back on the right economic track. We have won greater confidence in our abilities and more respect internationally as a member of the Group of Seven or G-7, the world's leading industrialized nations. Mr. Speaker, there is a new entrepreneurial spirit in Canada, a new economic vitality, supported and encouraged by all levels of government that represent the key to a strong, dynamic and competitive nation. We must not forget that a good economic performance is what guarantees fair and generous social programs for the country. The Canada we are building for this decade and the next century will have to meet society's demands for a higher standard of living, environmental protection, better health care and a better education system.
How can we maintain our momentum and reach these objectives that will enable Canada to play an important role in the world economy? The answer is obvious. We must remain a united country. Social justice cannot exist without economic renewal. Economic renewal cannot exist without national reconciliation. This goal can be reached by ratifying the Meech Lake Accord, thus ensuring social peace and economic prosperity for Canada. Not only will the accord allow Quebec to regain its place in the Constitution but it will strengthen all of Canada. A strong federal government with strong provinces is essential to the country's success. The accord gives all provinces without exception an equal voice in changes to national institutions, important institutions like the Senate and the Supreme Court. That defines the new federalism. We believe it is the only way a country as big and as diversified as Canada can find its place on the international market and in a global society.

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
Meech Lake will unite the Canadian family while enabling all Canadians to proceed to the next stage of their constitutional and economic expansion. We will turn the page on the 1980s and open a new chapter on the 1990s. Meech Lake will give us the economic stability that is essential to attract foreign investment and prepare Canada for the international challenges of the coming years.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the question: Should Meech fail, should Meech not be ratified-and I think we are now well into the eleventh hour when, as political leaders of the country, we have to entertain the possibility that the Meech Lake Accord might not be ratified before June 23-we must seriously consider what might become of Canada after June 23.
Nobody can really predict the outcome of such an eventuality, and I must confess that, like anybody else, I do not have a crystal ball to gaze into the future. For sure, the sun will rise in the early hours of June 24. Still, Mr. Speaker, we have heard a number of possible scenarios, most of them not overly optimistic. I can tell you that if Meech Lake is not ratified, unfortunately I am among those whose outlook on the days ahead is rather grim. The signature of the Meech Lake Accord is a unique accomplishment which several former Prime Ministers have been unable to achieve. It is the result of efforts of goodwill and of a spirit of compromise and fairness which have been the hallmark of our country's history. And I am sorry to say that, should Meech Lake fail, that spirit will be the first victim.
The accord was initiated when Premier Bourassa put his five basic conditions on the table and the other nine premiers accepted to take Quebec back into the constitutional family. It was said repeatedly that those five conditions are the most reasonable ever asked by a premier from Quebec. Jack Pickersgill had this to say about Quebec's willingness to compromise, as shown in its conditions, and about the consequence of failure: "If Quebec is rejected, if this agreement becomes a disagreement and if such an opportunity to get the approval of Quebec's constitutional authorities is lost, I believe that we will not get another chance before another generation and never with such reasonable terms." As I was saying, that willingness to compromise will be the first victim of the failure of the accord. And the message that Canada will send to the rest of the world if this accord fails, after three years of discussions and after being signed by all eleven First Ministers, will be most
disconcerting. How will the international community react? Economic impacts are already being felt. Several foreign investment projects are already being delayed or shelved.
If the accord should fail, Mr. Speaker, what we would lose next I am afraid would be the confidence of other countries which do business with Canada. A major force is at stake, although we cannot assess its impact just now. I can assure you that there would be an impact both nationally and internationally. Political uncertainty and disagreement are not conducive to foreign investments. This burden would be made heavier as a result of our constitutional situation. The progress we have made so far in the area of Senate reform, Indian rights, women's rights, as well as the constitutional expectations raised in other groups would be short-lived. It would be difficult, if not impossible, to carry out further constitutional reform in the absence of Quebec around the constitutional table.
Mr. Speaker, I have listed three major victims of a possible failure of the accord. However, I sincerely believe that what would suffer most would be our pride, pride in ourselves as a people who have always shown understanding, compassion, justice and tolerance, pride in our own country, this great and magnificent land which is the envy and admiration of many other nations. Those who would cause this accord to fail, for whatever reason-and I will not mention any name-would have difficulty explaining to Quebecers on June 24 that Canada said no to them once more. They would find it difficult to explain to Westerners and Atlantic Canadians that the Senate reform is impossible. They would find it difficult to explain to our trading partners that while walls are crumbling down all over the world, that nations are seeking a global market, we, as Canadians, have erected new barriers to make us less competitive. They will be hard pressed to explain to their children how they could let Canada drift apart.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, earlier this evening I spoke of options, of opportunities. In the next few days, we will have the option and the opportunity to say yes to Quebec and, as much if not more important, to say yes to Canada. Mr. Speaker, as a Canadian and a Quebecer, I would not want to intrude in any provincial jurisdiction, but I simply want to support the motion before the House this evening and urge all Canadians from coast to coast to take that step ahead, to say yes and proceed to
June 20, 1990

the next stage, to continue to build this great and magnificent country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Meech Lake Accord was a flawed document from the very beginning. It is flawed both in process and in substance. This document has torn our country as it has never been tom before, and that is the result of its flaws and the Prime Minister's penchant to conquer by discord.
There is no doubt that Quebec should be brought into the Constitution, but this document, with all its flaws, I believe will not work. That is why I must oppose it.
This discord was hatched in darkness and nurtured on fear. It has nothing to commend its passage. Moreover, it ignores Canada's first people and that has nurtured anger, fear, discrimination and despair. It has been a classic example of how a constitutional document should never be undertaken. Its genesis occurred in secret and grew on doubt, confusion, suspicion and misinformation.
For three years the Prime Minister repeated over and over again that the document had to be accepted as it is. Not an i could be undotted or a t uncrossed. Then we had that marathon, week-long spectacle here in Ottawa where the Prime Minister rolled the dice. What a cynical way to build a nation's most fundamental document and to build respect among colleagues. Not being satisfied with rolling the dice, he had to brag that he did it deliberately and thus inflamed the atmosphere to the awful state we have today.
A constitution must involve the people of a nation, not just the First Ministers. It must reflect the views, the aspirations, the hope and the will of all of the people. It cannot be hatched in darkness, in secret, in manufactured desperation.
The people must have a constitution that takes into account all of the people and especially our aboriginal peoples. By any ethical standard, they should have been
Government Orders
the very first to be consulted and to have their grievances adjudicated in fairness and generosity.
I want to say, and I will do so briefly, something about this canard that Quebec was left out of the first round. Sir, this is just not true. It is true that Quebec was not there, but Quebec was not there because the Levesque government chose not to be there for its own reasons.
We must have a complete, proper and functional constitution, but it must be consummated for all of the people, bom in light, and approved by all. Anything less, Sir, I can neither support nor accept. A valid constitution belongs to the people, not to the government.
Mr. Speaker, we come to life and sometimes forget that we are finite beings, but we are not. However, our country should outlast us all for many generations after all of us will have been forgotten. The world may little note nor long remember what we say here, but our descendants will long remember what we do here. Let us not fail them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague from Miramichi for giving me the opportunity to use the rest of the time allowed to the Liberal Party to take part in this important debate. I think it is appropriate to put the debate into the context of a motion that the government is proposing and that urges the Manitoba and Newfoundland legislatures to complete the ratification of the Constitutional Amendment, 1987 before June 23 1990, Saturday of this week, so that Canadians can complete an important act of nation-building and thereby open up the process for Canada's future constitutional development, including the important issues of Senate reform, of aboriginal rights and linguistic rights, of territorial participation in the federation and of providing a process for a continuing review of the operation of the Constitution of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, that is more or less what the motion proposes and we, on this side, hope that the two provinces that are still hesitating will hear the message that members of this House are sending and accept by the deadline of June 23 the constitutional proposals known as those of the Meech Lake Accord. This motion

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
reminds me of moments in 1986 and 1987 when the Meech Lake Accord was discussed in this House and at the Liberal Party Convention held here in Ottawa. In November of 1986, the National Convention of the Liberal Party approved a proposal very similar to the motion which is before the House today. I want to remind the House that it was we of the Liberal Party that proposed to amend the Meech Lake Accord precisely to strenghten that accord and to give it a national relevance. Here is, in substance, what was contained in the resolution proposed in November 1986 by the Liberal Party. We proposed adding a preamble to the Constitution to preserve and promote the linguistic duality and to recognize Quebec's distinctiveness, the multicultural character of Canadian society, the contribution made by native people, as well as the advantage of developing the Canadian economic union.
We introduced in this House nine constitutional amendments which were all defeated by the government. It has now come back with a motion very similar to what we were proposing three years ago.

History will say that this Liberal Party proposed three years ago some important amendments to strengthen the constitutional amendment. We do not have the pretension that we knew all about the process and that we would be able to propose things that would be perfect. I am not that naive. It is the first time since 1982, since we patriated our Constitution, that we Canadians go through the process of amending our Constitution. It is a lengthy process, a complicated one, one which, in my opinion, and I guess it is an opinion shared by many Canadians after this experience, is faulted, is in need of change.
Over the last few years in trying to explain to people in my riding, at the University of Ottawa, in my meetings with constituents, in meetings even with public servants not very long ago, I asked the simple question: "What does Meech mean to you? What does Meech mean to us? What does Meech mean? What does it encompass?"
I issued the challenge that if anybody in the room could tell me what the five conditions of getting Quebec into the constitutional fold are, I would buy him or her and a guest a supper at the Parliamentary Restaurant.
I never lost that bet, never once, and I made it umpteen times at the University of Ottawa. Nobody could give me the five conditions. Yet here we are wondering today why we are getting that kind of reaction. Well, I share the blame with all of us here in this House. We did not succeed in getting the message across to Canadians. We did not succeed in making them understand that we are not trying to make Quebec any better, greater or more powerful than any of the other provinces, but are trying to recognize the distinctiveness of that province.

Mr. Speaker, the majority of Quebecers speak French. Quebec is the only province with a French majority. It has a different Civil Code, which has applied since Napoleon and is unique to this province. It has cultural and social traditions-as evidenced, for instance, in its music and its poetry-it is a distinct society in the Canadian context. It might not be the only one, but it really is one. I recognize it, and so did my party.
Secondly, it was said that Quebec would have its say in immigration matters. The Cullen-Couture agreement exists since 1976 or 1977, I think- It was agreed that through the Meech Lake Accord, all provinces would be given that same right. That does not strike me as such a big deal! These powers already existed under our statutes, but now they would be enshrined in the Constitution, for all provinces if they agree. I think that was pretty clear.
Third, Mr. Speaker, there was the matter of veto rights for Quebec on constitutional amendments. There was also the federal government's spending powers in areas under provincial jurisdiction. There was a desire to restrict those powers. There is nothing new here. It was discussed in 1970, in Victoria, and in 1976 here in the House. This is not new. There was the question of Senate reform and giving the provinces the right to submit a list of candidates, and also that Quebec, since it has a different legal system-the Civil Code-would from now on be entitled to appoint three justices to the Supreme Court.
That is what Meech boils down to, and that's all. However, many Canadians are still very hazy about all this. Today I heard some very eloquent speeches in which it was said that the whole issue had been so poorly explained that today, Mr. Speaker, there is resentment and hatred in this country, and it's true, and it is just
June 20, 1990

because people don't understand. I find this very depressing, because once properly explained, it is a matter that is certainly not difficult to understand.

In affirming the constitutional role of the elected legislators of this federation of ours, and their right to decide, which is what we are going through now in this process, all this motion does is urge that Manitoba and Newfoundland exert efforts to bring about full ratification of the constitutional accord of 1987.
We have affirmed that deep commitment to this country. We would like to reaffirm that constitutional amendments can be made with care, understanding and generosity.
I think people have read into Meech much more than is actually there. I have heard some of the speakers on the government side today say that will be a disquieting and worrisome on June 25, June 26, or thereabouts, but I join some of my colleagues on this side. I think that if we do not get Meech it may not be the end of Canada. I hope and pray that it is not, but it will be a different Canada, Mr. Speaker. I can tell you that. I believe that strongly.
Will it be more generous, more understanding to the native people and their rights, to the minorities and then-rights? Will the majority of Canadians, English speaking, be more understanding of the minorities after if Meech does not pass? I do not believe that.
Will they be more caring, more generous? I do not believe they will be. I do not think that if Meech is defeated that that will make the majority more understanding of the minority expectations, dreams, or rights, for that matter.
A Constitution is made for minorities, because we are all in some sense part of a minority. God knows we have minority rights now in our Constitution; minority rights are there. They are not always applied, I agree. I could give the House possibly a long speech on minority rights in this country.
I was the one who got up on my feet the day after the Prime Minister announced the Meech Lake Accord, the Langevin Meech Lake Accord, and asked the Prime
Government Orders
Minister about promoting minority rights across this land. I thought that was the normal thing; preserve, yes, but promote also because preserve means status quo, promote looks forward, moves. I was told to be patient, that it will come in the second round. I was veiy disappointed.
Since then I have asked the Prime Minister in this House many times to convene a federal-provincial conference and get on with solving our constitutional impasse. I was told: "Wait, it is not the time. My emissary, Senator Murray, is out there consulting with the provinces". I understand that process.
However we are now at the eleventh hour. I say to the Prime Minister: if this thing does not go through and if they do not hear our plea in Manitoba and Newfoundland, there is only one person that I will blame and that is the Prime Minister of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the hon. member's remarks. I certainly have to agree with him that we are at the eleventh hour. Second, there are objections to the high priority which Meech Lake gives to Quebec's constitutional demands while failing to address the constitutional demands of other groups. I just heard from my hon. friend that everybody is talking about minority rights. I think it is very interesting to note that that is so important. Finally, there is this rigid amending formula that I have mentioned in this House so many times as well.

June 20,1990

Come June 24 or June 25, can we say as members in the federal Parliament of Canada that Canada is bigger than Meech Lake, or is Meech Lake so overpowering that absolutely nothing can be done? subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House for debate today is that:
The House urges the Manitoba and Newfoundland Legislative Assemblies to exert efforts to bring about full ratification of the Constitution Amendment, 1987 by June 23, 1990, so that Canadians can complete an important act of nation-building and thereby open the process for Canada's future constitutional development, including the important issues of Senate reform, of aboriginal rights and linguistic rights, of territorial participation in the federation, and of providing a process for a continuing review of the operation of the Constitution of Canada.
I want to stand and speak in support of the motion. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I am probably the least partisan member in this House and I think all members recognize that. On the question of the future of Canada, I cannot find it in my partisan heart to actually see this issue in
partisan terms. I cannot see the issue in partisan terms, so I am not going to involve myself in assigning blame. I am not going to blame the Prime Minister and I am not going to blame the provinces. I want to spend my time trying to explain why I would recommend to the legislatures of Manitoba, Newfoundland and Labrador that they support and pass the Meech Lake Accord with the attachment of June 9.
I do this because I recall very vividly three years ago. I remember the meeting at the Langevin building and I remember that weekend very well. I am not a betting person but I was prepared to take bets and I did not give the Prime Minister a snowball's chance in hell of coming out of that weekend meeting with any sort of agreement. I recall that very vividly.
I think I speak for all members in this House when I say how surprised we were that a unanimous agreement came out of that. In fact, on Monday morning, following that culmination of the Meech Lake process, everyone stood in this House and gave the Prime Minister a standing ovation. I did, and my colleagues in this party did. We all stood because we recognized that finally Quebec was pulling up its chair at the constitutional table and was going to participate now in the building of this nation.
It was an important element in the whole process of constitutional development. We were all very pleased. There were 10 premiers' signatures on that document, and the Prime Minister's signature. Ten and one; 11 signatures.
I have talked to a lot of young people. What they cannot understand at all in this country is whether a person's signature is worth anything any more. Is not the person's word and signature a bond any more? That is what young people say to me.
I was talking to a young chap the other day who said: "Well, if they signed it, they should stick by it, and if there are things you don't like, you work to change them". And all of this malarkey about process. Every Canadian has a different process, probably a lot better process than was followed. But that is the process that was inherited. You talk about process in 1982? It did not even go to the provincial legislatures.
June 20, 1990

If one were to examine in retrospect the document that former Prime Minister Trudeau gave to the country, people today would find fault with the notwithstanding clause. Where has there ever been a perfect constitution? Name the constitution that is perfect. Name the law that is perfect.
I saw a law come through Parliament-one page, two clauses-and we did it all in 15 minutes. It went to the Senate, and it found there that there was a comma in the wrong place which changed the whole meaning. It had to come back to Parliament and go through the process again in 15 minutes. It is not a perfect document and nobody says it is.
The Meech Lake Accord, of course, is not a perfect document. I want to say that I cannot accept the fact that it was made by 11 elitist people, 11 people of privilege. Of course not. They are elected. The premier of Ontario, whether I like it or not, he is not in my party, he was elected by the majority of people in the province of Ontario. Therefore, he represents the people of Ontario. The integrity is in the fact that he is elected. This is a democracy. They are not people of privilege. They are people who are elected.
So those 11 people signed the document, and eight legislatures ratified it. Two have not; Manitoba and New Brunswick.
There was a change of government in Newfoundland and that government deratified it. What a cockamamie way of making a constitution. Can you believe it? Who would ever come back and sit at the table thinking that there is integrity in this group and they would stick with what they have agreed to? By the time the ink is dry on the document, you find half the governments have changed. They have new stripes, new motivations, new politics and they do not like it. Throw it out. What a heck of a way to operate a country.
I have talked to people who are not from this country. They are absolutely amazed that we are risking the breakup of this nation, as we know it today, over this question: How many angels can dance on the head of a pin?
When one province came into Confederation, it was written into the Constitution you need to have a colour for the margarine. Believe it or not.
Government Orders
I say that the people who signed the document have a responsibility to have it ratified. They had a responsibility. I do not think it is out of place for us, as a federal Parliament, with elected members to have a national vision of Canada. I represent the riding of Nickel Belt, but my first commitment is to Canada because I am in a national Parliament. Therefore, I do not think it is beyond the realm of possibility for the federal Parliament to ask two of its confederated partners, namely Manitoba and Newfoundland and Labrador, to pass the Meech Lake Accord. I think it is quite within our responsibility to do that. I have no compunction whatsoever in asking those two provinces to ratify the Meech Lake Accord.
There is no question in my mind that the whole process of Meech Lake was to bring Quebec into the constitutional family. The Edmonton declaration where the nine premiers of the provinces-the Prime Minister was not present-declared that the next round of constitutional talks was to bring Quebec into the constitutional family. That was the purpose. If we do not fulfil that commitment, we put in jeopardy any future changes to the Constitution of this country.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, the offer made to aboriginal peoples is a fair one. I ask them, through the medium of this television, to reconsider. It is a fair proposal.
Meech Lake was signed and the ratification was supposed to take place, but it did not take place. Then started the dance. I could find a lot of fault with the way the Prime Minister may have handled it, but that is beside the point. The whole process of bringing the premiers together was to reach some consensus on getting this passed. The whole purpose is the welfare of the nation. That is the overriding concern. I cannot fault the Prime Minister for attempting to use every opportunity to make the premiers recognize their responsibility.
I have been really impressed with some people in this whole process. I want to tell you that I was very impressed with the Premier of Alberta, who actually stuck to his guns at one of his conventions in the Province of Alberta. He stuck to his support for Meech Lake, and won. If ever a person had as a concern Senate reform, it was Don Getty. He went into the Meech Lake Accord with the concept of a Triple E Senate. He did not come out with a Triple E Senate. I suspect he recognized

June 20, 1990
Government Orders
that the greater concern was to bring Quebec into the constitutional family.
I think people are putting their heads in the sand if they do not sense the mood across the river. It is not one of frenzy, but it is quiet certainty.
I recall very well the referendum debate. I was sitting on the sidelines. I saw all the municipalities across the country passing motions and sending them to Quebec. My municipality sent a motion which said: "Oh, Quebec, we love you, we love you. Just say no, and we will make it all right". That is what we hear. Just ask: "Will you love me as much tomorrow as you love me now?" That is what happened. I see the same dance happening again. We are sending all the cards saying: "We love you". Well, I do not think it will work this time. Once caught, twice shy. We have a responsibility as federal parliamentarians. That responsibility is the question of seeing Canada whole, as it is.
Meech is not the end, Meech is the beginning. It is promised in the attached document that we will look at and correct the process. That is fine. We will do that. But I think the first priority, and one that we owe the next generation of Canadians, is to deliver this country as we know it today on to them so they can build on this and make it a better country.
That is why I stand and speak in favour of the motion. It should be approved and, God, I hope it is.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some comments and then I would like to ask the hon. gentleman from Nickel Belt a question.
Mr. Speaker, I share his view. I absolutely support the Meech Lake Accord and I am convinced it is not only the right move, it is the best move for the country at this time.
I also share his view and recommend to all Canadians, particularly those in Newfoundland and Manitoba, and our aboriginal citizens everywhere, that we consider that the truly positive and constructive benefits of the Meech Lake agreement will bring a common direction for our country, committed at last to new constitutional progress, a new Senate, aboriginal reform, aboriginal rights,
pride in a common vision of our country, common identity, economic stability and new prosperity, a renewed international strength and influence and the time and energy for other things, other challenges such as the environment and the economy.
I would like to congratulate and commend all those Canadians such as the hon. gentleman from Nickel Belt who have participated in this debate on the Meech Lake Accord over the past three years and who have stood so solidly behind it.
In particular, tonight I would like to commend and congratulate those legislators in Newfoundland and Manitoba who are wrestling with this issue at this very moment. I am confident that they will discharge their duty in the best interests, not only of their provinces, but of all of Canada.
In the final analysis when we talk of certainty, there can only be certainty where there is trust. Surely we have now learned that only where there is trust is it possible that a great country such as Canada can find its true potential and its destiny.
In these final days we do place our trust in our fellow citizens in Manitoba and Newfoundland. I do not believe they will let us down.
I believe there has been a paralysis in the constitutional affairs of Canada ever since the patriation of the Constitution. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman from Nickel Belt if he believes that the constitutional paralysis that we have endured for so many years will now be cured with the passage of the Meech Lake Accord and with the existence at the one constitutional table of all the provinces and the federal government of Canada.

subtopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 RATIFICATION BY MANITOBA AND NEWFOUNDLAND LEGISLATURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. gentleman for his question.
I want to respond appropriately because when the Constitution of 1982 was negotiated in the kitchen of a room in the Chateau Laurier it seemed that Rene was not in the kitchen with Dinah in the discussions on the constitution.
Rene Levesque was not there and all the other premiers who were there came up with a deal. They did not hesitate to say that Levesque was in high dudgeon and left. That is too bad.
June 20, 1990

But Quebec was out of it and did not attend constitutional conferences after that. In fact the ones the Prime Minister referred to with respect to aboriginal people failed, with five provinces and the federal government voting for it, and Quebec was not there.
A major player represents she million people. How could we exclude six million people from the negotiating table? If they are not at the negotiating table, in fact our family is not complete. There is somebody missing at the table.
I think the Meech Lake Accord brought Quebec in. Certainly after the Meech Lake Accord was signed, it was a departure to see the Premier of Quebec talking about our country, our Canada. Meech Lake provides the opportunity for further changes to the Constitution and the accompanying document. Now all these things can go forward. I think it is very important that Meech Lake be approved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with only a couple of minutes left, I must say that it is a great privilege for me to have the opportunity to be the last speaker in this debate.
As the hon. member who has just finished said, and as Churchill said: "We are near the end and we are at the end of the beginning", for Canada is still a very young nation. We have only just begun our constitutional development.
There are three days left, and two provinces are in final debates leading toward ratification of the Meech Lake Accord. I have always had a sense of faith about this issue. Sometimes it does seem to defy logic. This evening they are still debating in Manitoba and Newfoundland the ultimate destiny of this accord. If we want to contemplate the worst, we can be very worried about it. For Canada, I prefer to believe in the best.
These great issues bring out the best in us. For Manitoba, for Newfoundland and for every province, obviously there have been some difficult concerns subject by subject, clause by clause, word by word. There is compelling evidence that Meech Lake is good for Canada. Therefore, if it is good for Canada, it is good for every province and for every Canadian.
As we in Canada continually struggle for a common sense of national vision and identity, we sometimes lose sight of the very distinctions which make our nation great. Canada is comprised of many different meanings for many different people. What distinguishes this country, though, is its very capacity to promote and protect such differences while remaining true to the ideal of one united land.

June 20, 1990

As we look to Canada's future with this vital issue still to be resolved in the next few days, let us reaffirm our common commitment to building this country in tolerance and respect for one another. I believe and I feel sure, Mr. Speaker, that you believe that that is what Canada is really all about.
